title: FoxP3+ Regulatory T-Cells in Canine Cutaneous Lymphoma and Their Role in Immune Modulation.
abstract: Background/aim Regulatory T cells (T regs ) are immunosuppressive lymphocytes that maintain immune homeostasis but may also facilitate tumor immune evasion. Their role in canine cutaneous lymphoma (CCL) remains insufficiently understood. We hypothesized that dogs with CCL would exhibit increased T reg levels in both peripheral blood and tumor tissue, thereby contributing to local and systemic immune modulation. Our objective was to evaluate T reg levels in blood and skin of dogs with CCL compared with healthy controls. Materials and methods Twenty-four dogs were enrolled: 12 with T-cell cutaneous lymphoma confirmed by histopathology and immunohistochemistry and 12 clinically healthy controls, recruited from a veterinary teaching hospital population. In this prospective study, circulating T regs were quantified by flow cytometry, and FoxP3 + cells in skin were evaluated by immunohistochemistry. Statistical analyses included t-tests, non-parametric tests, and Kaplan-Meier survival analysis. Results Dogs with CCL had significantly higher circulating T regs than controls (10.84±1.18% vs . 5.67±0.89%, p =0.0021). FoxP3 + cells were detected exclusively in neoplastic skin (mean, 8.27±5.71%), with no labeling in healthy skin ( p =0.0007). No significant differences were observed between epitheliotropic and non-epitheliotropic subtypes. T reg levels and the T reg /CD8 + ratio were not associated with survival outcomes ( p >0.20). Conclusion Dogs with CCL demonstrated increased T regs in both peripheral blood and intratumorally, suggesting a role of these cells in CCL-associated immunomodulation. Although T reg levels were not prognostic in this cohort, their accumulation highlights potential therapeutic targets in veterinary oncology.

title: Prostate-directed Radiotherapy in Selected Patients With Metastatic Castration-sensitive Prostate Cancer: A Real-world Case Series.
abstract: Background/aim Prostate-directed radiotherapy (RT) improves outcomes in selected patients with metastatic castration-sensitive prostate cancer (mCSPC), particularly those with low metastatic burden. However, real-world information regarding its use after response to systemic therapy remains limited. This study describes the treatment characteristics, safety, and clinical course of selected patients with mCSPC who received prostate-directed RT. Patients and methods We retrospectively reviewed an institutional RT database containing 396 patients who initiated prostate-directed RT between April 2015 and March 2026. Thirteen patients had mCSPC at RT initiation and were included. Prostate-directed RT was considered after a marked prostate-specific antigen (PSA) decline and confirmation of no radiographic progression during first-line systemic therapy; no prespecified PSA threshold was used. Patient characteristics, RT details, RT-related adverse events, and clinical outcomes after RT completion were evaluated. Results Eight patients had low-volume and five had high-volume disease. The median interval from initiation of first-line systemic therapy to RT was 8.4 months. The median PSA decline before RT was 99.9% (interquartile range=98.9-99.9%), and the median PSA level before RT was 0.028 ng/ml. All patients received intensity-modulated RT, and residual metastatic lesions were included in the RT target volume in six patients. All patients completed RT. No grade ≥2 acute genitourinary or gastrointestinal toxicity was observed, and no late RT-related toxicity occurred among the 11 patients evaluable for late toxicity. During follow-up (median, 39.6 months) after RT, four patients developed castration-resistant disease and four experienced radiographic progression. No post-RT local events or prostate cancer-specific deaths occurred; one patient died of an unrelated cause. Conclusion In this small, highly selected cohort of patients demonstrating favorable initial responses to systemic therapy, prostate-directed RT was feasible and well tolerated, with no grade ≥2 acute RT-related toxicity, no late toxicity among evaluable patients, and no local events. Comparative efficacy cannot be determined because of the retrospective design, small sample size, and absence of a non-RT control group.

title: Complete Response Demonstrated by [ 11 C]methionine-PET Imaging of a Patient With Squamous-cell Carcinoma of the Tongue Treated With Chemotherapy, Immunotherapy and Methionine Restriction Without Radiation or Surgery: A Potential New Low-toxicity Treatment Paradigm for a Recalcitrant Disease.
abstract: Background/aim Head and neck squamous-cell carcinoma (HNSCC) is associated with substantial morbidity. Treatment of locally-advanced disease commonly involves surgery, radiotherapy, and systemic therapy, which may result in functional impairment and treatment-related toxicity. Methionine addiction, known as the Hoffman effect, is a metabolic hallmark of cancer that is targeted by methionine restriction. We report here a patient with locally-advanced HPV-positive squamous-cell carcinoma of the tongue who achieved a complete response following chemotherapy combined with methionine restriction and subsequent immunotherapy, without surgery or radiotherapy. Case report A 58-year-old man was diagnosed with HPV-positive squamous-cell carcinoma arising from the base of the tongue with extensive cervical lymph-node involvement (cT1N3M0). The patient elected to avoid surgery and radiotherapy because of concerns regarding functional impairment and disfigurement. Treatment consisted of seven cycles of docetaxel, cisplatinum, and 5-fluorouracil combined with a low-methionine diet and oral recombinant methioninase (o-rMETase). Pembrolizumab was initiated during the fifth chemotherapy cycle and continued as maintenance therapy. The cervical tumor rapidly regressed and became clinically undetectable after the initial treatment cycles. Follow-up [ 11 C]methionine-PET/CT and [ 18 F]FDG-PET/CT demonstrated no evidence of active disease, consistent with a complete response. The patient remains clinically well without evidence of recurrence and continues pembrolizumab therapy and methionine restriction. Conclusion The present case demonstrates a complete clinical and metabolic response in a patient with locally-advanced HPV-positive tongue squamous-cell carcinoma treated with combination chemotherapy, methionine restriction, and pembrolizumab without surgery or radiotherapy. Although the present findings suggest that methionine restriction may have potential as an adjunct to systemic treatment in HNSCC, additional case series and prospective clinical studies are required to determine the efficacy, safety, and generalizability of this therapeutic approach.

title: Preoperative Prediction of Lymph Node Metastasis in Colorectal Cancer Using Routinely Collected Clinical Data: Multicenter Retrospective Machine Learning Model Development and External Validation Study.
abstract: Background Preoperative nodal assessment in colorectal cancer (CRC) remains imperfect, and uncertainty regarding pathological lymph node metastasis (LNM) may persist despite conventional imaging. Machine learning using routinely available preoperative information may provide complementary patient-level risk estimates without requiring radiomic feature extraction or molecular testing. Objective This study aimed to develop and externally validate machine learning models for preoperative estimation of pathologically confirmed LNM risk in patients with newly diagnosed CRC undergoing direct radical surgery without preoperative anticancer treatment, and to assess whether multivariable prediction adds information beyond clinical tumor stage (cT) alone. Methods This multicenter retrospective study included 2725 patients from 2 hospitals. The internal cohort (n=1074) was split into training (n=753) and internal test (n=321) sets, while 1651 patients from a second center formed the external validation cohort. Candidate predictors were routinely available preoperative clinical, laboratory, tumor-marker, imaging-based, and endoscopic biopsy variables. Predictors were selected using univariable and multivariable logistic regression (LR). Seven algorithms were evaluated: random forest (RF), support vector machine (SVM), LR, decision tree (DT), extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), naive Bayes (NB), and light gradient boosting machine (LightGBM). Performance was assessed using discrimination, threshold-dependent classification metrics, calibration, and decision curve analysis (DCA). Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) were used for interpretation. Sensitivity analyses compared the selected predictors with all candidate predictors and cT alone. Results Six predictors were retained: BMI, preoperative carcinoembryonic antigen, primary tumor site, cT, histological type, and tumor differentiation. RF was selected based on internal test performance. It is intended for research-stage adjunctive risk stratification and should not replace imaging, pathological evaluation, or clinical judgment. Prospective validation in broader populations and clinical settings is required before implementation.

title: Trustworthiness Evaluation of Medical Vision-Language Models: A Scoping Review and a Proposed Minimum Evaluation Checklist.
abstract: Background Medical vision-language models combine images and text to answer questions, generate reports, and support image interpretation. Task accuracy alone does not establish whether their outputs depend on relevant visual evidence or remain reliable under changes in the input. Objective We aimed to describe how trustworthiness is evaluated in medical vision-language models, identify gaps in evaluation and reporting, and develop a preliminary minimum evaluation checklist. Methods We conducted a scoping review using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews. We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and IEEE Xplore for English-language publications from January 1, 2022, to March 25, 2026. Eligible reports were peer-reviewed full papers that evaluated an image-and-language model in a medical imaging context and reported a measured result on at least one of eight trustworthiness dimensions. One reviewer charted the studies and a second verified the extraction. We summarized evaluation practices descriptively and applied the proposed eight-item Minimum Trustworthiness Evaluation Checklist (MiTEC) retrospectively. We did not perform a risk-of-bias appraisal. Results : We identified 516 records, screened 506 database records at title and abstract, and assessed 72 unique reports after merging duplicate full-text entries. The revised synthesis includes 29 studies: 11 journal articles and 18 conference papers. Robustness was evaluated in 11/29 (37.9%), hallucination in 7/29 (24.1%), distribution shift in 6/29 (20.7%), and visual grounding in 5/29 (17.2%). Interpretability and fairness were each evaluated in 4/29 (13.8%); uncertainty or confidence reliability in 2/29 (6.9%); and safety in 1/29 (3.4%). Two studies used a text-only baseline, and four used at least one image-reliance control. No included study was confirmed to report a formal calibration metric or a selective-prediction curve. Retrospective MiTEC scoring yielded 41 reported items among 232 study-item pairs (17.7%). Conclusions Evaluation practices varied across the included studies. Image-reliance controls, formal calibration measures, and subgroup analyses were uncommon. MiTEC is an author-proposed item set that requires independent testing and stakeholder consensus. The findings describe the included sample; incomplete linkage of preprints to published versions limits claims about the wider literature. Clinicaltrial

title: Refined Exclusion in Medical AI: Data Justice and Patient Safety Governance.
abstract: Medical AI is often evaluated using aggregate measures of discrimination, calibration, and accuracy. However, these measures can obscure clinically important variation across patient groups, institutions, devices, and workflows. This viewpoint defines refined exclusion as a governance condition in which an AI system appears successful in aggregate, while uncertainty, error, or reduced clinical reliability is concentrated in populations that are insufficiently represented, measured, validated, or monitored. The concept does not replace algorithmic fairness, hidden stratification, dataset shift, or subgroup performance analysis. It connects these mechanisms to a distinct consequence: an unequal distribution of safety that remains inadequately detected or corrected. Drawing on purposively selected, illustrative evidence from population health management, chest radiography, dermatology, computational pathology, medical foundation models, and clinical measurement, we distinguish model-level disparity, patient safety signals, and documented patient harm. We then frame data justice as a complementary governance approach with distributional, procedural, and substantive dimensions. The proposed lifecycle decision gates address intended use, subgroup learnability, data provenance, validation, procurement, local deployment, monitoring, updates, and patient feedback. Each gate links minimum evidence to decision authority and 1 of 4 actions: proceed, enrich or validate, restrict use, or pause or retire. Governance intensity should be proportionate to clinical risk and evidentiary uncertainty. By linking subgroup evidence gaps to institutional decisions and corrective action, the framework shifts attention from whether a model performs well on average to whether its safety is demonstrable for the populations and settings in which it will be used.

title: Improving Postpolypectomy Surveillance Decisions Using an Automated Analysis of Colonoscopy and Histopathology Reports: 2-Center Validation Study.
abstract: Background Postpolypectomy surveillance intervals derived from colonoscopy findings and histopathology should be guideline-based, yet these are frequently not adhered to, contributing to under- and oversurveillance. This motivates a more structured and automated approach to improve adherence. Objective We developed and evaluated an automated, implementable, guideline-aligned decision support tool that extracts colorectal polyp features from free-text colonoscopy and histopathology reports and produces auditable surveillance recommendations. Methods We extracted paired colonoscopy and histopathology reports from a National Health Service (NHS) trust and designed a 4-stage prompting pipeline using open-weight large language models to separate multispecimen histopathology reports into individual containers ("pots"), align endoscopic findings with specimens, and normalize each pot into a structured schema. The surveillance intervals were then computed by a deterministic rule engine encoding guideline rules. We evaluated extraction performance on 100 procedures (215 pots), assessed surveillance recommendation performance on a same-site cohort (n=100), and performed external validation on a cohort from a second trust (n=100). A separate retrospective audit compared automated recommendations and observed routine scheduling against a clinician-derived reference based on full electronic health record review in 127 patients. Results Key extraction fields showed end-to-end accuracy (specimen type=0.995; location=0.981; diagnosis=0.981; excision completeness=0.949), with mean report-level pot comprehensiveness of 0.968 (SD 0.112). Overall surveillance recommendation accuracy was 0.96 (95% CI 0.90-0.98) at Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust (GSTT) and 0.93 (95% CI 0.86-0.97) at Sandwell and West Birmingham NHS Trust (SWB) and showed strong class-level performance (no follow-up F 1 -score of 0.98 at GSTT and 0.97 at SWB; site check F 1 -score of 0.93 at GSTT and 0.91 at SWB; 3-year follow-up F 1 -score of 0.86 at GSTT and 0.80 at SWB; cancer alert F 1 -score of 1.00 at GSTT and 1.00 at SWB). The comparison to current clinical practice showed that the tool would improve guideline adherence primarily by reducing potential undersurveillance. Conclusions This hybrid approach using open-weight large language models for structured extraction and guideline-encoded rules for decision-making can generate accurate, lightweight, and auditable postpolypectomy surveillance recommendations. Such a tool has the potential to improve safety netting and guideline adherence in NHS colonoscopy workflows.

title: Reducing Annotation Costs Using Knowledge Distillation for Label‑Efficient Negation Detection in Radiology Reports: Multisite Internal Validation Study.
abstract: Background Negation in radiology reports (eg, "no evidence of dissection") is essential for accurately conveying diagnostic information. Clinical natural language processing systems, however, often fail to determine whether findings occur within negated or speculative contexts, leading to excessive false keyword alerts, noise in information extraction, and reduced precision in downstream clinical or research applications. Transformer models have advanced detection capabilities but require costly expert labeling. Large language models (LLMs) may provide label-efficient alternatives through few-shot prompting or knowledge distillation. Objective This study aims to systematically evaluate LLMs and transformer models under different supervision strategies, including comparisons of expert-labeled and LLM-distilled transformers, teacher LLMs (GPT-5.3 Chat, Gemma 4, and Qwen3.6-Plus), sampling approaches, and direct few-shot LLM inference, to determine whether LLM inference or LLM-based distillation can substitute for human labeling in radiology-report negation detection while reducing annotation costs. Methods We reused and analyzed 6000 deidentified English-language radiology reports from 3 hospital branches. Three LLMs-GPT-5.3 Chat, Gemma 4, and Qwen3.6-Plus-performed 0-, 5-, and 10-shot inference to identify negations and speculations unrelated to abnormal findings and generate pseudo-labels for transformer fine-tuning (Bio_ClinicalBERT [Bio + Clinical BERT model], BERT [Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers], and ALBERT [A Lite Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers]). We trained models using human-labeled or LLM-distilled supervision across 28 training data scales (n=42-4200) and 3 data sampling seeds and compared them across multiple supervision and training conditions encompassing backbone, label source, and sampling strategy. We assessed performance using keyword-level precision, recall, and F1-score with paired bootstrap tests (10,000 replicates). Results We refined 1000 report annotations (interrater κ=0.957) and fine-tuned 1260 transformer models. Human-labeled transformers consistently outperformed distillation-labeled ones, with the largest gap at small training scales (ΔF1-score ≈0.042; adjusted P<.001), which narrowed at larger scales (ΔF1-score ≈0.022; adjusted P<.001). Teacher model choice had minimal effect on distilled performance. All 3 human-labeled transformer backbones (BERT, ALBERT, and Bio_ClinicalBERT) achieved high keyword-level F1-scores (0.982-0.985 under their best conditions; n=4200). In the 10-shot setting, GPT-5.3 Chat (F1-score 0.974) modestly underperformed human-labeled transformers in the large-sample range (ΔF1-score=0.009; adjusted P=.047) and significantly outperformed Gemma 4 (F1-score 0.957; adjusted P=.01) and Qwen3.6-Plus (F1-score 0.950; adjusted P<.001) in the bootstrap analysis. GPT-5.3 Chat labeled reports at approximately US $0.018 per report and became less expensive than manual annotation when expert hourly wages exceeded US $0.64-1.50. Conclusions Human-supervised transformers remain the strongest baseline, but frontier LLMs such as GPT-5.3 Chat offer comparable performance with minimal supervision. LLM-based distillation offers a cost-effective alternative with only minor performance loss. Dataset scale proved more influential than sampling strategy. Additionally, superior teacher performance yielded no proportional gains through distillation, as open-weight or low-cost teachers achieved comparable results. If supported by external validation, the proposed label-efficient framework could enable accurate and affordable negation detection and rapid domain adaptation.

title: Detection of Cervical Nodal Metastasis in Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma Using Elastic Scattering Spectroscopy: Ex Vivo Diagnostic Modeling Study.
abstract: Background Cervical nodal metastasis remains one of the strongest determinants of treatment planning and prognosis in oral squamous cell carcinoma. Histopathology remains the reference standard, but it does not provide immediate information at the point of surgical specimen assessment. Elastic scattering spectroscopy (ESS) offers rapid, label-free optical interrogation of tissue microstructure, and may support ex vivo nodal assessment. Objective This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of ESS combined with machine learning classification for ex vivo detection of cervical lymph node metastasis in patients with oral squamous cell carcinoma. Methods We conducted a single-center observational ex vivo diagnostic modeling study in patients with oral squamous cell carcinoma undergoing primary tumor resection and neck dissection. A total of 3 ESS spectra were acquired from each bivalved lymph node before routine histopathological processing. Internal validation used repeated nested 5-fold cross-validation grouped by patient, so every spectrum and lymph node from a patient remained in the same fold. All preprocessing, scaling, dimensionality reduction, within-model-family configuration, and hyperparameter tuning, probability calibration where required, and decision-threshold selection were restricted to training data within the nested validation process; comparisons between candidate model families were exploratory and were based on pooled patient-grouped out-of-fold predictions. Spectrum-level probabilities were aggregated within each lymph node, and histopathology was the reference standard. Results A total of 52 patients were assessed for eligibility, 45 were included, and 280 fresh lymph nodes were assessed by ESS; 96 were pathology positive, and 184 were pathology negative. Of 840 acquired spectra, 760 passed quality control. Of the 280 nodes, 274 retained at least 2 usable spectra and comprised the analytical cohort; 6 pathology-negative nodes yielded no analyzable node-level ESS result. The hybrid model was selected because it had the highest pooled patient-grouped out-of-fold node-level area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), with an internally validated, exploratory estimate of 0.966 (95% CI 0.929-0.988). The same out-of-fold predictions informed model-family selection and performance reporting; this estimate does not represent independent validation of a prospectively fixed final model. At the cross-validation-derived summary threshold, secondary descriptive operating characteristics were sensitivity 93.8% (95% CI 86.4%-97.6%), specificity 95.5% (95% CI 90.1%-98.3%), accuracy 94.9% (95% CI 90.4%-97.3%), positive predictive value 91.8% (95% CI 82.9%-96.3%), and negative predictive value 96.6% (95% CI 92.4%-98.8%). The Brier score was 0.063, with calibration-in-the-large of -0.03 and a calibration slope of 0.94. Patient-level sensitivity was 96% and specificity was 90%. Pathology-positive and pathology-negative nodes also showed differences across amplitude-related and shape-related spectral features. Conclusions ESS showed promising ex vivo discrimination of metastatic cervical lymph nodes in this single-center model-development and internal-validation study. The findings support further investigation of ESS as a potential pathology-triage adjunct rather than a replacement for histopathology.

Pathology-positive and pathology-negative nodes also showed differences across amplitude-related and shape-related spectral features.

Conclusions

ESS showed promising ex vivo discrimination of metastatic cervical lymph nodes in this single-center model-development and internal-validation study. The findings support further investigation of ESS as a potential pathology-triage adjunct rather than a replacement for histopathology.

title: AI-Assisted Carotid Ultrasound for Nonexpert Use in Primary Care Cardiovascular Prevention: User-Centered Iterative Development Study.
abstract: Background Carotid ultrasound is traditionally confined to specialist settings because examination quality and diagnostic reliability are highly dependent on the operator's technical skill and experience. Recent advances in AI-assisted ultrasound may enable task shifting to primary care staff and support the integration of personalized visual risk communication into routine preventive care. Visualization of subclinical atherosclerosis has been shown to strengthen cardiovascular risk communication and support preventive engagement. However, limited evidence exists on how such technology can be practically integrated into routine primary care workflows and what conditions are required to support use by nonexpert operators. Objective This study aimed to describe an iterative user-centered design process enabling nonexpert use of AI-assisted carotid ultrasound for visualizing subclinical atherosclerosis in primary care cardiovascular disease prevention. Methods We conducted a user-centered, iterative study within the Västerbotten Intervention Programme in northern Sweden. Fourteen nurse assistants from 4 primary care centers representing urban, rural, and remote rural settings tested an AI-assisted carotid ultrasound prototype with real-time guidance and artery segmentation in their primary care work environment, while 15 nurse assistants participated in semistructured interviews. Structured system-interaction observations were conducted during prototype testing. Interview data were analyzed using inductive thematic analysis informed by Braun and Clarke's approach, while data from structured system-interaction observations were analyzed pragmatically to identify usability and workflow issues relevant to the iterative development process. Results The thematic analysis of interview data identified 4 themes describing nurse assistants' experiences and conditions for implementation: technology that fits the everyday primary care work; system guidance as a prerequisite for effective use; practical, peer-supported learning for confidence in clinical use; and confidence in the patient encounter. Observations identified recurring usability challenges related to ergonomics, probe handling, interface navigation, image acquisition, and time pressure. These findings led to iterative refinements, including redesigned interface navigation, simplified data entry, added audio feedback, enhanced probe support, and revised training materials. Conclusions This user-centered study identified key practical, organizational, and educational conditions for integrating AI-assisted carotid ultrasound into routine preventive care by nonexpert staff in primary care. The findings suggest that successful implementation will depend not only on technical capability but also on ergonomic and workflow fit, intuitive system guidance, peer-supported learning, and confidence in patient communication. These findings provide a foundation for future validation and implementation studies.

title: Chitosan Nanoparticles Combined With Titanium-Prepared Platelet-Rich Fibrin for Socket Preservation in Postextraction Sites: Protocol for a Single-Arm Clinical, Radiographic, and Histomorphometric Study.
abstract: Background Alveolar ridge resorption following tooth extraction can compromise subsequent implant placement. Socket preservation techniques aim to minimize dimensional changes and promote favorable bone healing. Chitosan nanoparticles combined with titanium-prepared platelet-rich fibrin represent a biologically active approach to ridge preservation. Objective This study aims to evaluate longitudinal changes in alveolar ridge dimensions and bone quality following socket preservation using chitosan nanoparticles combined with titanium-prepared platelet-rich fibrin. Methods This is a single-arm prospective clinical study involving systemically healthy participants requiring tooth extraction. Clinical, radiographic, and histomorphometric assessments will be performed at baseline and at follow-up visits at 3 and 6 months. Statistical analysis will be conducted using within-subject repeated-measures approaches. Results No external funding was received for this research. The manuscript was submitted before recruitment of participants had started and no clinical data had been collected or analyzed. Clinical, radiographic, and histomorphometric outcomes will be evaluated to assess changes in the dimensions of the alveolar ridge, bone density, and quality of regenerated bone during the postextraction healing period. Clinical and radiographic evaluation will be performed at baseline, 3 months, and 6 months. Histomorphometric analysis will be performed on bone core biopsy samples taken at the time of implant placement. The results of the study will be reported after data collection and analysis. Conclusions This protocol outlines a standardized approach to evaluating the clinical, radiographic, and histomorphometric outcomes of socket preservation using chitosan nanoparticles combined with titanium-prepared platelet-rich fibrin. The findings from this study may inform the design of future controlled clinical trials. Trial registration Clinical Trials Registry of India CTRI/2025/06/089715; https://tinyurl.com/4u6698xs. International registered report identifier (irrid) PRR1-10.2196/79532.

title: Quality Assessment and Model Training Impact of Synthetic Images in Medical Diagnostic Imaging: Systematic Review.
abstract: Background AI has increasingly been used to generate synthetic images to overcome the scarcity of large, regulatory-compliant medical image datasets. However, their quality and actual utility for algorithm development across deep learning architectures, medical settings, and image types have been poorly assessed. Objective This study aimed to review the use of synthetic images for algorithm development and to assess their quality and effects on downstream algorithms trained on these images, according to AI architecture, medical setting, and image type. Methods The authors conducted a systematic review of studies published between January 2020 and September 2025. PubMed, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and Embase were searched for peer-reviewed studies evaluating synthetic images generated from human medical imaging data. Data were extracted for imaging modalities, generative architectures, image-quality assessment methods, downstream model performance, explainability approaches, reproducibility practices, and risk of bias. Given substantial heterogeneity and incomplete statistical reporting, findings were synthesized descriptively. Results A total of 160 studies were included. Generative adversarial network-based architectures dominated image generation (119 studies, 74.4%), although hybrid and diffusion-based approaches became increasingly represented in recent years. Image-quality evaluation was highly heterogeneous: 50 studies included human-reader evidence, and 101 reported an automated image-quality assessment. Synthetic-only training generally underperformed real-data training, including a median Dice similarity coefficient change of -10.2% for segmentation. Adding synthetic data to real training sets was associated with median improvements in classification precision (+7.8%), recall (+5.3%), F 1 -score (+5.5%), accuracy (+4.3%), and area under the curve (+4.0%), while the median Dice coefficient improvement was +1.2%. Explainability evidence was reported in 68 (42.5%) studies and was rarely validated against expert annotations. Reproducibility reporting was inconsistent, and only 38% (60/160) of studies were judged to have low overall risk of bias. Conclusions Unlike previous reviews restricted to particular diseases, imaging modalities, or generative architectures, this review provides a cross-domain quantitative synthesis of both synthetic-image quality assessment and downstream model performance. Synthetic images currently appear more valuable as a complement to real training data than as a replacement, with modest improvements in classification performance, smaller gains in segmentation, and generally poorer performance with synthetic-only training. For researchers, developers, and regulators, these findings highlight the need for standardized multimethod image-quality evaluation, complete reporting, and rigorous external validation before synthetic-image pipelines are translated into clinical AI applications.

title: Comparison of Two AI Chatbots for Diagnosis and Providing Treatment Suggestions in Retinopathy of Prematurity: Retrospective Study.
abstract: Background Retinopathy of Prematurity (ROP) is a leading cause of preventable childhood blindness; yet, a global shortage of experienced pediatric ophthalmologists impedes timely diagnosis and treatment. While emerging AI chatbots are promising clinical decision-support tools in some ophthalmic diseases, their performance in ROP diagnosis and providing treatment suggestions remains uncertain. Objective This study aimed to compare the performance of Google's Gemini 2.5 Pro and OpenAI's ChatGPT o4-mini in ROP diagnosis and providing treatment suggestions against the gold standard of clinical consensus. Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted on 70 infants (140 eyes) with treatment-requiring ROP, each providing structured clinical text data and wide-field fundus images. We adopted a 2-stage prompting strategy for AI chatbots, instructing them first to generate ROP diagnoses (including zone, stage, and presence of plus disease), and subsequently to provide treatment suggestions. After collecting the generated responses, we assessed their performance by comparing the consistency of their diagnosis and treatment suggestions with the consensus gold standard. Furthermore, 2 independent specialists quantitatively assessed the outputs of Gemini 2.5 Pro and ChatGPT o4-mini using the ROP-specific Global Quality Score (GQS), which is a 5-point scale ranging from 1 (unusable) to 5 (excellent). Statistical significance was set at P <.05, and all statistical analyses were performed using R (version 4.4.1; R Foundation for Statistical Computing). Results For the tasks of ROP zoning and staging, the consistency rates between Gemini 2.5 Pro and ChatGPT o4-mini were 79.3% (111/140) vs 85.7% (120/140; zone), 64.3% (90/140) vs 70.0% (98/140; stage), respectively. For the task of treatment requirement, the rates (also referred to as sensitivity) were 93.6% (131/140) vs 90.7% (127/140), respectively. None of these differences were statistically significant ( P >.05). However, Gemini 2.5 Pro showed significantly better performance in plus disease identification (consistency: 108/140, 77.1% vs 80/140, 57.1%; P =.006), while ChatGPT o4-mini demonstrated significantly higher guideline adherence in treatment modality suggestions based on gold-standard ROP diagnoses (consistency: 91/140, 65.0%; vs 55/140, 39.3%; P =.01). Compared to Gemini 2.5 Pro, ChatGPT o4-mini performed better in providing ROP treatment suggestions (GQS score; P =.001), while the 2 AI chatbots had comparable GQS scores in diagnostic tasks. Conclusions ChatGPT o4-mini shows greater promise in generating evidence-based treatment suggestions based on gold-standard diagnoses, whereas Gemini 2.5 Pro shows advantages in visual interpretation, supporting its potential for targeted ROP diagnostic screening, particularly in identifying plus disease. As these AI chatbots continue to evolve, their performance merits further validation using larger cohorts.

title: Novel Sensors and Data-Driven Approach to Support Prevention, Diagnosis, and Treatment Planning of Cerebrovascular Accidents: Protocol for a Multimodal Data Collection Study With Novel Sensors.
abstract: Background Stroke is the second leading cause of death worldwide. Cerebrovascular diseases (CVDs), including strokes and transient ischemic attacks (TIAs), cause long-term disabilities and economic burdens. Strokes can be ischemic, caused by blood clots; or hemorrhagic, caused by bleeding in the brain. Immediate diagnosis and treatment are crucial. Proper management of TIAs is essential due to the high risk of subsequent strokes. Currently, wearable sensors, AI-based prediction, and automatic video analysis are not used in CVD diagnosis and recovery estimation. Objective This paper describes the design, cohort characteristics, and multimodal dataset of the Stroke-Data study conducted at 2 university hospitals in Finland. Although findings from individual components of the study have been reported elsewhere, this paper provides the first comprehensive description of the overall study design, cohort, and multimodal data collection protocol. The study collected a unique multimodal dataset comprising sensor data, video recordings, clinical assessments, questionnaires, and health record data from healthy controls and patients with stroke and TIA to support the development of AI, sensor-based, and video-based methods for CVD diagnosis and recovery estimation. Methods Stroke-Data was a prospective national multicenter study conducted at Oulu University Hospital and Kuopio University Hospital from October 2021 to December 2022. A rich multimodal dataset from patients with stroke and TIA and healthy controls was collected by study nurses and a research assistant. Inclusion criteria for patients were age >18 years and a diagnosis of cerebrovascular accident or TIA within the previous 3 days. Healthy control participants were aged 18 years and older and had no major chronic diseases, although blood pressure and cholesterol medications were permitted. Data collection included electroencephalogram; electrocardiogram; near-infrared spectroscopy; accelerometers to analyze gait and balance; retinal fundus images; video recordings of neurological examinations to analyze the face, body movements, and speech; clinical assessments; questionnaires; and electronic health records. Results In total, 263 participants were recruited, of whom 123 were controls (median age 59, IQR 45-72 years; female: 84/123, 68.3%), 31 were patients with TIA (median age 71, IQR 60-80 years; female: 8/31, 25.8%), and 103 were patients with stroke (median age 70, IQR 59-76 years; female: 42/102, 41.2%, sex data missing from 1 participant). A total of 6 participants were excluded (5 had diagnoses other than TIA or stroke and 1 control participant had a previous CVD). Conclusions We successfully conducted a multicenter multimodal data collection study on healthy controls and patients with stroke and TIA. This protocol paper provides a comprehensive methodological description of the Stroke-data study, serving as a reference for previously published and future analyses based on the dataset. The protocol is unique in combining physiological sensor data, video recordings, clinical assessments, questionnaires, and health record data from patients with stroke and TIA and healthy controls in a multicenter setting. title: Periodontitis Risk Assessment and Prevention Planning: Comparative Study of Multimodal Large Language Models and Periodontist Evaluations.
abstract: Background Periodontitis is one of the most prevalent yet preventable oral diseases, as indicated by multiple clinical and radiographic factors. As these factors are recorded in electronic health records (EHRs), their reuse offers opportunities for personalized risk assessment and targeted prevention. Predictive AI and traditional machine learning models support fragmented detection tasks but lack the integration of textual and imaging predictors. Emerging multimodal large language models (M-LLMs) show promise in combining these data sources for clinical assessment. Evaluating the capabilities of M-LLMs and comparing them against the current clinical standard are therefore essential to determine their potential as digital assistants. Objective This study aimed to evaluate the ability of M-LLMs to assess periodontitis risk and suggest prevention strategies, based on EHR data and radiographic findings. Each M-LLM was individually evaluated by periodontal experts, benchmarked against other models, and compared with a periodontist as a reference. Methods A vignette study was conducted following TRIPOD (Transparent Reporting of a Multivariable Prediction Model for Individual Prognosis or Diagnosis) guidelines for the evaluation of LLMs. Ten periodontal vignettes were created, each including a panoramic radiograph and textual EHR data. Three LLMs capable of reasoning and handling multimodal data were compared to a periodontist who generated outputs manually, based on the same prompts and input data. Periodontal experts rated all outputs across 6 predefined criteria on a 5-point Likert scale. Statistical analyses evaluated overall performance per model and tested whether performance varied per model, scenario complexity, or rater. Results GPT o1 Pro and Claude Sonnet 4 showed strong performance, with 86.7% and 85.6% of ratings deemed acceptable-comparable to the periodontist's output (87.8%). Gemini 2.5 Pro was rated significantly lower than both the periodontist and the other models (59.4% acceptable; P <.002). Radiographic interpretation consistently received lower scores than other abilities across all models and the periodontist, with Gemini rated below the acceptable threshold. The time required for completion ranged from approximately 10 seconds for Claude to 37 seconds for Gemini; 3 minutes, 22 seconds, for GPT; and 5 minutes, 57 seconds, for the periodontist. Conclusions M-LLMs demonstrated strong reasoning abilities in periodontal assessment. Across all models, unacceptable elements were consistently related to errors in radiographic interpretation, though refined prompting or newer model versions may improve this. Notably, even when radiographic findings were incorrect and plaque-retentive factors were absent, outputs were still rated well, indicating that EHR data alone provide a substantial basis. For clinical applicability, M-LLMs must at least perform comparably to a periodontist and meet the quality standards set by periodontal experts-a bar that GPT and Claude appear to approach.

title: Machine Learning and Deep Learning for the Diagnosis of Cervical Degenerative Diseases: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: Background Cervical degenerative diseases are a global public health issue, and their incidence is rising worldwide. Although an increasing number of studies on traditional machine learning (TML) and deep learning (DL) have been conducted in the detection and segmentation of cervical degenerative diseases and have reported promising task-specific results, the performance of these models has not yet been systematically analyzed. Objective This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to summarize and evaluate existing evidence on TML and DL approaches for diagnosing cervical degenerative diseases, thereby comprehensively guiding future research and clinical applications. Methods This systematic review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) guidelines. A comprehensive literature search was conducted on PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, Web of Science, Scopus, and the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE Xplore) from January 2000 to June 2026, supplemented by backward and forward citation searching in Scopus. Studies evaluating TML and DL algorithms for diagnosing cervical degenerative diseases using medical imaging were included. Methodological quality was assessed using the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 (QUADAS-2) tool and the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies AI (QUADAS-AI) tool. For the primary diagnostic accuracy meta-analysis, data were synthesized using a bivariate mixed-effects logistic regression model. Sensitivity and specificity were summarized separately using random-effects meta-analysis with the Knapp-Hartung adjustment, and 95% prediction intervals (PIs) were reported. Certainty of evidence was assessed using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation) approach. Results This systematic review included 30 studies, of which 21 involved a total of 25,301 patients included in the meta-analysis. The pooled sensitivity and specificity were 0.92 (95% CI 0.89-0.96; 95% PI 0.80-1.00) and 0.88 (95% CI 0.84-0.91; 95% PI 0.72-1.00), respectively. The positive likelihood ratio (LR) was 8.36 (95% CI 6.14-11.36), and the negative LR was 0.07 (95% CI 0.04-0.11). The area under the summary receiver operating characteristic (SROC) curve was 0.96 (95% CI 0.94-0.97). Leave-one-out analyses did not materially alter the pooled estimates. High risk of bias was identified in 4 studies using QUADAS-2 and in 17 using QUADAS-AI. The overall certainty of evidence was rated as low according to the GRADE approach. Conclusions TML and DL models demonstrated satisfactory diagnostic performance for cervical degenerative diseases, although external validation was limited. Unlike previously published reviews in this field, this study provides pooled estimates of the diagnostic performance of TML and DL for cervical degenerative diseases and indicates that, given between-study heterogeneity and low certainty of evidence, AI should currently be used as clinical decision support rather than an independent replacement for physicians.

title: Automated Lewis Score Estimation for Small Bowel Crohn Disease Using Capsule Endoscopy: Retrospective Cohort Study.
abstract: Background Small bowel capsule endoscopy (SBCE) is widely used to evaluate small bowel involvement in Crohn disease (CD); however, manual Lewis score calculation is time-consuming and susceptible to interobserver variability. Objective This study aimed to develop and preliminarily validate a multitask deep learning system for automated Lewis score estimation in patients with small bowel CD undergoing SBCE. Methods We developed Eval-Model, a multitask framework integrating You Only Look Once (YOLO)-style lesion detection and localization for ulcers and edema, a stenosis classification branch, and a long short-term memory-based temporal regression module. The primary dataset comprised SBCE examinations from 814 patients at the Children's Hospital of Fudan University. In this dataset, 725 (89.1%) cases were included for lesion-level annotation, and 89 (10.9%) cases with expert-consensus Lewis scores were used for scoring model development and internal testing. These 89 cases comprised 49 (55.1%) training cases and 40 (44.9%) internal test cases. All splits were performed at the patient level. A retrospective same-center temporal validation cohort of 20 consecutive cases from 2026 and 5 control cases were used for preliminary assessments of temporal robustness and specificity. Results In the 40-case internal Lewis score test set, Eval-Model achieved a mean squared error of 14.693 (95% CI 8.72-22.15), root mean squared error of 3.833 (95% CI 2.95-4.71), mean absolute error of 2.9 (95% CI 2.1-3.8), R 2 of 0.82 (95% CI 0.70-0.90), and explained variance of 0.83 (95% CI 0.72-0.91). For lesion recognition, the model achieved an overall mean average precision of 0.94 with an inference time of 15 ms per frame. In the 20-case same-center temporal validation cohort, the mean squared error was 26.848 (95% CI 12.51-45.33), the root mean squared error was 5.182 (95% CI 3.54-6.73), the mean absolute error was 3.3 (95% CI 2.2-4.6), R 2 rounded to 1.00 (95% CI 0.98-1.00), and the explained variance rounded to 1.00 (95% CI 0.98-1.00). These temporal estimates require cautious interpretation because of the small, same-center cohort. Conclusions Eval-Model demonstrated preliminary feasibility for automated Lewis score estimation from SBCE in small bowel CD. The system may serve as a standardized adjunct to expert review, but larger multicenter prospective validation with independent external annotation is required before clinical deployment.

title: Cross-Domain Chest Radiograph Report Generation Under Dataset Shift: Bidirectional Audit Study.
abstract: Background Cross-domain chest radiograph report generation may produce formally valid reports that are nevertheless repetitive, weakly case-specific, or missing clinically relevant findings. These failures can be missed when evaluation relies on a single language-overlap or clinical-label score. Objective This study aimed to evaluate cross-domain report generation with a bidirectional layered audit, characterize direction-specific and end point-specific failure profiles under a composite training-side control and 3 decoding policies, and explore whether selected audit dimensions remained informative for a contemporary medical vision language model. Methods A fixed R2Gen-style system was evaluated bidirectionally on 575 IU X-ray and 401 MIMIC-CXR (Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care Chest X-Ray) target records. The audit included surface validity, complete-report recurrence and concentration, a predefined prefix end point, lexical diversity, official Stanford CheXpert/NegBio labels, paired cluster-bootstrap inference, and blinded review by 2 medical trainees. The primary human audit included 210 reports from 70 randomly sampled cases, with blinded adjudication of unresolved primary end point disagreements. A 60-report targeted panel was used for failure-mode analysis. Separately, a fixed MedGemma 1.5 4B configuration generated reports for all 976 records. Results In MIMIC-CXR-to-IU X-ray transfer, out of 575 reports, ON (protocol-defined training-side control enabled)+B4 (beam search with a beam size of 4) reduced the predefined recurrent prefix from 575 (100%) to 8 (1.4%; Holm-adjusted P =.002). However, 569 (99.0%) ON+B4 outputs still belonged to exact duplicate groups. In IU X-ray-to-MIMIC-CXR transfer, the 14-category CheXpert/NegBio micro- F 1 was higher for ON+B4 than for OFF (protocol-defined training-side control disabled)+B4 (0.1687 vs 0.0744; Holm-adjusted P =.01). This apparent advantage was not broad-based: after cardiomegaly was excluded in a post hoc descriptive sensitivity analysis, the difference changed from +0.0944 to -0.0610. Text-level tracing showed that the original contrast was mainly driven by a labeler response to recurrent, semantically normal heart-size wording. Across the primary human-audit cells, major omissions occurred in 12 to 15 out of 35 reports, and major unsupported findings occurred in 10 to 16 of 35 reports, with no consistent configuration ordering observed. The exploratory MedGemma micro- F 1 was 0.4722 on IU X-ray and 0.4340 on MIMIC-CXR, but 381 out of 575 (66.3%) IU outputs belonged to exact duplicate groups. Conclusions No configuration performed consistently well across end points, and no single metric captured all forms of cross-domain degradation. The MedGemma stress test suggested that recurrence and label-traceability checks remain useful across architectures, although it was not a matched performance comparison. Cross-domain report generators should undergo bidirectional evaluation, final-text verification, and image-grounded human review before external validation or clinical deployment.

title: AI for Poststroke Epilepsy: Scoping Review of Imaging-Based Prediction Models and Implications for African Settings.
abstract: Background Poststroke seizures (PSS) and poststroke epilepsy (PSE) are important neurological complications associated with poorer functional recovery, increased mortality, and reduced quality of life after stroke. Neuroimaging plays a central role in identifying patients at increased risk, and recent advances in AI have enabled the development of imaging-based prediction models that may improve individualized risk stratification. However, the current evidence remains fragmented, and the extent to which these approaches are applicable to African health care settings is unclear. Objective This scoping review aimed to chart the existing global evidence on the development of imaging-based prediction models that can help in predicting PSS and PSE, especially AI-based ones. The purpose was to look into the imaging techniques, computational algorithms, and validation methodologies used and the representation of African populations. Methods This scoping review was performed using the Joanna Briggs Institute methodological framework, and the results were presented based on the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) framework. Articles searched using databases such as PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar involved the application of computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), angiography imaging techniques, radiomic markers, or multimodal neuroimaging techniques in statistical and AI-based prediction models for seizure-related outcomes after stroke. Results Twenty-three studies published between 2005 and 2026 met the eligibility criteria. The evidence demonstrated a clear methodological evolution from conventional imaging-based prediction models to radiomics, machine learning, deep learning, explainable AI, and multimodal approaches. MRI and CT were the predominant imaging modalities, with cortical involvement, lesion location, infarct volume, hemorrhagic transformation, and quantitative radiomic features emerging as the most frequently reported imaging predictors. Most AI models relied on internal validation, while relatively few underwent external validation. The evidence base was concentrated in East Asia, Europe, and North America, with no eligible imaging-based AI models having been developed or externally validated using African datasets. Conclusions Imaging-based AI for predicting PSS and PSE has progressed rapidly, but important methodological and geographical gaps remain. Limited external validation, heterogeneous reporting, and the absence of African development and validation cohorts restrict confidence in the generalizability of existing models. Future research should prioritize the development of explainable imaging-based AI models using representative African neuroimaging datasets and their external validation in multicenter studies.

title: Multiparametric Magnetic Resonance Imaging in a Prospective Cohort of Living Kidney Donors, Recipients, and Healthy Controls and Correlations With Markers of Renal Function, Fibrosis, and Aging (MPRENAL): Protocol for a Longitudinal Observational Study.
abstract: Background Renal fibrosis is the final common pathway of chronic kidney disease progression and a critical histological predictor of renal function decline and allograft failure. Routine clinical monitoring with estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and albuminuria is insensitive to fibrosis development. Renal biopsy is invasive and subject to sampling bias, which limits repeated assessment, thus necessitating noninvasive imaging biomarkers. Multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (mpMRI) characterizes renal structure and function noninvasively. Individual MRI measures have been associated with fibrosis and with declining renal function. However, longitudinal validation against histology and measured glomerular filtration rate (mGFR) remains limited. Objective This prospective longitudinal observational study aims to validate mpMRI against histological fibrosis assessed by kidney biopsy in kidney transplant recipients (KTRs), and compare the time-dependent trajectories of imaging and functional markers across living kidney donors (LKDs), KTRs, and healthy control (HC) cohorts. Methods The planned sample includes 32 LKDs, 32 KTRs, and 32 HCs. Up to 40 KTRs may be recruited to account for attrition. Baseline assessments are performed before transplantation for LKDs and KTRs, and at enrollment for HCs, with follow-up assessments at 3, 12, and 24 months. mpMRI is performed at 3 tesla (3 T). The MRI protocol includes structural longitudinal relaxation time (T1)-weighted and T2-weighted imaging, T1 mapping, T2 mapping, transverse relaxation time (T2*) mapping, diffusion-weighted imaging, pseudocontinuous arterial spin labeling, non-contrast enhanced angiography, and phase-contrast measurement of renal artery flow. Glomerular filtration rate will be measured by [ 99m Tc]Tc-diethylenetriaminepentaacetic acid (DTPA) clearance. A baseline allograft biopsy is taken during transplantation surgery, with protocol biopsies at 3, 12, and 24 months. Fibrosis is quantified using stereology. The primary outcome is the longitudinal association between the corticomedullary T1 difference and histologically determined renal fibrosis in KTRs across all 4 biopsy time points. Secondary analyses include longitudinal divergence of MRI and functional markers across cohorts, diagnostic performance for fibrosis, and predictive value for mGFR decline in KTRs and LKDs. Linear mixed models will be used to study longitudinal associations. Three additional MRI measures will be tested in a fixed sequence to control multiplicity. Receiver operating characteristic curve analysis will assess diagnostic performance. Results The study was funded in October 2023. Recruitment for the multiparametric renal magnetic resonance imaging (MPRENAL) study commenced on October 29, 2024. As of March 2026, 42 participants were enrolled, and data collection is ongoing. Recruitment is anticipated to close in February 2027, with final study visits by March 2029. The primary results are expected to be published in 2030. Conclusions Successful completion of this study is expected to provide robust histological validation of mpMRI and establish its utility as a noninvasive tool for monitoring renal health.

Multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (mpMRI) characterizes renal structure and function noninvasively. Individual MRI measures have been associated with fibrosis and with declining renal function. However, longitudinal validation against histology and measured glomerular filtration rate (mGFR) remains limited.

Objective

This prospective longitudinal observational study aims to validate mpMRI against histological fibrosis assessed by kidney biopsy in kidney transplant recipients (KTRs), and compare the time-dependent trajectories of imaging and functional markers across living kidney donors (LKDs), KTRs, and healthy control (HC) cohorts.

Methods

The planned sample includes 32 LKDs, 32 KTRs, and 32 HCs. Up to 40 KTRs may be recruited to account for attrition. Baseline assessments are performed before transplantation for LKDs and KTRs, and at enrollment for HCs, with follow-up assessments at 3, 12, and 24 months. mpMRI is performed at 3 tesla (3 T). The MRI protocol includes structural longitudinal relaxation time (T1)-weighted and T2-weighted imaging, T1 mapping, T2 mapping, transverse relaxation time (T2*) mapping, diffusion-weighted imaging, pseudocontinuous arterial spin labeling, non-contrast enhanced angiography, and phase-contrast measurement of renal artery flow. Glomerular filtration rate will be measured by [99mTc]Tc-diethylenetriaminepentaacetic acid (DTPA) clearance. A baseline allograft biopsy is taken during transplantation surgery, with protocol biopsies at 3, 12, and 24 months. Fibrosis is quantified using stereology. The primary outcome is the longitudinal association between the corticomedullary T1 difference and histologically determined renal fibrosis in KTRs across all 4 biopsy time points. Secondary analyses include longitudinal divergence of MRI and functional markers across cohorts, diagnostic performance for fibrosis, and predictive value for mGFR decline in KTRs and LKDs. Linear mixed models will be used to study longitudinal associations. Three additional MRI measures will be tested in a fixed sequence to control multiplicity. Receiver operating characteristic curve analysis will assess diagnostic performance.

Results

The study was funded in October 2023. Recruitment for the multiparametric renal magnetic resonance imaging (MPRENAL) study commenced on October 29, 2024. As of March 2026, 42 participants were enrolled, and data collection is ongoing. Recruitment is anticipated to close in February 2027, with final study visits by March 2029. The primary results are expected to be published in 2030.

Conclusions

Successful completion of this study is expected to provide robust histological validation of mpMRI and establish its utility as a noninvasive tool for monitoring renal health.

title: Metastasis Extraction From Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Clinical Notes Using Large Language Model-Based Classification: Retrospective Comparative Study.
abstract: Background Identification of metastasis status in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is a critical part of understanding disease prognosis, treatment courses, trial eligibility, and population-level cancer surveillance. However, metastasis status is inconsistently recorded in structured cancer registry fields, since manual abstraction of clinical notes is often an error-prone process. This challenge highlights an opportunity for leveraging large language models (LLMs) to conduct high-scale metastasis extraction from real-world clinical documentation. Objective We conducted a retrospective, multicohort comparative evaluation of 3 distinct LLMs for 2 independent classification tasks: overall metastasis presence at any site and brain/central nervous system (CNS) metastasis presence. We evaluated model performance on 2 independent NSCLC cohorts: one with registry labels and another with manual annotations. We further explored whether our methods could analyze clinical documentation and recover missing information in structured registry fields. Methods Patient cohorts were derived from the Winship Cancer Institute. Cohort 1 (n=579 patients; 24,887 notes across 69 note types; 2023-2025) used registry-linked metastasis fields as the reference standard. Cohort 2 (n=22 patients; 644 radiology notes; 2010-2021) was drawn from 2 completed randomized trials and used dual-annotated labels (Cohen κ: 0.93 overall metastasis; 0.88 CNS metastasis) as the reference standard. We fine-tuned the GatorTron-base encoder model for each independent binary classification task. We evaluated MedGemma-27B-text and Llama 3.1-70B using zero-shot prompting. A separate cohort of 675 patients with missing registry labels was used for an exploratory missingness-recovery analysis, validated against annotations of a random subsample. Our best-performing model was used to conduct further site-specific metastasis classification, based on available registry data. Results More than half (675/1260, 54%) of initially identified cohort 1 patients had missing or unknown registry metastasis labels. MedGemma demonstrated the best performance in overall metastasis classification (cohort 1: F 1 -score=0.80; cohort 2 patient-level: F 1 -score=1.0; cohort 2 note-level: F 1 -score=0.93). For brain/CNS metastasis, Llama3 performed best in both cohorts (cohort 1: F 1 -score=0.79; cohort 2 patient-level: F 1 -score=0.93; cohort 2 note-level: F 1 -score=0.86). The fine-tuned GatorTron model showed strong performance for classification of overall metastasis in cohort 1 (F 1 -score=0.72). Error analysis indicated that several model errors reflected incomplete registry labels, ambiguous clinical language, or missing documentation. In the exploratory recovery analysis, model predictions agreed with manual annotations at an accuracy of 0.90 and F 1 -score of 0.89. Additional site-specific metastasis classification by MedGemma demonstrated high performance for liver metastasis (F 1 -score=0.82) and bone metastasis (F 1 -score=0.79). Conclusions All models demonstrated relatively high performance. The zero-shot generative models were more robust to nuanced documentation and context-dependent brain/CNS metastasis extraction. The fine-tuned encoder model demonstrated strong classification performance but may have been limited by potential inaccuracies in the registry reference standards during model training. This study further demonstrated the potential of LLMs in recovering plausible structured labels from narrative text, complementing cancer registries for metastasis ascertainment.

title: A Framework for Identifying and Understanding Cognitive Biases in Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Radiology.
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) creates new susceptibility to diagnostic error in radiology related to the cognitive processes by which radiologists' interpretations incorporate AI outputs. This Perspective presents a conceptual framework for cognitive biases in AI-assisted radiology linking specific biases to radiologist-AI interactions. The framework uses dual-process theory, recognizing fast intuitive and deliberate analytic modes of information processing, as an organizing model for understanding cognitive processes underlying radiologists' decisions and their potential contribution to bias. Across seven decision scenarios spanning image viewing, findings interpretation, and contextual integration, the framework examines how AI output timing, radiologist-AI agreement, trust calibration, and reader expertise influence decision-making. We identify adaptive heuristics that support efficient decisions but, when misapplied or overrelied upon, increase susceptibility to complacency, confirmation, automation, distrust, anchoring, and usual implication bias, and increase behavioral risk of use without qualification. We highlight AI paradoxes emerging from the framework of despecialization, system fragility, and deskilling. Finally, we propose strategies targeting these cognitive biases, including education and experiential learning, workflow and interface design, clinical oversight, and performance monitoring. This framework provides a structured basis for generating testable hypotheses and designing AI-assisted radiology systems that preserve the strengths of human expertise and AI while supporting calibrated reliance.

title: Cloud-Based AI Application for Classifying Arteriovenous Hemodialysis Vascular Access Aneurysms: Findings from a Masked Multicenter Derivation Cohort Study.
abstract: Background In hemodialysis patients, arteriovenous fistulas (AVF) are the preferred vascular access for most hemodialysis patients. However, aneurysms of the AVF can lead to severe complications, including rupture and life-threatening exsanguination. To address this risk, we recently developed, trained, and validated a convolutional neural network capable of classifying digital images of arteriovenous aneurysms captured via mobile devices as showing either "Advanced" or "Not Advanced" aneurysms. This cloud-based aneurysm classification application (ACA) aims to facilitate early detection of advanced aneurysms, potentially reducing morbidity and improving outcomes. Our study aimed to compare the diagnostic performance of ACA with in-person aneurysm assessments by physicians specialized in vascular access care. Methods We conducted a single-masked, multicenter, observational, cross-sectional study at two vascular care centers with a catchment area of 21 hemodialysis clinics. Using mobile devices, research staff captured images of arteriovenous accesses and uploaded them to the cloud. The ACA then computed the probability of "Advanced" and "Not Advanced" aneurysms. Separately, physicians masked to the ACA results performed thorough physical and ultrasound examinations of the AVF and classified aneurysms as "Advanced" or "Not Advanced". Physician classifications served as the ground truth for ACA performance analysis. Results We analyzed 720 images from 120 incenter hemodialysis patients (six images per patient). Mean patient age was 62 years, 66 were male. Physicians classified 26 patients (22%) having "Advanced" aneurysms and 94 (78%) having "Not Advanced" aneurysms. The ACA achieved an AUROC of 0.908 (95% confidence interval: 0.843-0.963). At the maximum Youden index, ACA classified 42 aneurysms (35%) as "Advanced" and 78 (65%) as "Not Advanced," yielding a sensitivity of 96% and a specificity of 82%. Conclusion The ACA demonstrated promising accuracy in this initial masked evaluation. Further validation in larger, independent cohorts and under real-world conditions is warranted before broader clinical deployment.

title: Implementation of novel approaches for management and treatment of brain tumours
abstract: Primary brain tumours remain among the most difficult cancers to treat because of their molecular heterogeneity, infiltrative growth and the blood–brain barrier (BBB), which restricts drug delivery. For almost two decades, management of glioblastoma, the most common malignant primary brain tumour in adults, has rested on maximal safe resection followed by radiotherapy with temozolomide. Recent years have brought a more differentiated picture. Integrated molecular classification (WHO CNS5) and DNA methylation profiling have sharpened diagnosis; fluorescence-guided surgery and tumour treating fields have extended the established armamentarium; the IDH inhibitor vorasidenib (hazard ratio for progression or death 0.39; 95% CI 0.27–0.56 versus placebo) and BRAF/MEK inhibition with dabrafenib plus trametinib have delivered the first clearly biomarker-directed successes in adult and paediatric glioma respectively; and immunotherapy, including checkpoint blockade, dendritic cell vaccination and intraventricular CAR T cells, is under active investigation with mixed results. Regulatory approvals of vorasidenib (2024) and dordaviprone (2025) have since extended the biomarker-directed options, and ultrasound-mediated BBB opening illustrates a delivery-focused strategy. In parallel, machine-learning tools now support tumour classification, segmentation and response assessment, and are well placed to inform patient selection, end-point definition and trial design. This review summarises the clinical evidence for each approach, highlights pharmacological issues (CNS penetration, response end-points, safety and exposure–response relationships) and discusses barriers to implementation, including trial design, external validation of AI tools and equitable access.

title: Diagnostic Tools to Establish the Presence of Peripheral Arterial Disease in People With Diabetes (DMPAD): A Multicenter Comparative Diagnostic Accuracy Study.
abstract: Objective Accurate diagnosis of peripheral arterial disease (PAD) in people with diabetes is critical, but the accuracy of common bedside tests remains uncertain. This study evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of five bedside tests-ankle brachial pressure index (ABPI), exercise ABPI, toe brachial pressure index (TBPI), visual Doppler, and audible Doppler. Results were compared against the reference standard of computed tomography angiography (CTA) or magnetic resonance angiography (MRA). Research design and methods A prospective multicenter diagnostic accuracy study was conducted across 16 sites in the U.K. Participants aged ≥18 years, with a history of diabetes (symptomatic and asymptomatic), without contraindications to CTA or MRA, PAD status known on imaging, or a known history of PAD intervention, were eligible to partake. Patients were recruited from both primary and secondary care. Radiologists, blinded to index test results, used the ANGIO scoring system, with ≥50% stenosis defining PAD. The primary outcome was test sensitivity. Results From April 2022 to November 2023, 604 participants were enrolled; 536 completed the study with valid reference imaging. PAD was identified in 37% of participants. Sensitivity was low across all bedside tests: audible Doppler (36%, 95% CI 27-45), visual Doppler (42%, 95% CI 33-51), TBPI (55%, 95% CI 46-64), ABPI (41%, 95% CI 32-50), and exercise ABPI (41%, 95% CI 31-51). Conclusions In people with diabetes, visual Doppler, audible Doppler, ABPI, TBPI, and exercise ABPI demonstrated poor diagnostic performance for PAD and should not be considered as accurate diagnostic tools in this population.

title: Type 2 Diabetes and Longitudinal Changes in Cortical and Trabecular Bone Density, Microarchitecture, and Strength: The Framingham Study.
abstract: Objective To gain insight into higher fracture risk in individuals with type 2 diabetes, we determined the association of type 2 diabetes glycemic status and severity with longitudinal changes in peripheral bone density and microarchitecture. Research design and methods We conducted a longitudinal study of 769 participants from the Framingham Study who underwent high-resolution, peripheral, quantitative computed tomography (HR-pQCT) at the tibia and radius in 2012-2016 and 2021-2023 (mean 8-year follow-up). Linear regression models estimated mean 8-year percent changes in bone measures across indicators of diabetes severity, adjusting for age, sex, weight, and height. Results The mean age was 67 ± 7 years, and 59% of participants were women. More than half (57%) were normoglycemic (fasting plasma glucose [FPG] <100 mg/dL, not on any treatment), 31% had prediabetes (100 ≤ FPG ≤125 mg/dL), and 12% had type 2 diabetes (FPG >125 mg/dL or on treatment). Adjusted mean percent changes in HR-pQCT bone measures were similar across diabetes severity, including glycemic status, use of diabetes medications, duration of diabetes, and HbA1c. For example, cortical volumetric bone mineral density at the radius changed by -1.50% (95% CI -2.43, -0.56) in type 2 diabetes and -1.96% (-2.53, -1.39) in prediabetes, compared with -2.42% (-2.86, -1.97) in normoglycemia (reference group; all P > 0.05). Conclusions The magnitude of peripheral bone loss over 8 years did not differ between individuals with type 2 diabetes and those with normoglycemia, suggesting that bone deterioration alone does not explain the higher fracture risk in older adults with type 2 diabetes. Future studies should address other contributors to skeletal fragility.

title: Five predictors of meningioma surgery: an AI analysis.
abstract: Background Meningioma surgery aims to preserve neurological function, usually measured by the Karnofsky Performance Scale (KPS), but predicting postoperative KPS change remains challenging. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 397 meningioma resections from 14 Italian centers. Preoperative clinical and MRI features (age, tumor size, eloquent-area location, vessel and cranial-nerve involvement, prior surgery, baseline KPS, etc.) were used to train classifiers (logistic GAM, weighted logistic regression, linear/RBF SVM, random forest) with cross-validation. We compared performance to the Staartjes et al. GAM_MCS model (predicting KPS drop ≥10). Results All models achieved only moderate discrimination for new deficits: AUC ≈0.65-0.70 (Staartjes2 GAM_MCS 0.692; logistic regression 0.694). Predicting major changes was more accurate: for KPS drops ≥20 or ≥30 points, AUC ≈0.76-0.77, and for any postoperative improvement AUC ≈0.81, whereas 10-point declines were hardest (AUC ≈0.70). For example, weighted logistic regression yielded AUCs of 0.697, 0.765, 0.762, and 0.811 for predicting KPS drops ≥10, ≥20, ≥30, and any improvement, respectively. The most important predictors were anatomical complexity factors: eloquent-area involvement, major vessel manipulation, and tumor size (consistent with the "Big Five" risk factors). Meningioma surgery aims to preserve neurological function, usually measured by the Karnofsky Performance Scale (KPS), but predicting postoperative KPS change remains challenging.

We retrospectively analyzed 397 meningioma resections from 14 Italian centers. All models achieved only moderate discrimination for new deficits: AUC ≈0.65-0.70 (Staartjes2 GAM_MCS 0.692; logistic regression 0.694). The most important predictors were anatomical complexity factors: eloquent-area involvement, major vessel manipulation, and tumor size (consistent with the "Big Five" risk factors).

Preoperative anatomical complexity remains the dominant predictor of postoperative functional outcome. Logistic-based ML classifiers had moderate overall accuracy but better performance for extreme outcomes (major decline or clear improvement).
