title: Impact of ROI delineation methods on the repeatability of quantitative indices in 99mTc-MAG3 diuretic renography.
abstract: Background To assess how two different region-of-interest (ROI) delineation strategies - whole-kidney ROI and cortical ROI - affect the intra- and interobserver repeatability of quantitative indices in 99m Tc-MAG3 diuretic renography. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 85 patients (mean age 52.3±17.2 years) who underwent standardized 99m Tc-MAG3 diuretic renography for renal function assessment. Whole-kidney and cortical ROIs were generated using manual and semi-automated techniques. Intraobserver repeatability was assessed by repeated analysis by an experienced radiographer with an interval of one month between processing sessions. Interobserver repeatability was assessed by independent analysis performed by an experienced radiographer and a junior radiographer. Extracted parameters included differential renal function (DRF), time to maximum counts (T max ), and time to half-peak counts (T 1/2 ) per side (T maxR , T maxL and T 1/2R , T 1/2L , respectively). Repeatability was assessed using Bland-Altman analysis, Lin's concordance correlation coefficient (CCC), and Fleiss' kappa for ordinal T 1/2 classification. The Pitman-Morgan test was applied to compare intraobserver variance between whole-kidney and cortical ROI-derived parameters. Results Intraobserver repeatability was high across both ROI strategies (whole-kidney ROI, cortical ROI) and delineation methods (manual, semi-automated). DRF demonstrated minimal bias and narrow 95% LoA (whole-kidney ROI: 0.02±1.40% and 0.04±3.29% for manual and semi-automated delineation; cortical ROI: 0.15±1.32% and 0.38±3.06%, respectively), with high CCC values (whole-kidney ROI: 0.991 and 0.955; cortical ROI: 0.992 and 0.961, respectively). T max also showed substantial agreement, with small bias and high CCC values. T 1/2 classification demonstrated almost perfect intraobserver repeatability, with weighted kappa values for T 1/2R of 0.906 and 0.867 for whole-kidney ROIs and 0.870 and 0.850 for cortical ROIs using manual and semi-automated delineation, respectively. Interobserver repeatability was likewise high overall, although agreement was consistently slightly lower for cortical compared with whole-kidney ROIs. For DRF, interobserver CCC values were 0.978 versus 0.971 for manual delineation and 0.944 versus 0.916 for semi-automated delineation for whole-kidney and cortical ROIs, respectively. For manual T 1/2R classification, weighted kappa was 0.902 for whole-kidney ROIs and 0.717 for cortical ROIs. Conclusions Quantitative indices in 99m Tc-MAG3 diuretic renography showed high intra- and interobserver repeatability irrespective of ROI strategy. Among renal function metrics, repeatability was highest for DRF, while T max and T 1/2 also demonstrated high repeatability with only minor sensitivity to ROI selection. Both whole-kidney and cortical ROI approaches yielded reliable measurements, although cortical ROI delineation showed slightly lower interobserver agreement, suggesting greater sensitivity to operator-dependent variability.

title: Facial esthetic medicine in dentistry: botulinum toxin and hyaluronic acid fillers for smile-face harmonization.
abstract: Orofacial treatment planning is being redefined by the convergence of minimally invasive facial aesthetic medicine and aesthetic dentistry. Specifically, hyaluronic acid (HA) dermal fillers and botulinum toxin type A (BoNT-A) are being employed more frequently as adjuncts to maximize smile-lip-face harmony. The scope of non-invasive or minimally invasive facial aesthetic medicine for dentists has also been clarified by regulatory changes in Italy, underscoring the importance of competency-based training and organized risk management. The objective is to give a narrative summary of BoNT-A and HA fillers' indications, clinical procedures, integration into dental workflows, and safety concerns in dental practice, with a focus on perioral applications and complication management. In addition to focused searches in Google Scholar and important consensus texts (2000-2025; chosen updates through early 2026), a narrative search was carried out in PubMed/MEDLINE and Scopus. Systematic reviews, clinical trials, and expert consensus statements on face injectables and adverse event management were prioritized. There is evidence to support BoNT-A as a conservative adjunct for gummy smiles caused by hyperfunctional lip elevators, some lower-face dynamic rhytids, and masseter hypertrophy and bruxism-related myofascial pain, providing clinically meaningful reductions in pain, improvements in muscular and joint function, and favorable aesthetic outcomes. HA fillers may be used as a "finishing step" following orthodontic, periodontal, or restorative treatment to enhance lip contour and perioral soft-tissue support. Filler-induced vascular occlusion is the most important safety concern; early detection and prompt hyaluronidase treatment are essential, and ultrasound mapping is becoming more and more recommended for high-risk areas and tailored care. As an orofacial harmonization method, facial aesthetic medicine can be incorporated into modern dentistry as long as indications are conservative, patients are properly chosen and given consent, and clinics are prepared and trained to handle complications. Future studies should establish competency-based training pathways for dental professionals and standardize outcome measurements.

title: [Thoracic pain in an adolescent with a large intrathoracic mass].
abstract: Introduction Background: Ganglioneuromas are rare benign tumors of the sympathetic nervous system that predominantly occur in children and adolescents. They are most commonly located in the posterior mediastinum and often remain asymptomatic until they reach a considerable size. Case Presentation: We report the case of an adolescent who presented with intermittent right-sided chest pain. Chest radiography revealed a large intrathoracic mass, which was further characterized by computed tomography as a well-circumscribed right paravertebral lesion without radiological signs of malignancy. Ultrasound-guided transthoracic biopsy established the diagnosis of ganglioneuroma. Following multidisciplinary discussion, the patient underwent complete robot-assisted thoracoscopic resection. Histopathological examination confirmed a benign ganglioneuroma measuring 11.5 cm in maximum diameter. The postoperative course was uneventful, and the patient was discharged on the second postoperative day. At outpatient follow-up, the patient was asymptomatic and clinical as well as radiological examinations were unremarkable. Conclusion: Although rare, ganglioneuroma should be considered in the differential diagnosis of posterior mediastinal masses in adolescents presenting with persistent or recurrent chest pain and dyspnea. Cross-sectional imaging followed by histopathological confirmation is essential for diagnosis. Complete surgical resection is both diagnostic and curative, with an excellent prognosis.

title: Optical neuronavigation facilitates transcranial surgical access to the equine pituitary gland.
abstract: Objective To evaluate the feasibility of an optical neuronavigation-guided transcranial approach to the equine pituitary gland, compare pituitary tissue acquisition using MRI versus CT guidance, and assess an automated tissue resection device versus a standard biopsy needle. Methods 13 equine cadaver heads from horses euthanized for reasons unrelated to the study were used. A fiducial array was secured to the frontal bone before imaging; 7 heads underwent CT, and 6 heads underwent MRI. Images were imported into a neuronavigation system for 3-D reconstruction, surgical planning, and registration. Eighteen pituitary biopsy samples were obtained: 7 using a neuronavigation-guided automated morcellation and aspiration device and 11 using a standard biopsy needle. All samples were processed with hematoxylin and eosin staining, and histologic evaluation was performed by a veterinary pathologist blinded to biopsy technique and imaging modality. Results Pituitary tissue was confirmed histologically in 7 of 13 heads overall (53.8%): 6 of 6 MRI-guided heads (100%) and 1 of 7 CT-guided heads (14.3%). Both biopsy techniques were applied to each of the 6 MRI-guided heads (paired design); the automated morcellation device yielded pituitary tissue in 4 of 6 heads (66.7%), compared with 2 of 6 heads (33.3%) using the standard biopsy needle. Conclusions Optical neuronavigation enabled feasible transcranial access to the equine pituitary gland in cadaveric specimens, with tissue acquisition improved using MRI guidance and automated morcellation. Clinical relevance These findings support further investigation of neuronavigation-guided hypophysectomy as a potential treatment for pituitary pars intermedia dysfunction in horses.

title: Dogs and cats undergoing surgery for penetrating thoracic trauma have high survival despite frequent complications, and imaging may underestimate injury severity.
abstract: Objective To describe clinical and radiographic findings in dogs and cats with surgically confirmed penetrating thoracic trauma and evaluate associations with outcomes. Methods This retrospective, multicenter observational study reviewed records from 5 referral hospitals to identify dogs and cats with surgically confirmed penetrating thoracic trauma between July 1, 2010, and July 31, 2025. Inclusion required thoracic radiographs, surgical reports, and perioperative records. Results A total of 86 dogs and 5 cats were identified. Mean animal trauma triage score was higher in nonsurvivors (7.6 ± 2.4; n = 20) than survivors (5.2 ± 2.5; 71). Radiographic findings included pneumothorax (73.6%), pulmonary contusions (65.9%), and rib fractures (62.6%). Computed tomography findings often identified more injuries. Time from presentation to surgery did not differ in survivors versus nonsurvivors. Lung lobectomy was performed in 24.2% of patients and was more common in nonsurvivors (45.0% vs 18.3%). Intra- and postoperative complications occurred in 56% and 51.7% of patients, respectively. Survival to discharge was 78.0% (71 of 91 patients), with a median hospitalization of 3.3 days (range, 1 to 12 days). Among 55 patients with follow up, 11 (20%) had complications related to thoracic trauma. Conclusions Surgical management of penetrating thoracic trauma was associated with a high survival rate despite frequent complications. Animal trauma triage is a useful prognostic indicator. Computed tomography may alter treatment plans. Clinical relevance Clinicians should anticipate higher injury severity than anticipated based on routine imaging and examination. Higher animal trauma triage scores were associated with nonsurvival and may provide useful prognostic information. Close monitoring is needed following surgery for penetrating thoracic trauma.

title: Morphometric analysis of male and female inner ear structures in Caucasian population using three-dimensional modeling and oriented bounding box.
abstract: Objectives This study aims to determine the standard morphometric structure of male and female inner ear structures in the Caucasian population by analyzing computed tomography (CT) images of 130 people without hearing or balance complaints. Methods Three-dimensional (3D) models of the semicircular canals (SC), vestibule, and cochlea were created using semi-automatic segmentation. Angles between SCs were calculated using oriented bounding boxes (OBB). Size, volume, radius of curvature, canal diameters, common crus dimensions, central bone island areas, and cochlear and vestibule volumes were measured. Results Although significant deviations from 90° on a case-by-case basis were observed in SC pairs, no statistically significant deviation from orthogonality was detected. While there was no significant difference between SC angulations, there were significant gender differences between other inner ear morphometric measurements. Conclusions This study has shown that reliable SC angulation measurements can be made on conventional CT images with the OBB method, which has not been used for this purpose before. Significant differences were found between inner ear morphometric measurements of Caucasian male and female populations.

title: Giant intracranial neurocysticercosis mimicking brain tumors: Two illustrative cases with a practical neurosurgical decision-making algorithm.
abstract: Background Giant parenchymal neurocysticercosis (NCC) is a rare Taenia solium infection that can mimic neoplasms or cystic lesions. Its appearance, mass effect, and risk of neurological deterioration may complicate diagnosis and management, especially when surgery is considered. Case description We present two cases of giant parenchymal NCC initially diagnosed as intracranial neoplasms because of radiological findings and mass effect. Both patients underwent surgery for neurological deterioration and diagnostic uncertainty. In the first case, intraoperative findings suggested NCC, later supported by response to antiparasitic therapy. In the second, frozen section and histopathology confirmed NCC, allowing modification of the oncological procedure and avoidance of extensive resection. Both patients received antiparasitic treatment and had favorable clinical outcomes. Literature review showed that surgery in giant intracranial NCC has been driven by mass effect, neurological deterioration, or diagnostic uncertainty. Conclusion Giant parenchymal NCC should be included in the differential diagnosis of large cystic intracranial lesions, especially in patients exposed to endemic regions. When findings are inconclusive and deterioration or mass effect is present, surgery may confirm diagnosis and guide further treatment. Intraoperative pathology can avoid unnecessary resection.

In the second, frozen section and histopathology confirmed NCC, allowing modification of the oncological procedure and avoidance of extensive resection. Both patients received antiparasitic treatment and had favorable clinical outcomes. Literature review showed that surgery in giant intracranial NCC has been driven by mass effect, neurological deterioration, or diagnostic uncertainty.

Conclusion

Giant parenchymal NCC should be included in the differential diagnosis of large cystic intracranial lesions, especially in patients exposed to endemic regions. When findings are inconclusive and deterioration or mass effect is present, surgery may confirm diagnosis and guide further treatment. Intraoperative pathology can avoid unnecessary resection.

title: Radiation-induced meningioma and high-grade glioma following craniospinal irradiation for medulloblastoma: a case report.
abstract: Background Cranial irradiation is known to carry the risk of late intracranial toxicities, most notably the development of secondary intracranial neoplasms. Both meningiomas and gliomas can develop as radiation-induced tumors. Radiation-induced meningiomas represent the most common secondary tumor in patients who have previously undergone cranial irradiation. Secondary gliomas are the second most common secondary tumor in patients with prior cranial radiation. Case description We present the case of a patient with a history of medulloblastoma who received craniospinal irradiation at the age of 29 years. She remained disease-free for nearly two decades until developing an occipital meningioma at the age of 53, which recurred despite surgery and radiotherapy. Eight years later, she was diagnosed with a high-grade astrocytic neoplasm within the prior radiation field. Despite additional treatment, her disease rapidly progressed, and she expired. Conclusion This case highlights the late oncogenic risk associated with prior cranial irradiation in long-term survivors and emphasizes the necessity of lifelong clinical and radiographic surveillance. Uniquely, the patient developed two distinct radiation-induced neoplasms, suggesting heterogeneous secondary tumorigenesis following radiation exposure.

title: Severe early postoperative brainstem infarction after vestibular schwannoma resection: A case report and literature review.
abstract: Background Postoperative brainstem infarction is a rare and potentially devastating complication of vestibular schwannoma resection. While symptomatic arterial narrowing is recognized in other contexts, its role in posterior fossa tumor surgery remains poorly defined. We report a case of severe brainstem infarction and analyze the diagnostic challenges in instances where definitive vascular injury could not be confirmed. Case description We report the case of a 36-year-old woman who developed severe neurological deterioration immediately after resection of a right cerebellopontine angle vestibular schwannoma. The procedure was uneventful, with no major intraoperative hemorrhage or vascular injury and minor subarachnoid blood contamination during tumor resection. Initial postoperative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), including diffusion-weighted imaging, showed no hemorrhagic or ischemic lesions; however, repeat MRI with magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) on postoperative day 1 demonstrated right midbrain and upper pontine infarction associated with mild narrowing of the right posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries. Because the vascular narrowing was modest and digital subtraction angiography, serial vascular imaging, and direct assessment of perforator involvement were unavailable, vasospasm was considered a possible but unconfirmed contributing mechanism. Alternative etiologies, including perforator injury, traction-related ischemia, microembolic phenomena, thrombosis, transient hypoperfusion, or early radiologically occult ischemia, could not be excluded. Despite intensive care management, including intravenous nimodipine, the patient developed severe persistent neurological deficits, with a Karnofsky Performance Status of 40 at 3-month follow-up. Conclusion This case highlights the diagnostic complexity of severe early postoperative brainstem infarction. Mild posterior circulation narrowing on MRA may raise suspicion for a vascular-related process, but it should not be interpreted as definitive evidence of causality in the absence of digital subtraction angiography, serial vascular imaging, or direct assessment of perforator involvement. In patients with unexplained neurological deterioration after posterior fossa surgery, early vascular imaging and broad consideration of vascular and ischemic mechanisms are essential to guide management and avoid overattribution to a single pathophysiological process.

title: Calvarial erosion secondary to epithelioid glioblastoma: A molecularly characterized case report.
abstract: Background Epithelioid glioblastoma (eGBM) is a rare, aggressive IDH-wildtype glioblastoma of children and young adults. It is typically B-Raf proto-oncogene, serine/threonine kinase (BRAF) valine-to-glutamic acid substitution at amino acid position 600 (V600E)/ cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor 2A (CDKN2A)/ cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor 2B (CDKN2B) -altered. Calvarial erosion with extracranial extension is exceptionally rare and may mimic primary calvarial or extra-axial tumors. Case description A 16-year-old girl presented with a 2-week history of headache and a new-onset generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Neuroimaging revealed a superficially located left temporal intra-axial lesion with heterogeneous enhancement, extensive vasogenic edema, focal dural enhancement, and a through-and-through temporal squamous bone defect suggesting transdural extension. The patient underwent a left temporal craniotomy and tumor resection. The temporal squama was completely eroded, and the tumor breached the dura and extended beyond the inner table, confirming extracranial spread. Gross-total resection, including involved bone and dura with reconstruction, was achieved without postoperative complications or neurological deficit. Histopathology showed eGBM, central nervous system World Health Organization grade 4, with rhabdoid features, necrosis, subpial condensation, and meningeal involvement. Molecular profiling demonstrated BRAF V600E, telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT) promoter -146C>T, CDKN2A/2B homozygous deletion, and methylthioadenosine phosphorylase (MTAP) loss, with isocitrate dehydrogenase 1 (NADP+) (IDH1)/ isocitrate dehydrogenase 2 (NADP+) (IDH2) and H3F3A wildtype, low tumor mutational burden, and microsatellite stability. Despite standard chemoradiotherapy, the patient passed away 6 months after diagnosis. Conclusion eGBM may present with calvarial erosion and surgically confirmed extracranial extension in pediatric patients. Recognition of skull defects and dural enhancement should prompt planning for en bloc resection of invaded bone and dura with reconstruction and early comprehensive molecular testing to identify actionable targets such as BRAF V600E.

title: Cervicothoracic intramedullary teratoma in a 6-year-old child: A case report.
abstract: Background Intramedullary spinal teratomas are rare, accounting for 0.1% of spinal tumors. We report the successful surgical management of an extensive mature intramedullary teratoma (C6-T6) in a 6-year-old female presenting with spastic gait. Case description Despite the absence of intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring (IONM), a T4-T6 laminoplasty and microsurgical resection were performed. Histopathology confirmed a benign cystic teratoma. Postoperatively, the patient achieved complete clinical recovery at 24 months. Conclusion This case demonstrates the feasibility of total resection for a rare pediatric intramedullary tumor in a resource-limited setting where IONM was unavailable. Furthermore, it highlights the application of laminoplasty as a useful technique for maintaining spinal stability and facilitating recovery.

title: Efficacy of arterial spin labeling magnetic resonance perfusion in differentiating recurrent or residual high-grade glioma from post-treatment changes: A retrospective hospital-based study.
abstract: Background Differentiating true recurrence or residual disease from treatment-related changes in patients treated for high-grade glioma (HGG) remains a major diagnostic challenge, because both produce contrast- enhancing lesions on conventional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Arterial spin labeling (ASL) is a non- contrast perfusion technique that quantifies cerebral blood flow using magnetically labeled arterial blood water as an endogenous tracer. We evaluated the efficacy of ASL magnetic resonance (MR) perfusion in distinguishing recurrent or residual HGG from post-treatment changes. Methods This retrospective hospital-based study analysed 71 patients (>18 years) with histopathologically proven GRADE 3 and 4 GLIOMA who had received post-operative radiotherapy and/or chemotherapy and presented with a focal enhancing lesion. All had undergone 3.0 T MRI, including three-dimensional pseudo- continuous ASL. Relative cerebral blood flow (rCBF) and qualitative perfusion pattern (red/hyperperfusion vs. blue/hypoperfusion) were correlated against a reference standard of histopathology ( n = 22) or a predefined composite clinico-radiological standard based on ≥6 months of serial follow-up imaging ( n = 49); tumors were classified per the World Health Organization 2021 central nervous system classification. Diagnostic performance and a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) cutoff were derived. Results Recurrence/residual disease was confirmed in 21 patients (29.6%) and post-treatment change in 50 (70.4%). Mean rCBF was significantly higher in recurrence (2.33 ± 0.602) than in post-treatment change (1.058 ± 0.302; Mann-Whitney U, p < 0.0001). The red perfusion pattern was seen in 20 of 21 recurrences and only 1 of 50 post-treatment cases ( p < 0.0001). ASL achieved sensitivity 95.0%, specificity 98.0%, positive predictive value 95.0%, negative predictive value 98.0% and accuracy 97.1%, with almost-perfect agreement with the reference standard (κ = 0.93). ROC analysis yielded an area under the curve of 0.911 with an optimal rCBF cutoff of 2.04 (sensitivity 90.0%, specificity 98.0%). Diagnostic performance was comparable in the histopathology-confirmed subgroup (accuracy 95.5%) and the follow-up-confirmed subgroup (accuracy 98.0%). Conclusion ASL MR perfusion is a reliable, reproducible and contrast-free technique with excellent accuracy for differentiating recurrent or residual HGG from post-treatment changes, and is well suited to longitudinal surveillance where repeated gadolinium administration is undesirable.

title: Partially thrombosed anterior communicating artery aneurysm mimicking a suprasellar tumor: Microsurgical reconstruction after aneurysmotomy and ultrasonic thrombectomy.
abstract: Background Partially thrombosed intracranial aneurysms are uncommon lesions that may mimic intracranial neoplasms because of their heterogeneous radiological appearance and mass effect. When associated with broad-neck morphology and incorporation of adjacent vessels, treatment may require complex microsurgical reconstruction. Case description A 69-year-old woman with hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus underwent investigation after a mild traumatic brain injury. Initial computed tomography (CT) demonstrated a suprasellar lesion suggestive of a neoplastic process. CT angiography and digital subtraction angiography subsequently revealed a partially thrombosed anterior communicating artery aneurysm measuring 19 × 10 mm with a 6.6-mm neck and incorporation of the right A2 segment into the aneurysm neck. The patient underwent elective microsurgical treatment through a right fronto-orbital approach. Following temporary vascular control, aneurysmotomy and ultrasonic thrombectomy using the Clarity ® system were performed. Definitive reconstruction required sequential placement of eight permanent clips while preserving both A2 segments. Intraoperative fluorescein angiography confirmed adequate vessel patency. The patient remained neurologically intact, with a modified Rankin Scale score of 0 at 90-day follow-up. Conclusion Partially thrombosed anterior communicating artery aneurysms may mimic suprasellar tumors and represent an important diagnostic challenge. In selected cases with branch incorporation, broad-neck morphology, and significant thrombotic burden, microsurgical reconstruction remains a safe and effective treatment strategy. Aneurysmotomy combined with ultrasonic thrombectomy facilitates visualization of the true aneurysm neck and may assist complex clip reconstruction.

title: Hyperspectral imaging and machine learning in brain tumor surgery: Current evidence, clinical applications, and future directions.
abstract: Background Brain tumor surgery aims to achieve maximal safe resection while preserving neurological function; however, accurate intraoperative discrimination between tumor tissue and normal brain remains a major challenge. Hyperspectral imaging (HSI) has emerged as a promising label-free optical imaging modality that provides quantitative information on tissue biochemical and physiological characteristics. The integration of machine learning (ML) has further enhanced its potential for automated tissue classification and real-time intraoperative decision support. This narrative review summarizes the current evidence regarding HSI and ML in brain tumor surgery, highlighting technological principles, clinical applications, current limitations, and future directions. Methods This narrative review was based on a comprehensive literature search of PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar to identify studies evaluating the application of HSI and artificial intelligence (AI) in brain tumor surgery. The search strategy included combinations of the keywords " hyperspectral imaging ," " brain tumor ," " glioma ," " machine learning ," " deep learning ," " artificial intelligence ," and " neurosurgery ." Priority was given to peer-reviewed original research articles, narrative and systematic reviews, and clinically relevant investigations describing the technical development, intraoperative application, and translational potential of HSI in neurooncology. Landmark studies that established the foundations of HSI, together with recent publications reflecting advances in ML and clinical implementation, were preferentially included to provide both historical context and contemporary perspectives. Manual screening of the reference lists of key publications was performed to identify additional relevant studies. As a narrative review, this manuscript was intended to provide a critical overview of current evidence rather than a systematic assessment of the literature. Consequently, no formal study selection algorithm, quality assessment tool, or quantitative meta-analysis was performed. Results Current evidence indicates that HSI combined with ML enables accurate intraoperative tissue classification, improved tumor margin delineation, and emerging molecular characterization, including prediction of isocitrate dehydrogenase mutation status. Deep learning approaches generally outperform conventional ML techniques by integrating spectral and spatial information. title: Biportal endoscopic foramen magnum decompression and C1 posterior arch resection for Chiari malformation type I: Technical note.
abstract: Background Chiari malformation type I is commonly treated with posterior fossa decompression and C1 posterior arch resection to restore cerebrospinal fluid flow at the craniocervical junction. Although open microsurgical decompression remains the standard approach, minimally invasive techniques may reduce soft-tissue disruption and postoperative morbidity. Biportal endoscopy may provide adequate visualization and instrument maneuverability at the craniocervical junction. Methods A 60-year-old female presented with a 2-year history of progressive Valsalva-induced occipital headache and bilateral upper-limb paresthesias. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a 5.7 mm descent of the cerebellar tonsils without syringomyelia. The patient underwent biportal endoscopic suboccipital decompression and partial C1 posterior arch resection using a 30° endoscope, high-speed burrs, Kerrison rongeurs, radiofrequency, and continuous saline irrigation. No dural opening or duraplasty was performed. Results The operative time was 135 min, with minimal blood loss and no intraoperative complications. Postoperative CT confirmed adequate osseous decompression, including a 21 × 22 mm suboccipital craniectomy and a 10 mm C1 posterior arch resection. Postoperatively, the patient improved clinically without complications and was discharged on postoperative day 2. Conclusion Biportal endoscopic foramen magnum decompression with C1 posterior arch resection appears feasible in selected adult patients with Chiari malformation type I.

title: Parasitic rachipagus associated with complex spinal dysraphism: A case report.
abstract: Background Rachipagus is an exceptionally rare form of parasitic conjoined twinning characterized by dorsal fusion along the vertebral column and is frequently associated with spinal dysraphism. The coexistence of complex dysraphic anomalies and mature teratomatous differentiation is exceedingly uncommon and may complicate the distinction between parasitic rachipagus and mature teratoma. We report a rare case highlighting the diagnostic challenge and surgical management of this unusual entity. Case description An 8-month-old girl presented with a progressively enlarging congenital midline dorsal mass containing paired rudimentary limb-like appendages. Neurological examination was normal. Computed tomography demonstrated thoracolumbar spinal dysraphism, while magnetic resonance imaging revealed lipomyelomeningocele, type II split cord malformation (diastematomyelia), and tethered cord. Complete excision of the parasitic mass with surgical repair of the associated spinal dysraphism was successfully performed. Histopathological examination demonstrated mature adipose, fibrous, cartilaginous, and osseous tissues consistent with mature teratomatous differentiation. However, the characteristic clinical morphology, radiological findings, and intraoperative findings supported the diagnosis of parasitic rachipagus. The postoperative course was complicated by wound dehiscence requiring revision surgery. At 1-year follow-up, the patient remained neurologically intact with preserved bladder and bowel function. Conclusion This case expands the limited literature on parasitic rachipagus associated with complex spinal dysraphism. Mature teratomatous differentiation does not exclude the diagnosis of parasitic rachipagus, which should be established through integration of clinical, radiological, intraoperative, and histopathological findings rather than histopathology alone. Complete excision combined with appropriate neurosurgical management can achieve favorable long-term outcomes.

title: Intraoperative ultrasonography after dural closure for early detection of bleeding in cranial surgery.
abstract: Background Postoperative hematoma is a serious complication of cranial surgery and may require reoperation. This study evaluated intraoperative ultrasonography (US) performed immediately after dural closure and before bone replacement for detecting bleeding within the surgical cavity and confirming hemostasis. Methods This retrospective single-center observational study included 192 patients who underwent cranial surgery between January 2024 and October 2025. B-mode US was performed after dural closure in all cases. Postoperative brain computed tomography (CT) was obtained within 6 h. Intraoperative findings, postoperative imaging, and reoperation requirements were analyzed. Hematomas causing mass effect or neurological deterioration and requiring evacuation were considered clinically significant. Results Intraoperative US detected bleeding in 5 patients (2.6%). All underwent immediate re-exploration and additional hemostasis during the same surgical session, and none had hematoma on postoperative CT. Postoperative imaging demonstrated hematoma in 24 patients (12.5%) with negative intraoperative findings; 22 were managed conservatively and 2 (1.0%) required reoperation. These postoperative hematomas may have developed after dural closure during the interval before imaging. The overall reoperation rate was 1.0%. Conclusion US after dural closure is a safe and practical method for confirming hemostasis and detecting bleeding before completion of cranial surgery. Although it cannot predict small delayed hematomas, it may support immediate intraoperative intervention before wound closure.

title: Intraoperative detection of a false-negative facial motor evoked potential by direct facial nerve stimulation during vestibular schwannoma surgery: A case report.
abstract: Background False-negative transcranial facial motor evoked potential (FMEP) findings have previously been recognized retrospectively through discrepancies between preserved intraoperative FMEPs and postoperative facial palsy. To the best of our knowledge, no previous report has demonstrated a false-negative FMEP finding intraoperatively using direct facial nerve stimulation. We report the only false-negative case encountered among more than 100 cases monitored with FMEPs at our institution. Case description A 58-year-old man with a right Koos Grade II vestibular schwannoma underwent near-total resection with transcranial FMEP monitoring, free-running electromyography, and intermittent direct facial nerve stimulation. Reproducible FMEPs were obtained only with double-train stimulation and remained stable throughout tumor removal, with amplitudes never decreasing below 50% of baseline. Direct stimulation initially elicited stable responses at 0.4 mA at all tested sites. During the final stage of resection, stimulation at the internal auditory canal fundus produced a robust compound muscle action potential at 0.4 mA, whereas cisternal stimulation produced no response at 0.4 mA and only a minimal response at 0.7 mA. This discrepancy demonstrated severe segmental facial nerve conduction impairment despite preserved FMEPs. Postoperatively, House-Brackmann Grade V facial palsy developed and improved to Grade II by 6 months. Conclusion To the best of our knowledge, this is the first reported case in which direct facial nerve stimulation identified a false-negative FMEP finding intraoperatively rather than retrospectively from postoperative facial palsy. Serial direct stimulation at multiple facial nerve segments should be integrated with FMEP monitoring to detect occult conduction impairment and guide safe tumor resection.

title: Cerebellar hydatid cyst in an elderly woman: Case report and literature review.
abstract: Background Intracranial hydatid disease is an uncommon manifestation of cystic echinococcosis, accounting for only a small proportion of all cases of hydatid disease. Cerebellar involvement is exceptionally rare, with most reported cases occurring in pediatric patients and involving the supratentorial compartment. Consequently, cerebellar hydatid cysts represent a diagnostic challenge because their clinical and radiological features overlap with those of other cystic lesions of the posterior fossa. Case description A 68-year-old female presented with a several-month history of progressively worsening pulsatile headache, nausea, vomiting, vertigo, visual symptoms, and gait instability. Neurological examination revealed gait ataxia with right-sided lateralization. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a well-circumscribed multilobulated cystic lesion within the right cerebellar hemisphere measuring approximately 19 × 31 × 18 mm, characterized by thin internal septations and mild peripheral enhancement without an identifiable mural nodule. The radiological differential diagnosis included neoplastic, infectious, and parasitic lesions of the posterior fossa. The patient underwent suboccipital craniectomy with gross-total microsurgical excision of the lesion without intraoperative rupture of the cyst capsule. Histopathological examination demonstrated a laminated acellular cyst wall containing multiple protoscolices and refractile hooklets, confirming the diagnosis of hydatid cyst (cystic echinococcosis). Postoperative imaging confirmed complete lesion removal without hemorrhagic or hydrocephalic complications. The patient experienced progressive neurological improvement and was discharged in stable condition. Conclusion Cerebellar hydatid cysts are exceptionally rare lesions that should be considered in the differential diagnosis of cystic posterior fossa masses, particularly in endemic regions. Histopathological confirmation remains essential for definitive diagnosis, whereas complete surgical excision without cyst rupture remains the cornerstone of treatment. The advanced age of our patient further emphasizes the unusual nature of this presentation.

title: HRCT-Based Three-Dimensional Morphometric Analysis of the External Auditory Canal for Transcanal Surgical Planning and Navigation.
abstract: To establish a preliminary pathway-planning framework for continuum robotic navigation within the external auditory canal (EAC) by reconstructing the three-dimensional (3D) centerline and quantifying key anatomical parameters, including curvature index, volume, surface area, and canal dimensions, using high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT). A retrospective study was conducted in 75 adults (103 ears; 52 male and 51 female ears; mean age, 46.55 ± 12.37 years) who underwent temporal bone HRCT with a slice thickness of 0.67 mm. Three-dimensional reconstruction and centerline extraction of the EAC were performed using 3D Slicer software. Morphological parameters, including EAC length, mean radius, volume, surface area, and curvature index, were measured. Statistical analyses were performed using parametric or non-parametric tests according to data distribution. The mean EAC length was 29.92 ± 2.69 mm, mean radius was 3.29 ± 0.36 mm, volume was 1020.34 ± 207.64 mm3, surface area was 688.61 ± 97.81 mm2, and curvature index was 1.07 ± 0.04. Male participants exhibited significantly larger EAC dimensions than female participants, including greater volume (1082.79 vs. 956.66 mm3), surface area (725.12 vs. 651.38 mm2), and length (30.79 vs. 29.04 mm; all P < 0.05). Right-sided EACs demonstrated larger volume (1028.37 vs. 954.30 mm3) and greater radius (3.32 vs. 3.20 mm) than left-sided EACs (P < 0.05). EAC volume showed a strong positive correlation with radius (r = 0.904) and a moderate negative correlation with length (r = -0.341), suggesting two anatomical phenotypes: "slender" canals characterized by greater length and smaller radius, and "robust" canals characterized by shorter length and larger radius. This study presents a preliminary anatomical framework for continuum robotic navigation within the EAC based on centerline coordinates derived from 3D HRCT reconstruction. Quantitative morphometric parameters, including curvature index and canal radius, may provide important reference data for the design, validation, and trajectory planning of flexible robotic systems. The proposed methodology may also support future development of individualized transcanal surgical navigation and minimally invasive otologic interventions.

title: Diagnostic Musculoskeletal Ultrasound in the Evaluation of the Subacromial Bursa.
abstract: The subacromial and subdeltoid bursa commonly communicate and, for all intents and purposes, function as a single bursa. The subacromial bursa lies between the supraspinatus and the acromion process, while the subdeltoid bursa is the lateral extension of the subacromial bursa. These bursae function to limit frictional forces between the various structures. These bursae can become irritated and inflamed when they are impinged between the greater tubercle of the humerus and the acromion and/or the coracoacromial ligament when one lifts the shoulder into elevation and internal rotation. It is difficult to determine whether the bursa, the supraspinatus tendon, or both are irritated when diagnosing shoulder pain. An accurate diagnosis of bursitis is essential for appropriate treatment planning and optimizing patient outcomes. Diagnostic musculoskeletal ultrasound (MSKUS) has become a widely used imaging modality for assessing several shoulder pathologies. It offers a portable, real-time, and cost-effective alternative that is gaining traction in rehabilitation and sports medicine settings. MSKUS has emerged as a valuable, non-invasive imaging modality for evaluating shoulder bursal tissue. This manuscript will review the utility of MSKUS in evaluating the quality, size, and sonographic features of subacromial and subdeltoid bursal tissue, as well as the clinical implications for professionals in the rehabilitation field. By integrating MSKUS into clinical practice, providers can improve diagnostic accuracy, enhance diagnostic confidence, monitor healing progression, and guide rehabilitation strategies to achieve optimal patient outcomes for those with shoulder bursal injuries.

title: Baseline Brain Abscess Volume as a Predictor of Repeat Surgery: A Prospective Cohort Study.
abstract: Objective To evaluate whether baseline brain abscess volume predicts the need for repeat surgical intervention within 90 days after the index procedure. Study design An observational study. Place and Duration of the Study: Department of Neurosurgery, Medical Teaching Institution/Mardan Medical Complex, Mardan, Pakistan, from January 2024 to September 2025. Methodology Consecutive patients with a brain abscess confirmed by contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) who underwent surgical intervention and completed at least 90 days of follow-up were included. Patients with epidural or subdural empyema, fungal or tuberculous abscesses, and those managed non-surgically were excluded. Baseline abscess volume was estimated using the ellipsoid (ABC/2) method on contrast-enhanced imaging. The primary outcome was repeat surgical intervention within 90 days of the index surgery. Baseline abscess volume was compared between the groups, and logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses were performed. Results Fifty-three patients (mean age 28.9 ± 17.9 years; 64.2% male) were included. Fourteen patients (26.4%) required repeat surgical intervention within 90 days. Baseline abscess volume was significantly higher in patients requiring re-intervention compared with those who did not (28.55 ± 7.03 cm3 versus 21.18 ± 8.06 cm3, p = 0.004). In univariable logistic regression, the odds ratio (OR) for baseline volume was 1.128 per cm3; the 95% confidence interval (CI) was 1.032-1.234 (p = 0.008). ROC analysis demonstrated acceptable discrimination, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.752. Conclusion Larger baseline brain abscess volume was associated with an increased likelihood of repeat surgical intervention within 90 days. Baseline abscess volume may serve as a useful adjunct for early risk stratification; however, larger multicentre studies are required for validation. Key words Brain abscess, Abscess volume, Neurosurgery, Repeat surgery, Prognosis.

An observational study. Place and Duration of the Study: Department of Neurosurgery, Medical Teaching Institution/Mardan Medical Complex, Mardan, Pakistan, from January 2024 to September 2025.

Methodology

Consecutive patients with a brain abscess confirmed by contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) who underwent surgical intervention and completed at least 90 days of follow-up were included. Patients with epidural or subdural empyema, fungal or tuberculous abscesses, and those managed non-surgically were excluded. Baseline abscess volume was estimated using the ellipsoid (ABC/2) method on contrast-enhanced imaging. The primary outcome was repeat surgical intervention within 90 days of the index surgery. Baseline abscess volume was compared between the groups, and logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses were performed.

Results

Fifty-three patients (mean age 28.9 ± 17.9 years; 64.2% male) were included. Fourteen patients (26.4%) required repeat surgical intervention within 90 days. Baseline abscess volume was significantly higher in patients requiring re-intervention compared with those who did not (28.55 ± 7.03 cm3 versus 21.18 ± 8.06 cm3, p = 0.004). In univariable logistic regression, the odds ratio (OR) for baseline volume was 1.128 per cm3; the 95% confidence interval (CI) was 1.032-1.234 (p = 0.008). ROC analysis demonstrated acceptable discrimination, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.752.

Conclusion

Larger baseline brain abscess volume was associated with an increased likelihood of repeat surgical intervention within 90 days. Baseline abscess volume may serve as a useful adjunct for early risk stratification; however, larger multicentre studies are required for validation.

Key words

Brain abscess, Abscess volume, Neurosurgery, Repeat surgery, Prognosis.

title: Unusually long-term survival in a feline with Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP-like) disease without ACVR1 gene mutations.
abstract: Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP) is a rare genetic disorder characterized by heterotopic ossification within the connective tissues that affects the muscles, tendons, and joint capsules. It is an autosomal inherited condition caused by mutations in ACVR1, which is associated with ectopic bone formation. A 5-year-old neutered male outdoor cat, clinically diagnosed with FOP-like disease three years prior, presented for follow-up evaluation owing to an unusually long survival. New blood samples and radiographs were obtained to assess disease progression and investigate the patient's genetic background, with the aim of describing this case's clinical evolution and new genetic findings, and sharing the patient's exceptionally rare long-term survival with peers. Radiographic evaluation revealed severe progression of osteoarticular disease, partial to total resorption of previously deposited mineralized tissue, marked hypertrophy of the limb musculature, and an overall increase in radiographic muscular density. Genetic analysis confirmed the absence of the ACVR1 mutation. This is the first reported case of FOP-like disease in a cat in Uruguay, with no ACVR1 mutation detected and an unusually long survival of more than three years after diagnosis.

title: Anatomopathological features of uterine tube adenoma in a female dog.
abstract: The uterine tube is part of the female reproductive system responsible for connecting the ovary to the uterus. Neoplasms originating from the uterine tube are rare in both animals and humans, with few reports available in the veterinary literature. A 7-year-old mixed-breed bitch was presented with clinical signs of lethargy, weight gain, and abdominal distension. Ultrasonography and computed tomography revealed a large abdominal mass. The patient underwent exploratory laparotomy for surgical excision of the mass, which was found adhered to the right ovary. Grossly, the mass measured 27.5 × 22.5 × 5.5 cm, had a soft consistency, irregular contours, reddish coloration, and a papillary appearance. Histopathological evaluation revealed well-differentiated papillary projections lined by ciliated columnar epithelial cells, with positive expression of estrogen and progesterone receptors and low Ki-67 labeling index, supporting the diagnosis of uterine tube adenoma. Although these tumors may reach considerable dimensions, they are generally associated with a favorable prognosis. In the present case, the diagnosis was established based on the correlation of clinical, morphological, and histopathological findings.

title: Comparison of Commercial Fixed and In-House Tissue-Based and Live Cell-Based Assays for the Detection of Common Neuronal Surface Autoantibodies.
abstract: Autoimmune encephalitis (AIE) is diagnosed through detection of neuronal-surface antibodies (Abs) in serum and/or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Commercial biochip-based cell-based assay (CBA) using fixed cells and in-house CBAs using live cells may give incongruent results. We aimed to shed further light on features of AIE patients with discordant CBA results to establish factors related with diagnosis and treatment-response. A total of 45 patients found positive for N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR), leucine rich glioma inactivated 1 (LGI1), contactin-associated protein-like 2 (CASPR2)-Abs on routine screening done with fixed-CBA, were further tested using in-house live-CBA and tissue-based assay (TBA). Serum neurofilament light chain (NFL) levels were measured and response to immunotherapy was assessed in a follow-up period of 36.9±7.8 months. Thirty patients who were positive on both fixed and live-CBA/TBA, showed trends towards displaying limbic symptoms and EEG/MRI features suggestive of AIE. By contrast, most of the 15 patients with only fixed-CBA positivity failed to fulfill AIE criteria. Positivity on live CBA/TBA did not predict response to immunotherapy or coexisting cancers. Some patients in the fixed-CBA positive category exhibited features highly suggestive of autoimmune encephalopathy and elevated NFL levels. Lower disease severity, presence of viral prodromal findings, absence of autonomic symptoms and facial dyskinesia were associated with treatment response. Live CBA/TBA demonstrated higher diagnostic accuracy than fixed cell-based assays and substantially reduced the likelihood of false-positive antibody detection. Positive live-CBA/TBA results strongly coincide with definite AIE criteria. However, live CBA and NFL results fail to predict response to immunotherapy and identify coexisting cancers. This is putatively because some patients in the live-CBA/TBA negative category likely have immunotherapy-responsive neuroinflammatory disorders.

title: Predictors of Long-Term Disability in Multiple Sclerosis: Up to 10 Years of Follow-up in a Real-World Cohort Study.
abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) shows substantial interindividual variability in clinical course, yet early predictors of long-term disability remain incompletely defined. This retrospective cohort study aimed to investigate the impact of demographic characteristics, family history, comorbidities, and initial clinical and radiological features on disability progression over time. We retrospectively evaluated MS patients with respect to initial clinical presentation, relapse frequency, baseline magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) characteristics, early radiological progression, and acute relapse treatment. We also examined the association between recovery after the first relapse and long-term disability outcomes, assessed at years 1, 2, 5, and 10. Of the 346 patients, 69% were female, and the mean age was 43.4±11.0 years. Most patients had relapsing-onset disease (96%). Sensory symptoms and optic neuritis were the most common presenting symptoms, while motor and cerebellar onset were significantly associated with higher EDSS scores at years 1, 2, and 5. Relapse activity within the first year after diagnosis correlated positively with fifth-year EDSS, whereas relapse frequency prior to diagnosis showed no association with long-term progression. Neither the presence nor the number of contrast-enhancing MRI lesions predicted disability progression. Early clinical phenotype and early treatment response carry important prognostic information in MS. Motor or cerebellar onset, incomplete early recovery, and persistent relapse activity after diagnosis identify patients at higher risk for disability accumulation. Spinal cord involvement was the only MRI parameter associated with 10-year EDSS.

title: Outcome Prediction After [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA I&T in Metastatic Castration-Resistant Prostate Cancer: External Validation of a [ 68 Ga]Ga-PSMA-11 PET-Based Model with [ 18 F]F-Flotufolastat.
abstract: 177 Lu-prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA)-targeted radiopharmaceutical therapy is an established treatment for metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, though responses vary. A prognostic model using [ 68 Ga]Ga-PSMA-11 PET-derived parameters was developed to predict therapy outcomes. This retrospective analysis validates the model in an independent cohort imaged with [ 18 F]F-flotufolastat ([ 18 F]rhPSMA-7.3 PET) before [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA I&T. Methods: In total, 174 consecutive patients treated with [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA I&T at a single center were included in this analysis. The Cox proportional hazards models for overall survival (OS) and prostate-specific antigen (PSA) progression-free survival (PFS) and the logistic regression model for PSA response, as proposed in the prognostic model, were applied to our validation data. Model performance was evaluated using the Harrell concordance index (C-index) and calibration plots. OS, PSA-PFS, and PSA response were reported with median values and 95% CI, as well as stratified by published cutoff values into low- and high-risk groups. Results: The estimated OS probabilities were 60% (95% CI, 53%-68%) at 12 mo and 40% (95% CI, 33%-49%) at 18 mo. Our validation yielded a C-index of 0.71 (95% CI, 0.67-0.76) for OS prediction compared with a C-index of 0.72 (95% CI, 0.68-0.76) in the validation cohort. For PSA-PFS, the estimated probabilities were 56% (95% CI, 49%-65%) at 3 mo and 34% (95% CI, 27%-42%) at 6 mo, with a C-index of 0.62 (95% CI, 0.57-0.67) compared with a C-index of 0.71 (95% CI, 0.68-0.74) in the validation data. Low-risk patients had significantly longer OS (21.8 vs. 11.6 mo, P < 0.0001) and PSA-PFS (6.9 vs. 2.9 mo, P = 0.003) than did high-risk patients. The prognostic PSA response model showed slightly worse discrimination in our cohort (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, 0.71; 95% CI, 0.63-0.79) than with the validation data (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve; 95% CI, 0.78, 0.68-0.88). Conclusion: Our results indicate accuracy similar to that of the prognostic model for prediction of OS and PSA-PFS and for PSA response in an independent patient population undergoing [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA I&T radiopharmaceutical therapy with [ 18 F]F-flotufolastat instead of [ 68 Ga]Ga-PSMA-11.

title: Multimodal Visual Question Answering System for Survival Prognosis in PSMA-Targeted Radiopharmaceutical Therapy.
abstract: Large language models show great promise for clinical decision support but generally lack medical imaging integration. Therefore, vision-language models have been proposed, but there is little evidence on their performance, particularly compared with conventional machine learning. Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA)-targeted radiopharmaceutical therapy is a well-established treatment for metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC), but it is still not known which patients will be good long-term responders. Therefore, this study proposes a physician-inspired visual question answering (VQA) framework that emulates the structured integration of PSMA-directed imaging and clinical data used in routine clinical assessment for overall survival prognostication. Methods: As a proof of concept, we conducted a retrospective, multicenter study across 2 academic institutions that included 110 patients with mCRPC who were treated with either [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA I&T or [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA-617. Our VQA approach incorporates a 3-dimensional image encoder, the domain-specific language model RadBERT, and a cross-modal transformer to process baseline and interim (after 2 cycles) PET and SPECT images, clinical data, and clinical query. The model was trained to predict 24-mo survival, and performance was compared with state-of-the-art approaches. External validation was performed with the [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA-617 cohort. Results: The VQA model outperformed all state-of-the-art approaches while showing accuracy comparable to the query-free attention multimodal fusion model. Specifically, it achieved 81.8% accuracy (95% CI, 0.52-0.95) when integrating SPECT or PET images with prostate-specific antigen measurements. External validation of the VQA showed 71.9% accuracy (95% CI, 0.53-0.86) after few-shot fine-tuning, with further improvement over all state-of-the-art approaches in survival stratification. The VQA approach showed the closest calibration with the ground-truth survival distribution, with no significant differences observed (log-rank test, P = 0.76). Receiver operating characteristic analysis showed the highest area under the curve (0.75) among the evaluated models. Together, these findings suggest that the VQA approach demonstrated adaptability across different PSMA ligands while maintaining slightly improved yet comparable overall survival prognostic performance. Conclusion: By adopting a physician-inspired assessment workflow, the VQA framework shows advantages in integrating imaging and laboratory data for clinical decision support compared with conventional machine learning. The preliminary results indicate that VQA-based approaches warrant future evaluation for survival prognostication in patients with mCRPC who are receiving PSMA radiopharmaceutical therapy.

title: Toward a Biopsy-Free Diagnosis of Prostate Cancer: Potential of Combined 18 F-Flotufolastat PSMA PET and mpMRI.
abstract: This retrospective analysis aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of 18 F-flotufolastat PET/MRI for the detection of clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa). The primary objective of the study was to assess the proportion of patients for whom a prostate biopsy could be safely circumvented by combining the Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System (PI-RADS) from multiparametric MRI and quantitative data from PET. Methods: This study included 79 patients with suspicion of csPCa based on elevated prostate-specific antigen (>4 ng/mL) who underwent 18 F-flotufolastat PET/MRI before biopsy or surgical resection of the prostate. Analytic methods included receiver operating characteristic analysis, logistic regression, and threshold-based evaluation of PI-RADS and of SUV max Imaging findings were compared against histopathology. Results: csPCa (International Society of Urological Pathology grade group ≥ 2) was confirmed in 42 patients, whereas histopathology excluded csPCa in 37 patients. The combination of PI-RADS and SUV max resulted in an area under the curve (AUC) of 87.1%, outperforming PI-RADS alone (AUC of 75.2%) and SUV max alone (AUC of 80.7); however, differences were not statistically significant. A PI-RADS score of at least 3 and 18 F-flotufolastat PET showed comparable sensitivity (0.90 vs. 0.91) and specificity (0.42 vs. 0.32) in the detection of csPCa, when applying a low SUV max threshold (>4.5). Using a high SUV max threshold (>10.0) increased the specificity of 18 F-flotufolastat PET to 100%. Furthermore, combined PET/MRI increased the number of patients for whom csPCa can be reliably diagnosed to 28%, as well as increasing to 29% the number of patients for whom csPCa can be ruled out with a very high degree of certainty. Conclusion: This retrospective analysis suggests that prostate-specific membrane antigen PET/MRI can stratify patients with suspected prostate cancer into 3 groups: one with a very high likelihood of csPCa who may undergo definitive therapy without biopsy, one with a very low risk for csPCa who may not require biopsy, and an indeterminate group who still need biopsy. Overall, in our cohort, prostate biopsy would have been avoided in 57% of patients. Therefore, there is an urgent need for prospective studies on prostate-specific membrane antigen PET/MRI to reduce the number of unnecessary biopsies in men with suspected prostate cancer.

title: [ 68 Ga]Ga-SSO120 PET/CT Imaging in Pediatric Patients with Neuroblastoma: Biodistribution and Whole-Body Radiation Dosimetry.
abstract: The clinical standard for neuroblastoma detection is based on targeting the norepinephrine transporter with [ 123 I]MIBG, which has several challenges. Imaging the somatostatin receptor (SSTR) is a strong alternative. In contrast to standard DOTATATE, SSTR antagonist imaging with [ 68 Ga]Ga-satoreotide trizoxetan ([ 68 Ga]-SSO120) can potentially improve lesion detection as it targets both active and inactive SSTRs. We present the biodistribution and radiation exposure results of [ 68 Ga]Ga-SSO120 PET/CT imaging in pediatric patients with neuroblastoma. Methods: Patients age 3-7 y with stage 4 neuroblastoma received 2 MBq/kg of [ 68 Ga]Ga-SSO120, followed by a 60-min dynamic scan and a static PET/CT scan. SUV normalized to lean body mass (SUL max , SUL mean , SUL peak ) and time-activity curves were measured for suspected lesions and various tissue compartments. Tumor-to-liver and tumor-to-blood pool ratios were calculated. Radiation doses to various organs and the total-body effective dose were computed. Results: Five patients underwent dynamic [ 68 Ga]Ga-SSO120 PET/CT scanning, with a total of 17 neuroblastoma lesions. The median administered activity was 2.5 MBq/kg (range, 2.1-2.8 MBq/kg). At 60 min postinjection, the median tumor SUL max and SUL peak were 4.28 (range, 1.89-18.07) and 2.71 (range, 1.23-14.77), respectively, and the median tumor-to-liver ratio was 4.05. The highest exposure was in the bladder (22.3 ± 4.3 μSv/MBq). The effective dose was 0.088 ± 0.014 mSv/MBq. Conclusion: [ 68 Ga]Ga-SSO120 PET/CT was safe in pediatric patients with neuroblastoma, with a low effective radiation dose, and detected neuroblastoma lesions with a good target-to-noise ratio. Image acquisition at 30 and 60 min postinjection seemed equivalent.

title: Theranostic Approach Using Radioiodinated Trimethoprim Targeting E. coli Dihydrofolate Reductase in Engineered Cells.
abstract: Radiopharmaceutical therapy (RPT) has re-emerged as a potent approach for targeting tumors, particularly for the treatment of neuroendocrine tumors and prostate cancer expressing the somatostatin and prostate-specific membrane antigen receptors, respectively. In addition to endogenously expressed proteins specific for these cancers, RPT has been explored using synthetic, engineered expression of proteins in tumor tissues. An early example of this was the use of sodium iodide symporter delivered to tumors using viral vectors, which were subsequently treated with [ 131 I]NaI. This approach is complicated by the natural uptake in human tissues that express sodium iodide symporter (e.g., the thyroid). However, given the rapid acceleration of gene and cell therapies, expansion and re-exploration of the synthetic, genetically engineered RPT paradigm is warranted. This is especially true for RPT, which can be coupled with PET companion imaging agents. Methods: Here, we developed a β-emitter radiotherapeutic probe, radioiodinated trimethoprim ([ 131 I]I-TMP), and evaluated its therapeutic potential. In addition, we developed [ 124/125 I]I-TMP radiotracers for uptake and imaging studies. The selective cytotoxicity of [ 131 I]I-TMP toward E. coli dihydrofolate reductase (eDHFR)-expressing cells was evaluated using time- and dose-dependent responses. Biodistribution was characterized in healthy mice followed by small-animal PET/CT studies using a tumor xenograft model and [ 124 I]I-TMP. Finally, the eDHFR synthetic RPT approach was applied in murine cancer models to evaluate its cytotoxicity in tumors. Results: Radioiodinated trimethoprim radiotracers ([ 131/125/124 I]I-TMP) exhibited selective uptake in eDHFR-positive tumors both in vitro and in vivo. Small-animal imaging with [ 124 I]I-TMP demonstrated specific retention in I45-eDHFR tumors with negligible background signals. A dose-dependent and time-dependent cytotoxic effect was observed selectively in eDHFR cell lines. Furthermore, targeted treatment with [ 131 I]I-TMP led to a significant reduction in tumor volume expressing eDHFR compared with wild-type tumors or untreated controls. Conclusion: This synthetic RPT approach shows promise for future applications in targeted cancer therapies and genetic medicine, particularly in the realm of theranostic strategies that integrate trimethoprim-based companion imaging and radiotherapy for the treatment of cancer.

title: End-to-End PET/CT Interpretation and Quantification with an LLM-Orchestrated AI Agent: A Real-World Pilot Study.
abstract: Although deep learning models have improved individual PET analysis, image processing, and quantification tasks, end-to-end automation from raw DICOM data to quantitative clinical reporting remains limited, particularly in heterogeneous real-world settings. Methods: As a proof-of-concept, an autonomous large language model (LLM)-orchestrated multitool agent for end-to-end PET/CT interpretation was developed. A reasoning-based, text-based LLM selected appropriate series from raw DICOM, coordinated registration and SUV conversion, invoked segmentation and detection tools, generated maximum-intensity projections, called a vision-enabled LLM for interpretation, and synthesized structured draft reports. The system was retrospectively evaluated in 170 patients undergoing baseline [ 18 F]FDG PET/CT for lung cancer staging, with clinical reports serving as the reference standard. Results: The agent successfully completed the full end-to-end workflow from raw DICOM selection to structured draft report generation without human intervention in all 170 examinations. Primary tumor detection achieved 100% sensitivity. For nodal involvement, sensitivity was 84.8% and specificity was 39.4%, whereas distant metastasis detection showed 70.2% sensitivity and 65.0% specificity. Discrepancy analysis of 58 nodal and 57 metastatic mismatch cases revealed systematic false-positive findings related to reactive or physiologic uptake and false-negative findings involving small-volume or anatomically atypical metastases. Conclusion: LLM-orchestrated PET/CT agents enabled workflow-level automation from raw DICOM to quantification and structured draft reporting under real-world conditions. Although primary tumor detection was highly reliable, nodal and metastatic assessment revealed systematic limitations, supporting a collaborative role with continued expert oversight in complex clinical scenarios.

title: Prognostic Value of a Composite Score Incorporating Baseline [ 18 F]FDG PET/CT and [ 68 Ga]Ga-PSMA-11 PET/CT When Screening for [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA Treatment Eligibility (PROFILE Study).
abstract: We investigated the prognostic value of baseline [ 18 F]FDG and [ 68 Ga]Ga-PSMA-11 PET/CT in patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer treated with [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA-617. Methods: In this multicenter retrospective study, the associations between several clinical, biologic, and radiologic parameters and overall survival (OS) were tested in a development cohort using univariable analyses, followed by the construction of a multivariable Cox model. The PROFILE prognostic score was subsequently derived from this model, internally validated, and externally validated in an independent cohort. Results: Data from 174 patients from 3 centers were used to construct the multivariable Cox model. Five independent adverse prognostic factors were identified and incorporated into the PROFILE score: an SUV max exceeding 300% of the PERCIST threshold on [ 18 F]FDG PET/CT, a "nonhigh" classification on [ 68 Ga]Ga-PSMA-11 PET/CT using the visual PSMA tumor-to-salivary gland ratio, a baseline hemoglobin level of 11 g/dL or less, a baseline alkaline phosphatase level of greater than 220 IU/L, and a disease duration not exceeding 100 mo. The PROFILE score stratified patients into 3 risk groups and achieved a Harrell C-index of 0.67 (95% CI, 0.62-0.72). The median OS in the low-, intermediate-, and high-risk groups was 17.2, 13.0, and 8.6 mo, respectively ( P < 0.0001). These results were confirmed in 114 patients in an independent, single-center validation cohort, with median OS of 20.4, 14.3, and 8.8 mo ( P < 0.0001), respectively, and a C-index of 0.73 (95% CI, 0.68-0.78). Conclusion: The PROFILE score offers valuable prognostic information for patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer when considering the use of [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA-617 therapy.

title: Prognostic Value of 68 Ga-NOTA-AE105 uPAR PET/CT in Resected Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: A Single-Center Prospective Study.
abstract: Non-small cell lung cancer shows wide variability in outcomes after curative-intent resection. 18 F-FDG PET/CT is indispensable for staging but primarily reflects glucose metabolism rather than the invasion-related tumor biology that may contribute to recurrence. 68 Ga-NOTA-AE105 PET/CT images the urokinase-type plasminogen activator receptor (uPAR), a cell-surface mediator of local invasion and metastatic spread. We assessed whether preoperative 68 Ga-uPAR PET/CT is prognostic for postoperative recurrence. Methods: We conducted a single-center cohort study of patients with resectable lung adenocarcinoma or squamous cell carcinoma who were prospectively enrolled to undergo preoperative 68 Ga-uPAR PET/CT in addition to standard-of-care 18 F-FDG PET/CT. Primary tumor SUV mean and SUV max were measured for both tracers, and tumor tissue uPAR expression was quantified by immunohistochemistry (H-score). Postoperative recurrence was the primary endpoint and was analyzed in a competing-risks framework with death as a competing event. The primary prognostic analyses evaluated 68 Ga-uPAR SUVs, 18 F-FDG SUVs, and uPAR H-score as continuous variables using univariable cause-specific Cox models. A 1.5-y horizon was used for exploratory Youden-derived high versus low groups, for which cumulative incidence of recurrence was estimated using the Aalen-Johansen method. Trial registration number is NCT02755675 Results: Thirty-seven patients comprised the analysis cohort, of whom 14 developed recurrence during a median follow-up of 2.38 y (interquartile range, 1.97-8.20 y). Four patients died without prior recurrence. 68 Ga-uPAR uptake correlated with tumor tissue uPAR expression, whereas 18 F-FDG uptake did not. As continuous prognostic factors, higher 68 Ga-uPAR SUV max (hazard ratio, 2.16; 95% CI, 1.34-3.49; P = 0.002) and higher uPAR H-score (hazard ratio, 1.04 per unit; 95% CI, 1.01-1.08; P = 0.017) were associated with recurrence; 68 Ga-uPAR SUV mean showed borderline evidence of association ( P = 0.053), whereas 18 F-FDG uptake was not prognostic. Exploratory 1.5-y threshold analyses showed greater early recurrence in the high SUV mean and high H-score groups; the SUV max comparison did not reach statistical significance. Conclusion: Preoperative 68 Ga-uPAR PET uptake reflected tumor uPAR expression and was associated with early postoperative recurrence, whereas 18 F-FDG uptake was not prognostic in this cohort. These findings suggest that uPAR PET captures invasion-related tumor biology that is not fully reflected by glucose metabolism imaging. External validation is required.

title: Evaluating Interim Progression: First Posttherapy 177 Lu-PSMA SPECT/CT Relative to Baseline PSMA PET/CT.
abstract: Prostate Cancer Working Group 4 recommends using prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) PET for response assessment of patients with androgen pathway receptor modulator-resistant prostate cancer treated with 177 Lu-PSMA-617. For that purpose, the time interval between baseline PSMA PET and initiation of therapy is critical as interim disease progression may influence the performance of PET as a response assessment tool. Methods: We visually assessed the frequency of interim disease progression seen on the first posttherapy 177 Lu-PSMA-617 SPECT/CT in 87 patients with androgen pathway receptor modulator-resistant prostate cancer. The time interval between baseline PSMA PET and initiation of therapy, pretherapy prostate-specific antigen (PSA) measures, and treatment outcomes between patients with or without interim progression on SPECT/CT were also compared. Results: For the 32 patients (36.8%) with interim progression, the PET to therapy interval (88 d) was significantly greater than those without progression (42 d, P < 0.001) despite adjusting for age, Gleason grade, and PSA doubling time. A time interval between baseline PSMA PET and initiation of therapy exceeding 30 d was seen in approximately 94% of patients with interim progression. PSA response and overall survival were not impacted by interim progression. Conclusion: Baseline PSMA PET may not represent the true disease status if the first cycle of 177 Lu-PSMA-617 occurs more than 30 d after baseline PET.

title: 18 F-BMS-986192 PET to Predict Durable Response to Nivolumab in NSCLC: A Novel Approach Beyond PD-L1 Immunohistochemistry.
abstract: Programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1) immunohistochemistry, the current standard biomarker for predicting response to programmed death protein 1/PD-L1 checkpoint inhibitors in non-small cell lung cancer, has moderate predictive value among others because of tumor heterogeneity and limited biopsy representation, whereas PD-L1 PET/CT using 18 F-BMS-986192 enables noninvasive, whole-tumor assessment of PD-L1 expression and heterogeneity, potentially improving prediction of response to immunotherapy. Methods: In this prospective multicenter biomarker exploration study, patients with stage IV non-small cell lung cancer eligible for nivolumab-based therapies underwent baseline 18 F-BMS-986192 PET/CT, 18 F-FDG PET/CT, and tumor biopsy for PD-L1 immunohistochemistry before treatment initiation. The primary endpoint was durable clinical benefit, defined as progression-free survival (PFS) of 9 mo or greater, with secondary analyses assessing associations among tracer uptake, PD-L1 expression, survival outcomes, and PET-based radiomic features. Results: Of 91 enrolled patients, 77 were included in the final analysis of 18 F-BMS-986192 PET/CT. Although PD-L1 immunohistochemistry did not differ between patients with PFS of less than 9 mo versus 9 mo or greater, PD-L1 PET uptake in lung lesions was significantly higher in patients with PFS of at least 9 mo ( P = 0.01). Using an optimal mean SUV peak cutoff of 2.4, PD-L1 PET demonstrated a high negative predictive value (94%) for durable clinical benefit, with significant associations for both PFS and overall survival, particularly in patients receiving first-line treatment. Tracer uptake showed no correlation with 18 F-FDG uptake. Conclusion: 18 F-BMS-986192 PET/CT revealed interpatient PD-L1 variability. Low uptake in lung lesions predicted poor outcomes with high negative predictive value. 18 F-BMS-986192 PET/CT demonstrated stronger negative predictive value than did baseline PD-L1 immunohistochemistry in this cohort. These findings require prospective validation.
