title: Preoperative staging of gastric cancer: a prospective comparison of gastric filling ultrasonography and enhanced CT with implications for surgical decision-making.
abstract: Background Accurate preoperative staging is essential for optimizing treatment strategies in gastric cancer. While gastric-enhanced CT is widely used, its accuracy remains suboptimal, particularly for early-stage tumors. Gastric filling ultrasonography, a non-invasive technique using oral contrast to displace intraluminal gas, offers potential advantages in mural visualization. This prospective study compared the diagnostic performance of gastric filling ultrasonography and gastric-enhanced CT against postoperative pathological staging. Methods We enrolled 406 patients with histologically confirmed gastric cancer who underwent both imaging modalities prior to surgery. Preoperative T and N stages assigned by each modality were compared with pathological results. Diagnostic accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and area under the ROC curve (AUC) were calculated. McNemar's test was used for paired comparisons, DeLong test for AUC comparisons, and Kappa statistics for agreement assessment. Univariate logistic regression identified factors affecting ultrasound accuracy. Results For T-staging, overall accuracy was 72.7% (295/406) for ultrasound vs. 63.5% (258/406) for CT ( P < 0.001). Ultrasound significantly outperformed CT in T1 (81.5% vs. 56.3%, P = 0.009) and T2 (81.1% vs. 67.9%, P < 0.001) stages. For N-staging, accuracy was 82.0% (333/406) for ultrasound vs. 60.1% (244/406) for CT ( P < 0.001). Kappa agreement with pathology was substantial for ultrasound T-staging ( κ = 0.625) and N-staging ( κ = 0.748), compared with moderate agreement for CT ( κ = 0.508 and 0.395, respectively). In multivariate analysis, vascular infiltration was the only independent factor associated with ultrasound T-staging accuracy. Conclusions Gastric filling ultrasonography demonstrates superior accuracy over gastric-enhanced CT for preoperative T1/T2 and N-staging, with substantial agreement with pathological findings. This non-invasive and radiation-free examination method can serve as an effective complement to CT, and is particularly suitable for gastric cancer at the T1 and T2 stages. We have proposed a complementary imaging protocol to assist in surgical decision-making, which is expected to enable clinicians to make more accurate preoperative staging assessments for patients with gastric cancer. Registration It was registered in the ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05596864).

title: Modern hysteroscopic management of congenital uterine anomalies: current techniques, emerging technologies, and future directions.
abstract: Background Congenital uterine anomalies are clinically relevant in reproductive medicine, particularly among women with infertility, recurrent pregnancy loss, adverse obstetric outcomes, or obstructive symptoms. Hysteroscopy has transformed the management of correctable intracavitary anomalies by enabling conservative, image-guided reconstruction of the uterine cavity while avoiding the morbidity of historical abdominal metroplasty. Scope This narrative review critically examines contemporary hysteroscopic management of septate uterus, dysmorphic uterus, bicorporeal septate uterus and rare obstructive malformations, such as Robert's uterus. We discuss the implications of the ESHRE/ESGE, CUME, and ASRM classification systems; the role of three-dimensional transvaginal ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging in preoperative mapping; and the technical principles that guide metroplasty, cavity remodeling, ultrasound-guided hysteroscopy, office-based metroplasty, and staged approaches in complex anatomy. Discussion Bipolar saline-based platforms, miniaturized resectoscopes, bipolar needle electrodes, cold scissors, and selected tissue removal systems have expanded the therapeutic spectrum and improved safety. The evidence supporting surgery remains heterogeneous: the TRUST randomized trial challenged routine septum resection in unselected women, whereas data for T-shaped and other dysmorphic uteri remain largely observational. Emerging technologies, including laser platforms, artificial intelligence-assisted hysteroscopy, and robotic concepts, are promising, but currently lack prospective validation. Conclusion Optimal management should therefore be individualized, anatomy-driven, and grounded in shared decision-making, with careful preservation of endometrium and myometrium. Standardized reporting, multicenter registries, and prospective comparative studies are needed to define which patients benefit most from hysteroscopic correction.

title: Second-generation ICG fusion fluorescence endoscopy in pituitary neuroendocrine tumor surgery.
abstract: Objective This study investigated the clinical feasibility of integrating second-generation real-time indocyanine green (ICG) fusion fluorescence endoscopy into routine transsphenoidal surgical workflow for pituitary neuroendocrine tumors (PitNETs). Our focus was on describing the qualitative fluorescence patterns of PitNETs observed within the procedure-embedded 15-18 min delay window following administration of ICG, and evaluating the reproducibility of image interpretation. Methods This retrospective single-center descriptive feasibility study included 26 patients with PitNETs who underwent endoscopic transsphenoidal surgery. ICG was intravenously injected before sellar floor drilling, then after the tumor-pituitary interface was fully exposed, real-time fusion mode fluorescence endoscopy was maintained for continuous observation. Two independent observers retrospectively assessed fluorescence intensity and contrast patterns on video clips of intraoperative fusion fluorescence imaging. Interobserver agreement for binary fluorescence intensity grading and three-category contrast pattern classification (tumor-dominant, equivalent, and pituitary-dominant) was evaluated using Cohen's kappa coefficient (weighted kappa for ordinal pattern categories). Results Surgery under fluorescence guidance was successfully completed for all 26 patients, with no ICG-related adverse events. No intraoperative mode switching was required, and fluorescence signals remained stable within the delay window. The contrast pattern classifications were: tumor-dominant n = 8 (all clinically functioning PRL-PitNETs), equivalent n = 15 (multiple subtypes), and pituitary-dominant n = 3 (all elderly patients ≥65 years with non-functioning PitNETs). Interobserver agreement was excellent, with Cohen's kappa of 0.91 (95% CI: 0.85-0.97, P < 0.001) for binary fluorescence intensity grading and a weighted Cohen's kappa of 0.89 (95% CI: 0.82-0.96, P < 0.001) for contrast pattern classification. All postoperative adverse events were mild and resolved conservatively, with no permanent pituitary dysfunction. Conclusion Second-generation ICG fusion fluorescence endoscopy demonstrated preliminary technical feasibility and short-term safety for integration into transsphenoidal surgical workflow. The three fluorescence contrast patterns within the 15-18 min window show good interobserver agreement. The clinical utility of these patterns for tumor-pituitary interface assessment remains unproven and requires prospective validation.

title: Severe delayed gastric emptying combined with enteroparalysis after pancreaticoduodenectomy: a case report.
abstract: Background Pancreaticoduodenectomy is an important surgical procedure for treating diseases of the pancreatic head, periampullary region, and related conditions. However, due to its extensive surgical scope, long duration, and involvement of complex digestive tract reconstruction, postoperative gastrointestinal dysfunction remains relatively common. Among these, delayed gastric emptying (DGE) is a common complication after pancreaticoduodenectomy, while the occurrence of severe DGE combined with enteroparalysis is relatively rare, and its diagnosis and treatment remain challenging. Case presentation This article reports the case of a 69-year-old female patient who developed severe DGE complicated by intestinal paralysis after pancreaticoduodenectomy. The patient persistently experienced nausea, vomiting, and the inability to tolerate oral intake postoperatively. Although imaging studies suggested restricted passage at the gastrointestinal anastomosis, raising suspicion of obstruction, further laparoscopic exploration and gastroscopy revealed no definite mechanical obstruction. The patient received gastrointestinal decompression, nutritional support, internal environment management, and rehabilitation therapy. Enteral nutritional support was established through a jejunal feeding tube. After long-term comprehensive treatment, the patient's gastrointestinal function gradually recovered and eventually returned to oral intake. However, long-term follow-up showed that despite the recovery of gastrointestinal function, the patient still had a certain degree of decline in physical function and limited ability in activities of daily living. Conclusion Severe delayed gastric emptying complicated by enteroparalysis after pancreaticoduodenectomy is a rare but clinically challenging gastrointestinal dysfunction. This case suggests that persistent postoperative gastrointestinal dysfunction may present with clinical features resembling mechanical obstruction, therefore requiring comprehensive assessment integrating imaging, endoscopy, and dynamic clinical changes.

title: Adjunctive screw fixation and screw corridors for spiral tibial fractures involving the distal tibial articular surface: a retrospective case series.
abstract: Objective Building on a CT-based regional evaluation framework developed in our previous morphological study, this study retrospectively summarized the adjunctive screw corridors actually used and their fixation targets in spiral tibial fractures involving the distal tibial articular surface that were treated with intramedullary nailing combined with adjunctive screw fixation, and used representative intraoperative and postoperative images to illustrate the relationship between the adjunctive screws and the intramedullary nail. Methods This was a single-center retrospective case series of patients with spiral tibial fractures involving the distal tibial articular surface who underwent tibial intramedullary nailing combined with adjunctive screw fixation at the Department of Lower Limb Trauma, Honghui Hospital, Xi'an Jiaotong University, between May 2020 and May 2025. During the study period, 110 patients were treated with this combined fixation; 98 patients with a follow-up duration of at least 12 months and complete clinical and imaging records were included in the analysis, and 12 patients were excluded because of insufficient follow-up or incomplete imaging records. Two observers independently assessed the involvement of the posterior malleolar/Volkmann region, the anterior malleolar/Chaput region, and the medial malleolar region on preoperative CT, and Cohen's kappa was calculated from the original independent assessments obtained before consensus discussion. The four types of adjunctive screw corridors actually used were retrospectively summarized from operative records and postoperative imaging. All patients underwent adjunctive screw fixation before reaming and intramedullary nail insertion. Corridor use was summarized using descriptive statistics, and perioperative variables, time to full weight bearing, the American Orthopaedic Foot & Ankle Society (AOFAS) ankle-hindfoot score, the visual analog scale (VAS) pain score, the difference in ankle dorsiflexion angle between the affected and contralateral sides, and related complications were recorded. Results A total of 98 patients were included, comprising 62 men and 36 women, with a mean age of 45.67 ± 13.61 years. The posterior malleolar/Volkmann region, the anterior malleolar/Chaput region, and the medial malleolar region were involved in 76 (77.6%), 40 (40.8%), and 23 (23.5%) patients, respectively; single-region, two-region, and three-region involvement was present in 64, 27, and 7 patients. Interobserver agreement for the individual regions and for their combinations ranged from 95.9% to 98.0%, with kappa values of 0.924-0.957. The tibiofibular incisura, anterior cortical, posterior cortical, and medial malleolar corridors were used in 93, 8, 7, and 6 patients, respectively; 87 patients received a single corridor and 11 received multiple corridors. The number of adjunctive screws ranged from 1 to 4, with a mean of 1.23 ± 0.62. Mean operative time was 73.45 ± 7.88 min, mean intraoperative blood loss was 67.56 ± 10.46 mL, and mean follow-up was 16.13 ± 2.20 months. Ninety-seven patients were included in the analyses of time to full weight bearing and final functional outcomes. Mean time to full weight bearing was 64.81 ± 16.91 days; at the final follow-up, the mean AOFAS ankle-hindfoot score was 91.67 ± 3.13, the mean VAS pain score was 1.36 ± 0.50, and the mean difference in ankle dorsiflexion angle between sides was 6.06 ± 3.27 degrees. Two patients developed delayed healing of the anterior ankle incision used for distal locking screws, which healed after dressing changes, and one patient developed an infection at the tibial shaft fracture site and was treated with implant removal and antibiotic-loaded bone cement. Among the 98 patients with complete follow-up, no obvious articular redisplacement or fixation failure was observed on the available follow-up radiographs. Conclusion This retrospective case series summarized the four types of adjunctive screw corridors actually used when spiral tibial fractures involving the distal tibial articular surface were treated with intramedullary nailing combined with adjunctive screw fixation, and described the fixation target of each corridor. Representative images are used to illustrate, but do not systematically analyze, the relationship between the adjunctive screws and the intramedullary nail. These results provide descriptive information on the adjunctive fixation technique used in this cohort, and their value for guiding preoperative planning and surgical decision-making requires further validation.

title: Case Report: Solitary fibrous tumor (SFT) of cerebellum: report of 2 cases.
abstract: Objective To elucidate the neuroradiological characteristics, clinical manifestations, and surgical outcomes of intracranial cerebellar solitary fibrous tumors (SFTs) to improve diagnostic accuracy and therapeutic strategies. Method A retrospective analysis was conducted on the clinical data of two histopathologically confirmed cases of cerebellar SFT, supplemented by a review of the relevant literature. Results Both patients underwent total surgical excision followed by postoperative radiotherapy. At the latest follow-up, neither patient showed radiological evidence of tumor recurrence (Case 1: 18 months; Case 2: 12 months]). Given the potential for late recurrence in SFTs, long-term surveillance is mandatory. Conclusion Intracranial cerebellar SFTs are rare neoplasms that are frequently misdiagnosed despite exhibiting distinctive magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) features. Definitive diagnosis relies on histopathological and immunohistochemical analyses. In this study, MRI demonstrated T1-weighted imaging (T1WI) hypointensity or isointensity, T2-weighted imaging (T2WI) heterogeneity, and inconsistent post-contrast enhancement. Immunohistochemical evaluation revealed positivity for CD34, CD99, and STAT6. Prompt surgical intervention accompanied by adjuvant therapy was associated with a favorable prognosis.

title: Pseudo-cerebrospinal fluid rhinorrhea following endoscopic endonasal transsphenoidal surgery for PitNET: a case report and literature review.
abstract: Pseudo-cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) rhinorrhea, defined as non-CSF nasal discharge mimicking true CSF leakage, is a rare but clinically significant complication that may prompt unnecessary aggressive treatment. We report a case of a 64-year-old man who developed positional clear nasal discharge after endoscopic endonasal resection of recurrent pituitary neuroendocrine tumor (PitNET). Glucose oxidase testing was negative, and imaging demonstrated intact skull base reconstruction. Nasal endoscopy revealed bilateral crusting and purulent secretions without evidence of CSF leak. The condition was diagnosed as vasomotor rhinitis. Conservative management-including nasal debridement, antibiotic therapy, topical corticosteroids, and saline irrigation-led to complete symptom resolution. This case underscores the importance of differentiating pseudo-CSF rhinorrhea from true CSF rhinorrhea to avoid invasive interventions.

title: Brain re-expansion rate on the first postoperative day and risk of symptomatic recurrence after burr-hole drainage for chronic subdural hematoma.
abstract: Background Early brain re-expansion may indicate recurrence risk after chronic subdural hematoma evacuation. This study examined its association with 90-day symptomatic recurrence and its incremental prognostic value. Methods This retrospective study included 286 adults undergoing first-time burr-hole evacuation with closed drainage. Volumes on preoperative computed tomography and postoperative imaging at 22-26 h were used to standardize re-expansion to 24 h. Symptomatic recurrence required clinical deterioration, radiographic progression, and reintervention. Follow-up began at postoperative imaging and ended by postoperative day 90. Cause-specific Cox and Fine-Gray models used joint strata for brain atrophy and antithrombotic use, with additional adjustment for age, bilateral disease, and preoperative volume. Internal validation used 1,000 patient-level bootstrap samples with the stratum structure held fixed. Results Symptomatic recurrence occurred in 47 patients (16.4%); eight died before recurrence and 231 remained alive without recurrence. Each 10-percentage-point/24 h increase in re-expansion was associated with a lower cause-specific hazard (adjusted hazard ratio, 0.74; 95% confidence interval, 0.64-0.85) and subdistribution hazard (adjusted subdistribution hazard ratio, 0.74; 95% confidence interval, 0.65-0.85; both P < 0.001). Adding re-expansion increased the within-stratum Harrell concordance index from 0.657 to 0.695 (difference, 0.039; 95% confidence interval, -0.015 to 0.092; P = 0.155). The 90-day area under the receiver operating characteristic curve increased from 0.731 to 0.774 (difference, 0.042; 95% confidence interval, 0.001-0.083; P = 0.043). The full Fine-Gray model had an optimism-corrected Brier score of 0.116 and calibration slope of 0.89. Conclusions Faster first-day brain re-expansion was associated with lower symptomatic recurrence hazard after accounting for competing death. The internally observed increase in 90-day discrimination requires external validation before clinical application.

title: Case Report: Solitary fibrous tumor of the right temporal skull base with bone destruction and postoperative recurrence.
abstract: Background Solitary fibrous tumor (SFT) is a rare fibroblastic mesenchymal neoplasm of the central nervous system, and temporal skull-base lesions with destructive osseous change and extension toward the middle-ear region are uncommon. Case presentation A 60-year-old woman presented with acute right peripheral facial weakness. CT demonstrated expansile mixed lytic-sclerotic destruction of the right temporal bone and middle cranial fossa floor, and MRI showed a 46 × 38 × 36 mm lobulated mass with heterogeneous signal, irregular peripheral and nodular enhancement, central nonenhancing necrotic or cystic change, and adjacent temporal-lobe edema. Right frontotemporal microsurgical resection achieved gross-total macroscopic removal, although piecemeal resection rendered microscopic margins unassessable. Histology and immunohistochemistry supported SFT, with 4 mitoses/10 high-power fields, focal necrosis, nuclear STAT6 expression, weak partial CD34 expression, MDM2 immunoreactivity, and a Ki-67 labeling index of approximately 40%. Review of the available sections showed no morphologically distinct high-grade sarcomatous component. Under the 2021 CNS WHO framework, the documented mitotic count corresponds most closely to grade 1. Postoperative radiotherapy was recommended but declined. Telephone follow-up indicated that outside-hospital MRI reportedly showed tumor recurrence at 18 months and further enlargement at 27 months. The patient also reported that outside examinations showed no metastatic disease in the lungs, liver, or skeleton. During later follow-up, the family expressed concern that the patient might not tolerate another major surgical intervention, and continued clinical and imaging follow-up was recommended. Conclusion This case illustrates that a documented mitotic count within the CNS WHO grade 1 range does not exclude clinically significant local recurrence. In skull-base SFT, formal pathologic grading should be interpreted together with anatomic extent, margin assessability, proliferative features, and the certainty of local control when planning postoperative management and surveillance.

title: Age is the wrong axis: rethinking surgical selection for octogenarians with early-stage non-small cell lung cancer.
abstract: Lung cancer is increasingly a disease of older age, and as low-dose computed tomography screening extends into the ninth decade, a growing number of octogenarians present with early-stage, potentially curable non-small cell lung cancer. Faced with these patients, clinicians repeatedly ask a single question: is this patient too old for surgery? Recent prospective data show that selected octogenarians achieve long-term survival comparable to younger patients despite substantially higher complication rates, with quality of life that recovers over the first postoperative year. Yet the favorable result is attributed to careful selection that is rarely defined, and is seldom accompanied by any account of the patients who were assessed and not offered an operation. This article argues that chronological age is the wrong axis for the decision. Physiologic reserve, measurable through validated frailty instruments and established physiologic testing, predicts postoperative outcome far better than birth year, and aging is sufficiently heterogeneous that any age threshold misclassifies patients in both directions. A substantial competing risk of non-cancer death, compounded by overdiagnosis among screen-detected tumors, tempers the survival gain expected from aggressive treatment and makes overtreatment as real a hazard as age-based exclusion. A graded menu of options now exists, extending from minimally invasive lobectomy through sublobar resection and stereotactic ablative radiotherapy to active surveillance, and intensity should descend with reserve rather than with age. The task is to operationalize careful selection through structured geriatric assessment, multidisciplinary collaboration, prehabilitation, and shared decision-making, and to judge success by outcomes that older patients actually value.

title: Preoperative ovarian vascular parameters and perioperative factors associated with ovarian reserve marker decline after laparoscopic endometrioma cystectomy: a retrospective prediction study.
abstract: Background Laparoscopic cystectomy is a commonly used surgical treatment for ovarian endometrioma, but postoperative reduction in ovarian reserve markers is a recognized concern. Preoperative identification of women at increased risk may support counseling and surgical planning. This study evaluated whether multidimensional ovarian vascular and hemodynamic ultrasound parameters are associated with subsequent decline in ovarian reserve markers. Objective To evaluate the association of preoperative multidimensional ultrasound parameters with postoperative ovarian reserve marker decline and to develop an exploratory perioperative prediction model. Methods A retrospective cohort of 280 reproductive-age women undergoing laparoscopic ovarian endometrioma cystectomy (May 2021-May 2024) was analyzed. Transvaginal color Doppler ultrasound on menstrual cycle days 2-5 yielded 2D morphological parameters [ovarian volume [OV], antral follicle count [AFC]], 3D vascular parameters [vascularization index [VI], flow index [FI], vascularization-flow index [VFI]], and spectral Doppler parameters (resistance index [RI], pulsatility index [PI], peak systolic velocity [PSV], end-diastolic velocity [EDV]). Serum AMH, FSH, LH, and E2 were measured. Ovarian reserve markers were reassessed at 3, 6, and 12 months. The primary 6-month outcome was a study-specific composite decline in ovarian reserve markers. Exploratory multivariable logistic regression was used to construct a perioperative model, and internal optimism was estimated by 1,000 bootstrap resamples. Apparent discrimination was assessed by ROC analysis. Results At 6 months, 118 of 280 patients (42.1%) met the study-specific composite outcome. Women meeting the outcome had lower preoperative VI, VFI, FI, PSV, and EDV and higher RI and PI (all P < 0.01). Pearson correlations showed moderate associations of vascular parameters with 6-month AMH and FSH levels. AMH decreased after surgery in both groups, with a greater reduction in patients meeting the composite outcome; significant effects of time, group, and group-by-time interaction were observed (all P < 0.001). The exploratory perioperative logistic model retained age, bilateral cysts, preoperative maximum cyst diameter, intraoperative r-AFS score, preoperative VI, and preoperative RI. Higher VI was associated with lower odds of the composite outcome, whereas higher RI was associated with greater odds. The composite model had an apparent AUC of 0.888 (95% CI 0.845-0.923), which was higher than that of VI (AUC=0.702) or RI (AUC=0.699) alone. Bootstrap internal validation yielded a corrected AUC of 0.878. At a probability cutoff of >0.57, sensitivity and specificity were 76.3% and 90.1%, respectively, with a PPV of 84.9% and an NPV of 83.9%. Because r-AFS is intraoperative and no external validation was performed, this is a perioperative rather than a strictly preoperative model and requires external validation before clinical application. Conclusions Preoperative ovarian vascular and hemodynamic ultrasound parameters, particularly VI and RI, were associated with postoperative decline in ovarian reserve markers. The composite model showed good apparent discrimination and modest optimism on internal bootstrap validation; however, external validation and comparison with models incorporating established baseline ovarian reserve markers are required before clinical implementation.

title: Catastrophic acetabular wear following polyethylene liner dissociation with locking-tab damage after total hip arthroplasty: a case report.
abstract: Polyethylene liner dissociation is an uncommon but potentially severe complication of total hip arthroplasty (THA). Loss of the intended bearing interface can permit direct femoral-head-acetabular-shell articulation, with progressive shell wear, metallic debris deposition, and acetabular bone loss. A 73-year-old woman developed left hip pain after an accidental sprain in February 2025, having reported no hip-related symptoms after primary THA in 2020. The index Mindray implants included a 48-mm acetabular shell, a highly cross-linked polyethylene liner, a 28-mm femoral head, and a size-10 stem. Radiographs and CT with three-dimensional volume-rendered reconstruction were used to assess acetabular bone loss, classified as Paprosky type IIA. Revision revealed polyethylene liner dissociation, catastrophic shell wear-through, extensive black metallic debris deposition, and a well-fixed femoral stem. Partial locking-tab damage was identified on gross inspection, but formal retrieval analysis was not performed. Acetabular revision with iliac-crest autografting was performed while retaining the femoral stem. At 6 months, the Harris Hip Score improved from 46 to 82, and radiographs showed a stable acetabular component with evidence of graft incorporation. This case illustrates the potential for clinically occult progression from liner dissociation to catastrophic head-on-shell wear. Gross locking-tab damage did not establish the initiating failure mechanism. Component-preserving acetabular revision was associated with a favorable short-term clinical and radiographic outcome in this patient.

title: Deep learning for diagnostic and clinical decision support in companion animals: a systematic review of CNN- and LSTM-based approaches.
abstract: Early disease detection prior to the onset of advanced clinical signs remains a critical imperative in veterinary medicine. This systematic review provides a methodological synthesis of Convolutional Neural Networks and Long Short-Term Memory networks applied to diagnostic and clinical decision support in canine and feline patients, evaluating both algorithmic performance and clinical feasibility. Adhering to the PICO-CS framework and PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we queried Scopus and Web of Science for peer-reviewed studies published between 2021 and 2026, retrieving a final corpus of 57 primary studies. Eleven clinical domains were identified, with evidence heavily concentrated in Oncology (28.1%), Cardiology (15.8%), and Pulmonology (12.3%). CNN architectures predominated in spatial imaging modalities-including radiographs, clinical photography, ultrasonography, and microscopic imagery-whereas LSTM networks were deployed for temporal signals and sensor-derived telemetry. Binary classification tasks achieved the highest performance metrics (accuracy reaching up to 99%), whereas multi-class formulations exhibited broader variability due to dataset imbalance. Cross-study benchmarking revealed substantial heterogeneity in datasets, evaluation metrics, and validation protocols, while reliance on high-performance computational infrastructure poses a barrier to point-of-care deployment in resource-constrained clinics. We conclude that while deep learning architectures hold significant promise as clinical decision-support tools, transitioning to routine veterinary practice requires prospective external validation, representative open-access datasets, and lightweight models optimized for conventional clinical hardware.

title: Case Report: Presumptive subdural hemorrhage as a rare neurological manifestation of primary immune-mediated thrombocytopenia in a dog.
abstract: A 10-year-old female spayed mixed-breed dog was presented with a history of seizures and acute progressive intracranial signs. The neurological examination was consistent with multifocal brain disease. Clinical examination revealed ecchymoses, petechiae, and bilateral retinal hemorrhage. Clinicopathological evaluation identified severe thrombocytopenia [a platelet count of 9 × 10 3 /μL without clumps on manual smear evaluation] with an increased mean platelet volume. Coagulation testing (activated partial thromboplastin time and prothrombin time) and fibrinolysis markers (D-dimers, quantitative fibrinogen), infectious disease screening, and thoracic and abdominal imaging were within normal limits, establishing a diagnosis of primary immune-mediated thrombocytopenia (ITP). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed minimally expanded, bilateral crescent-shaped, extra-axial fluid accumulations overlying both cerebral hemispheres. Based on T1-weighted and T2-weighted hyperintensities and peripheral susceptibility artifact on T2*-weighted gradient-recalled echo (GRE) imaging, a late subacute subdural intracranial hemorrhage was diagnosed. Despite initial uneventful anesthesia and recovery, the dog experienced acute neurological deterioration and suffered cardiopulmonary arrest, suspected due to ongoing hemorrhage or brain herniation. This report describes a rare neurological manifestation of primary ITP in a dog. While canine ITP generally carries a favorable prognosis, life-threatening secondary intracranial hemorrhage can occur. Primary ITP should be considered as a differential diagnosis for an acute, progressive neurological presentation until a normal platelet count is confirmed.

title: A European algorithm and strategy for management of chronic postoperative inguinal pain (EurA-CPIP).
abstract: Background Chronic postoperative inguinal pain (CPIP) is a disabling complication affecting 8%-17% of all patients after inguinal hernia repair. It is a complex pain condition with several pathophysiological mechanisms involved, including neuropathic pain, inflammation, and mechanical effects (e.g., mesh or scar tissue). Management remains inconsistent, probably due to limited high-quality evidence, heterogeneous approach, and insufficient standardisation of outcomes. This study aimed to develop EurA-CPIP, a multidisciplinary treatment algorithm and prospective data-collection platform designed to support consistent phenotyping, step-up management, and standardised outcomes across centres, creating an iterative platform for future hypothesis-driven research and multicentre trials. Methods An international multidisciplinary working group from European tertiary referral centres developed the European Algorithm and Strategy for Management of Chronic Postoperative Inguinal Pain (EurA-CPIP). Development was informed by the evidence synthesis underpinning the updated international HerniaSurge guidelines and a critical appraisal of previously published CPIP algorithms. A pragmatic step-up algorithm was designed, integrating pharmacological, interventional, surgical and supportive treatments, with prospective outcome registration and planned data-driven revision on a regular basis. Results EurA-CPIP provides a multidisciplinary algorithm with entry at multiple levels depending on prior treatment attempts. The concept is to begin and, if needed, advance from conservative measures such as systemic medication and topical therapy, to more invasive treatments such as trigger point injections, and ultrasound-guided nerve blocks; predefined investigational add-ons (radiofrequency, cryoneurolysis, botulinum toxin A) are embedded after documented block response. Multidisciplinary team review precedes escalation to more invasive interventions such as surgery. A supportive and rehabilitative coping trajectory is integrated early on. Standardised outcomes include patient-reported pain outcomes, functional impairment, psychological factors, analgesic use, and patient global impression of improvement. Conclusion EurA-CPIP is a pragmatic consensus-based strategy intended to harmonise and improve specialised CPIP care while utilising existing and developing emerging therapies. Future research should investigate pathophysiology and intervention effects within this step-up algorithm.

title: Extended Reality for Image-Guided Small Animal Surgery: Current Evidence, Clinical Applications, and Future Directions.
abstract: Image-guided surgery has become an integral component of modern veterinary surgery using advanced imaging modalities, such as computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, ultrasonography, and fluoroscopy. Recently, extended reality (XR) technologies have emerged as promising tools to enhance image-guided surgical procedures by improving three-dimensional anatomical understanding, surgical navigation, and intraoperative decision-making. Although XR has gained considerable attention in human surgery, its application in veterinary surgery remains at an early stage. This narrative review aimed to provide a comprehensive overview of the current evidence regarding XR technologies in small animal surgery, with particular emphasis on their integration with preoperative and intraoperative imaging modalities. The available literature was reviewed to evaluate current clinical applications, technological developments and future perspectives. A literature search was performed in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science for studies published up to May 2026 using combinations of terms related to extended reality and small animal veterinary surgery. Original articles, case reports, pilot studies, technical reports, and reviews addressing clinical, experimental, or simulation-based applications were considered. Although several studies have explored the use of XR technologies for veterinary education, anatomical training, and diagnostic imaging instruction, relatively few investigations have assessed their direct application in clinical surgical practice. Potential applications have been described in orthopedic, oncologic, neurologic, cardiovascular, and minimally invasive procedures. Crucially, the currently available peer-reviewed evidence is restricted to canine patients, as no eligible feline studies were identified. Current evidence suggests that XR is an emerging technology with potential applications in canine surgical planning, image-guided procedures, and surgical training. Further prospective clinical studies are required to establish its clinical effectiveness, cost-effectiveness, and impact on surgical outcomes.

title: Rat Calvarial Defect Models in Bone Regeneration Research: A Narrative Review of Critical Size and Micro-Computed Tomography Outcome Reporting.
abstract: The rat calvarial defect model supports the preclinical evaluation of bone-regenerative approaches relevant to craniofacial reconstruction, including recombinant human bone morphogenetic protein-2 (rhBMP-2) and bone substitutes. However, its invasive nature requires study-specific harm-benefit assessment and application of the 3Rs. This narrative review used a structured PubMed search to examine spontaneous healing in defects smaller than 5 mm and μCT outcome reporting in untreated or control defects. Twenty-four studies of sub-5 mm defects and 45 μCT studies were included. Complete spontaneous healing was not reported in the sub-5 mm studies; only two μCT studies reported regeneration of at least 50% according to their respective outcome measures. Healing generally increased with longer observation periods and smaller defects, although methodological heterogeneity limited comparisons. Inconsistent reporting of acquisition parameters, segmentation thresholds, regions of interest, and numerical outcomes restricted reproducibility and data reuse. Within this PubMed-indexed evidence base, the findings support 5 mm defects as a practical model of incomplete spontaneous healing and indicate that smaller defects also do not reliably heal completely within the observation periods studied. These findings do not directly establish clinical benefit. Future studies should justify the least burdensome model capable of answering the research question, implement replacement, reduction, and refinement, and report standardized bone volume fractions, relevant measures of defect bridging, reproducible imaging methods, and reusable numerical data.

title: Gill Alterations in Adult Zebrafish Exposed to Avobenzone: Morphometric Profiling and Machine-Learning Analysis.
abstract: Gill histopathology is widely used in fish toxicology, but lesion scores and targeted measurements capture only part of the structural information in routine sections. We tested whether a morphometric profile could quantify avobenzone-related changes in adult zebrafish gills. The 40× dataset comprised gill sections from 35 adult zebrafish across five conditions represented in the image dataset: a 4-day solvent-control group and fish exposed to nominal avobenzone concentrations of 3 or 9 μg/L for 4 or 21 days. From 750 fields, quality control and automated segmentation yielded 503 accepted masks; 360 fields (72 per condition) were used in the balanced analysis. Thirty-nine descriptors quantified tissue geometry, interlamellar spaces, branch-like organisation, and thickness heterogeneity. Validation was repeated 30 times with all fields from each fish kept in the same partition. The time-matched 4-day control-versus-exposed comparison reached 89.4 ± 4.1% balanced accuracy. The 3-versus-9 μg/L comparison at 4 days reached 88.7 ± 4.6%, and 4 versus 21 days within the 9 μg/L group reached 88.5 ± 5.0%. Performance for direct five-condition classification was lower (68.4 ± 5.1%). Because 21-day control images were not included, exposure-related inference was restricted to the time-matched 4-day comparison. Morphometric profiling provides a quantitative complement to conventional histopathology while preserving individual fish identity as the grouping unit for image analysis.

title: Opportunistic Cardiovascular Assessment During Lung Cancer Screening with Low-Dose Computed Tomography: A New Window for Prevention.
abstract: Population-based lung cancer screening with low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) is expanding across Europe, including a publicly funded Polish programme starting in October 2026. Because screening-eligible individuals share substantial tobacco-related cardiovascular risk, LDCT also offers cardiovascular risk assessment without additional radiation. We conducted a narrative review of the PubMed literature published up to September 2026, prioritising guidelines, lung cancer screening cohorts and systematic reviews. We summarise the cardiovascular findings on non-contrast, non-electrocardiography (ECG)-gated LDCT: coronary artery, aortic valve, mitral annular and thoracic aortic calcification, ascending aortic dilatation, pericardial effusion, and pulmonary artery enlargement, as well as investigational cardiac volumetry, epicardial adipose tissue and artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted quantification. We grade each finding by reportability, defined downstream action and supporting evidence, and align reporting thresholds with the European Respiratory Society/European Society of Thoracic Imaging (ERS/ESTI) statement on incidental findings. LDCT cannot replace dedicated cardiac imaging or establish haemodynamic diagnoses. The prognostic value of coronary and aortic valve calcification and of ascending aortic dilatation is established, whereas the evidence for mitral annular calcification and pulmonary artery enlargement is more limited; observational data indicate that reporting these markers changes preventive management, but whether this improves cardiovascular outcomes has not yet been demonstrated. Standardised reporting, proportionate thresholds, and coordinated pathways linking radiology, pulmonology, primary care and cardiology are needed to translate incidental cardiovascular findings into scalable prevention and should be evaluated in implementation studies.

title: Spectral-Distribution Uncertainty Modeling for Robust Cross-Domain Medical Image Segmentation.
abstract: Domain generalization (DG) for medical image segmentation is commonly approached by simulating domain shifts through deterministic image transformations or feature perturbations. However, such methods implicitly assume that unseen domains can be approximated by predefined appearance variations. In this work, we challenge this assumption and hypothesize that medical domain shifts are more fundamentally characterized as uncertainty in spectral distributions. While anatomical structures are largely preserved across institutions, scanners, and acquisition protocols, substantial variations arise in image appearance, texture, and artifacts, which are predominantly manifested in the spectral domain. To test this hypothesis, we propose Spectral-Distribution Uncertainty (SDU), a frequency-aware DG framework that explicitly models uncertainty in the Fourier amplitude distributions of intermediate representations. By decomposing Transformer features into amplitude and phase components, SDU disentangles domain-specific spectral characteristics from domain-invariant anatomical semantics. Instead of imposing handcrafted frequency perturbations, SDU estimates spectral-distribution uncertainty during training and injects stochastic variations into the amplitude space, synthesizing diverse yet anatomically consistent representations that emulate potential unseen domains. Consequently, SDU expands the support of spectral feature distributions, enabling the model to learn representations that are robust to uncertainty-induced spectral shifts. Extensive experiments on retinal fundus and prostate MRI benchmarks demonstrate that SDU consistently outperforms state-of-the-art DG methods. Beyond empirical gains, these findings provide evidence that medical domain shifts are more appropriately characterized as uncertainty in spectral feature distributions, offering a principled perspective for generalizable medical image segmentation.

title: VesselRegNet: Multi-Scale Feature Fusion Network for Multi-Modal Joint Retinal Vessel Segmentation and Registration.
abstract: Multimodal retinal image registration remains challenging due to nonlinear intensity discrepancies and insufficient feature representation across modalities. To address these limitations, we propose VesselRegNet, a joint retinal vessel segmentation and registration framework based on multi-scale feature fusion. The model integrates a multi-scale semantic feature extraction module with a shared prediction head and rotation-equivariant constraints to enhance feature consistency. Unlike conventional approaches relying on binary segmentation masks, the proposed method utilizes dense semantic features to directly guide deformable registration. Experimental results demonstrate that VesselRegNet achieves an average Dice coefficient of 0.664 and SSIM of 0.645, achieving a relative improvement of 4.1% in Dice and 2.5% in SSIM over the strongest baseline (RetinaRegNet), and up to 11.9% improvement over general unsupervised registration frameworks. The proposed multi-scale fusion and joint learning strategy improves registration accuracy under complex retinal deformations.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Selective Prediction in Brain-Tumour MRI Classification: Selective Risk Reduction and Component-Wise Reliability Findings.
abstract: Background Automated brain-MRI analysis is usually judged by accuracy at a single operating point, yet a model that is accurate on average may still fail without signalling that it is about to fail. Selective prediction addresses this by allowing a model to abstain, but the resulting trade-off between coverage and risk is rarely quantified in medical imaging. Objective This study asks whether confidence- and entropy-based selective prediction produces a measurable reduction in selective risk in a biomedical vision-language classifier by concentrating errors among withheld cases, and at what coverage cost. Three further components of a brain-MRI-analysis framework-volumetric segmentation, glioma grading and structured report generation-are evaluated as complementary evidence about the reliability profiles of different modules, not as independent contributions. Methods A LoRA-fine-tuned LLaVA-Med classifier was evaluated on the 1000-image BRISC2025 test partition, with a disjunctive rejection rule based on softmax confidence and predictive entropy. Volumetric segmentation used nnU-Net v2 (3D full-resolution) on BraTS2020 with a three-fold ensemble evaluated on 74 held-out cases; glioma grading (high- versus low-grade) used DenseNet121 on multi-slice representations; report generation used Meta Llama 3.2 3B Instruct fine-tuned with QLoRA on structured findings. All proportions are reported with 95% Wilson score intervals under a single analysis plan documented before the reported analyses were finalised. Results Withholding 1.80% of predictions (95% CI 1.14-2.83) raised selective accuracy to 97.76% (95% CI 96.63-98.52) and reduced selective risk from 3.40% to 2.24%, a relative reduction of 34.1%. Withheld predictions were strongly enriched for errors (66.7% versus 2.24%; odds ratio 87.3, Fisher exact p = 4.6 × 10 -15 ), capturing 35.3% of all errors while issuing 99.38% of the predictions that were correct. Considered as a detector of its own errors, the rule has a balanced accuracy of 67.34%; this describes the binary rejection decision at the realised threshold and does not identify the AUROC of the underlying continuous score, which the single operating point leaves anywhere in [0.351, 0.996]. Because the per-sample probability vectors were not retained, the full risk-coverage curve, the rule ablations and calibration error could not be computed, and the thresholds (τ c = 0.6, τ H = 1.0) were selected empirically on an undocumented partition; the selective-prediction finding is therefore reported as a single-operating-point case study and is exploratory. Among the complementary components, three-fold ensembling improved held-out mean Dice from 0.7948 to 0.8150 (+0.0202), reported descriptively because the per-case values needed for a paired test were not preserved. Glioma grading did not achieve better-than-chance discrimination: balanced accuracy 49.91%, Cohen's κ -0.0023, Matthews correlation coefficient -0.0026, low-grade recall 8.96% (95% CI 5.81-13.57), and accuracy (74.03%) below a constant majority-class classifier (79.46%); the associated McNemar statistic is reported descriptively because slice-level observations are not independent. Report generation produced high automatic similarity scores (BERTScore F1 0.9513) that are not interpretable without baselines. Conclusions Confidence- and entropy-based abstention produced a measurable reduction in selective risk at low rejection rates, and it did so because errors concentrated among the cases were withheld by the confidence/entropy rule rather than because predictions were discarded indiscriminately. At the realised coverage the rule captured 65.5% (95% bootstrap CI 41.9-87.8) of the reduction achievable by an oracle that rejects only true errors. The component-wise comparison shows that this reliability behaviour cannot be assumed for every module: high aggregate accuracy and useful discrimination came apart in the grading task. These findings are component-wise and do not constitute an end-to-end, externally validated or clinically validated pipeline. The vision-language evaluation is at image level: BRISC2025 carries no patient identifiers, so patient-level independence cannot be established and the reported intervals should be read with that constraint in mind.
originalAbstract:
Background

Automated brain-MRI analysis is usually judged by accuracy at a single operating point, yet a model that is accurate on average may still fail without signalling that it is about to fail. Selective prediction addresses this by allowing a model to abstain, but the resulting trade-off between coverage and risk is rarely quantified in medical imaging.

Objective

This study asks whether confidence- and entropy-based selective prediction produces a measurable reduction in selective risk in a biomedical vision-language classifier by concentrating errors among withheld cases, and at what coverage cost. Three further components of a brain-MRI-analysis framework-volumetric segmentation, glioma grading and structured report generation-are evaluated as complementary evidence about the reliability profiles of different modules, not as independent contributions.

Methods

A LoRA-fine-tuned LLaVA-Med classifier was evaluated on the 1000-image BRISC2025 test partition, with a disjunctive rejection rule based on softmax confidence and predictive entropy. Volumetric segmentation used nnU-Net v2 (3D full-resolution) on BraTS2020 with a three-fold ensemble evaluated on 74 held-out cases; glioma grading (high- versus low-grade) used DenseNet121 on multi-slice representations; report generation used Meta Llama 3.2 3B Instruct fine-tuned with QLoRA on structured findings. All proportions are reported with 95% Wilson score intervals under a single analysis plan documented before the reported analyses were finalised.

Results

Withholding 1.80% of predictions (95% CI 1.14-2.83) raised selective accuracy to 97.76% (95% CI 96.63-98.52) and reduced selective risk from 3.40% to 2.24%, a relative reduction of 34.1%. Withheld predictions were strongly enriched for errors (66.7% versus 2.24%; odds ratio 87.3, Fisher exact p = 4.6 × 10-15), capturing 35.3% of all errors while issuing 99.38% of the predictions that were correct. Considered as a detector of its own errors, the rule has a balanced accuracy of 67.34%; this describes the binary rejection decision at the realised threshold and does not identify the AUROC of the underlying continuous score, which the single operating point leaves anywhere in [0.351, 0.996]. Because the per-sample probability vectors were not retained, the full risk-coverage curve, the rule ablations and calibration error could not be computed, and the thresholds (τc = 0.6, τH = 1.0) were selected empirically on an undocumented partition; the selective-prediction finding is therefore reported as a single-operating-point case study and is exploratory. Among the complementary components, three-fold ensembling improved held-out mean Dice from 0.7948 to 0.8150 (+0.0202), reported descriptively because the per-case values needed for a paired test were not preserved. Glioma grading did not achieve better-than-chance discrimination: balanced accuracy 49.91%, Cohen's κ -0.0023, Matthews correlation coefficient -0.0026, low-grade recall 8.96% (95% CI 5.81-13.57), and accuracy (74.03%) below a constant majority-class classifier (79.46%); the associated McNemar statistic is reported descriptively because slice-level observations are not independent. Report generation produced high automatic similarity scores (BERTScore F1 0.9513) that are not interpretable without baselines.

Conclusions

Confidence- and entropy-based abstention produced a measurable reduction in selective risk at low rejection rates, and it did so because errors concentrated among the cases were withheld by the confidence/entropy rule rather than because predictions were discarded indiscriminately. At the realised coverage the rule captured 65.5% (95% bootstrap CI 41.9-87.8) of the reduction achievable by an oracle that rejects only true errors. The component-wise comparison shows that this reliability behaviour cannot be assumed for every module: high aggregate accuracy and useful discrimination came apart in the grading task. These findings are component-wise and do not constitute an end-to-end, externally validated or clinically validated pipeline. The vision-language evaluation is at image level: BRISC2025 carries no patient identifiers, so patient-level independence cannot be established and the reported intervals should be read with that constraint in mind.

title: DU-KAN: A Dual-Domain Enhanced Deep-Learning Framework for Digital Pathology-Based Oxford MEST-C Assessment in Pediatric IgA Nephropathy.
abstract: Oxford MEST-C assessment of pediatric immunoglobulin A nephropathy (IgAN) relies on pathologists' interpretation of complex renal biopsy structures. Automated segmentation may support standardized quantification but is challenged by scale variation, weak boundaries, and small lesions. We developed DU-KAN, a stage-adapted U-KAN framework combining a shallow convolution-MaxViT dual-branch encoder with adapted heterogeneous feature fusion and wavelet-prototype skip enhancement. A single-center dataset of 532 periodic acid-Schiff-stained images from 278 children was partitioned at the patient level. On the held-out test set of 55 patients, DU-KAN achieved a mean Dice of 69.58% across eight classes, including background (95% patient-level bootstrap CI, 66.23-71.91), exceeding U-KAN by 3.56 percentage points (95% CI, 1.90-5.26). Foreground mean Dice was 65.42%. On the Synapse abdominal CT benchmark, mean Dice across eight organs was 87.21%, supporting cross-task architectural generalization, rather than external validation in pediatric IgAN. Segmentation outputs were further aggregated into case-level MEST-C-related indicators. In an exploratory 40-case evaluation, complete agreement across the five assessed indicators was 65.00% (26/40), while sensitivity was 37.50% for E (3/8) and 50.00% for T (1/2). The 97.50% agreement for T largely reflected the predominance of negative cases and did not establish reliable positive-case detection. DU-KAN improves the internal segmentation performance and achieves structured pathological quantification, which can provide auxiliary reference for clinical judgment of renal pathologists.

title: VLM-Based Mesh Segmentation Framework for DDH Robotic Ultrasound.
abstract: For robotic ultrasound targeting developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH), reconstructed infant body-surface meshes should preserve the target surface while excluding bed, support, and background geometry. This study proposes a structured vision-language model (VLM)-based multi-view segmentation method for infant phantom mesh cleanup. Text-guided 2D masks provide foreground and background evidence; mask-quality statistics and structured VLM assessments generate view-specific foreground-support weights that undergo deterministic risk suppression before target/non-target classification of 3D vertices. Hard voting and Rule-weighted voting were baselines under identical projection and post-processing settings. We evaluated one physical infant phantom across 150 separate acquisition-reconstruction trials under controlled conditions, each comprising 40 voting views and 10 held-out evaluation views, yielding 1500 manually annotated reference masks. Structured VLM voting achieved a Balanced score (intersection over union minus the 2-pixel tolerant leakage rate) of 0.804 ± 0.085, versus 0.801 ± 0.084 and 0.793 ± 0.086 for Rule-weighted and Hard voting. This leakage rate was 0.087 ± 0.043, versus 0.089 ± 0.042 and 0.092 ± 0.043; mean Coverage remained similar (0.992-0.993). The Balanced-score gain and leakage-rate reduction relative to Rule-weighted voting remained significant after Holm correction (adjusted p = 0.029 and p = 0.033, respectively). Validation using real-infant data, 3D reference standards, and closed-loop robotic scanning is still required.

title: Cross-Dataset Generalization of Deep Learning for Retinal Vessel Segmentation in Fundus Images: External Evaluation from DRIVE to CHASE_DB1.
abstract: Automated retinal vessel segmentation can support quantitative analysis of fundus photographs and facilitate measurement of vascular characteristics associated with ocular and systemic disease. Although deep-learning methods achieve high segmentation performance on benchmark datasets, their reliability may decrease when applied to images obtained under different acquisition conditions. This study evaluated the cross-dataset generalizability of a U-Net segmentation architecture incorporating an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet34 encoder. Sixteen images from the DRIVE dataset were used for model training and four were retained for in-domain validation. Images were resized to 256 × 256 pixels and processed using a consistent normalization pipeline, while spatial and photometric augmentation was applied during training. Without target-domain retraining or domain adaptation, the trained model was subsequently evaluated on the independent CHASE_DB1 dataset. Segmentation performance was assessed using the Dice coefficient, intersection over union (IoU), and sensitivity, together with qualitative examination of predicted vessel maps. On the held-out DRIVE images, the model achieved a Dice coefficient of 0.7263, IoU of 0.5703, and sensitivity of 0.7201. On CHASE_DB1, performance decreased to 0.6269, 0.4573, and 0.5502, respectively. The disproportionately larger reduction in sensitivity indicated an increased frequency of missed vessel pixels under cross-dataset evaluation. Qualitative examination showed greater fragmentation and omission of fine and peripheral vascular structures in CHASE_DB1 images. These findings demonstrate that within-dataset performance may overestimate the robustness of retinal vessel segmentation models when transferred to a different imaging domain. External evaluation should therefore form an important component of retinal imaging artificial intelligence research. Future work should investigate higher-resolution processing, vessel-width-specific evaluation, multi-domain training, domain-adaptation strategies, and larger multicentre datasets to improve model generalizability.

title: ABR-DeepLabV3+: Adaptive Boundary-Refined Multi-Backbone DeepLabV3+ for MRI Brain Tumor Segmentation.
abstract: Accurate brain tumor segmentation from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is essential for diagnosis, treatment planning, surgical guidance, and quantitative tumor assessment. However, automated segmentation remains challenging due to the heterogeneous tumor appearance, irregular morphology, weak tissue contrast, and ambiguous tumor boundaries. Conventional encoder-decoder segmentation models, including DeepLabV3+, can capture multi-scale semantic information but may still produce boundary inconsistencies when tumor margins are diffuse or visually similar to surrounding tissues. To address this limitation, this study proposes ABR-DeepLabV3+, an Adaptive Boundary-Refined Multi-Backbone DeepLabV3+ framework for MRI brain tumor segmentation. The proposed framework integrates an Adaptive Boundary Refinement (ABR) module after decoder fusion to enhance boundary-sensitive feature representation before final mask prediction. Four encoder backbones, namely InceptionResNetV2, Xception, MobileNetV2, and ResNet50, were evaluated under the same framework using the Figshare Brain Tumor Segmentation (FBTS) dataset consisting of 3064 MRI images from meningioma, glioma, and pituitary tumor classes. The evaluation employed patient-level train-validation-test partitioning together with patient-grouped five-fold cross-validation to reduce subject-level information leakage between data subsets. Experimental results show that ABR-DeepLabV3+ with Xception achieved the best overall test performance, with accuracy of 0.9994, Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) of 0.9753, and Jaccard Index (JI) of 0.9519. ResNet50 also achieved competitive performance with DSC of 0.9732 and JI of 0.9478, while MobileNetV2 demonstrated strong class-wise performance for meningioma and pituitary tumors. For the Xception configuration, the component-wise ablation analysis showed that Full ABR achieved higher performance than both plain DeepLabV3+ and an ordinary convolutional refinement control. Relative to plain DeepLabV3+, Full ABR increased DSC from 0.89002 to 0.97530 and JI from 0.80183 to 0.95190, while reducing the 95th-percentile Hausdorff Distance (HD95) from 8.72 to 3.28 pixels and the Average Symmetric Surface Distance (ASSD) from 2.41 to 0.87 pixels. Five-fold cross-validation showed that the Xception-based configuration achieved the highest mean DSC of 0.9017 and mean JI of 0.8258 among the evaluated backbones; however, the lower cross-validation mean relative to the single-split test result indicates sensitivity to patient-level data partitioning rather than unconditional evidence of robustness. Qualitative analysis using segmentation overlays, error heatmaps, and prediction-region heatmaps illustrated representative patterns of contour agreement and localized residual segmentation error without interpreting prediction-derived heatmaps as internal model attention or attribution. Overall, the findings indicate that the proposed ABR design improves within-dataset tumor-region overlap and boundary agreement relative to plain DeepLabV3+ under the evaluated experimental conditions, while external validation and repeated-run statistical evaluation remain necessary to establish broader generalizability and reproducibility.

title: Theranostic Imaging Agents: Integrating Molecular Diagnostics, Precision Therapeutics, and Artificial Intelligence.
abstract: Theranostic imaging agents combine molecular diagnosis, targeted therapy and monitoring of treatment response into a single paradigm of precision medicine. This review summarizes the current development and translational landscape of theranostic imaging agents, covering molecular targets, imaging platforms, principles of agent design, nanotheranostics, radiotheranostics, and disease-specific applications. Particular emphasis is given to clinically validated and emerging targeting strategies using prostate-specific membrane antigen, somatostatin receptors, fibroblast activation protein, C-X-C Chemokine Receptor 4 (CXCR4), Human Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor 2 (HER2) and other disease-associated biomarkers. Moreover, the review addresses Positron Emission Tomography (PET), Single-Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT), Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), optical, photoacoustic, Raman and multimodal imaging approaches, therapeutic payloads, stimulus-responsive systems, and pharmacokinetic optimization. Moreover, emerging applications of artificial intelligence, radiomics, radiogenomics, spatial and single-cell multiomics, liquid biopsy, digital pathology, personalized dosimetry, and digital twins are evaluated for their potential to improve patient stratification, treatment selection, response assessment and adaptive therapy. Despite tremendous progress, clinical translation is hampered by target heterogeneity, off-target accumulation, radionuclide availability, manufacturing complexity, dosimetric uncertainty, regulatory requirements, limited clinical validation, data interoperability, cost and unequal access. This review, overall, emphasizes the convergence of molecular imaging, targeted therapeutics, nanotechnology, and artificial intelligence in the development of next-generation theranostic platforms, and outlines critical priorities for their clinical translation.

title: Focused Ultrasound-Mediated Blood-Brain Barrier Opening for Enhanced Drug Delivery in Diffuse Gliomas: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Background/Objectives: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) severely limits the intratumoral delivery of systemically administered therapeutics in diffuse gliomas, including glioblastoma (GBM), contributing to the persistently poor prognosis of these tumors. Focused ultrasound (FUS) combined with microbubble agents enables transient, spatially targeted, and reversible BBB opening (BBBO), offering a non-invasive strategy to enhance drug delivery in this setting. Despite a rapidly growing body of clinical evidence, a systematic synthesis of outcomes across FUS platforms, drug regimens, and study designs is currently lacking. This systematic review aims to critically appraise the available clinical evidence on FUS-mediated BBBO for enhanced drug delivery in adult patients with diffuse gliomas. Methods: A systematic search of PubMed/MEDLINE and Scopus was performed using pre-specified search terms (last search: June 2026). Eligible studies included clinical trials and cohort studies enrolling adult patients (≥18 years) with histologically confirmed diffuse glioma (WHO grades II-IV) who underwent FUS-BBBO for therapeutic drug delivery enhancement. Two reviewers independently screened records and extracted data using a standardized form. Study quality was assessed using the NIH Quality Assessment Tool for Before-After Studies (single-arm studies) and the ROBINS-I tool (comparative studies). The review was retrospectively registered on OSF. Results were synthesized narratively due to study heterogeneity. Results: Eight publications from seven independent clinical studies were included. Across these publications, 68 patient entries were reported; however, because of overlapping populations across publications, the number of unique patients could not be precisely determined. Two FUS platforms were employed, with the ExAblate Neuro system (220-230 kHz) used in six out of seven cohorts. BBB opening was confirmed in all studies, with target sonication success rates of 92.4-100%. No procedure-related serious adverse events attributable to FUS-BBBO were reported across any study. Transient T2/SWAN hypointense foci were observed in a subset of patients, consistently asymptomatic and histologically benign. Direct intratumoral drug quantification was feasible in two pre-surgical studies, demonstrating a 2.2-fold increase in drug accumulation in FUS-treated versus untreated tissue ( p < 0.01). The only comparative study reported a statistically significant improvement in overall survival (median 31.3 vs. 19.3 months; HR 0.50, p = 0.009) and progression-free survival (median 13.5 vs. 8.1 months; HR 0.55, p = 0.020) versus the controls. Conclusions: FUS-mediated BBBO is a safe and feasible approach for enhancing drug delivery in adult diffuse glioma patients across multiple platforms and drug combinations. Preliminary comparative data suggest a potential survival benefit in newly diagnosed GBM; however, these findings are based on a single non-randomized study and require confirmation in prospective randomized controlled trials.

title: A SAM2 and VLM-Based Automatic Radiological Reporting System for Pneumothorax Detection.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Pneumothorax, caused by air accumulation in the pleural space, can lead to lung collapse and, if diagnosis is delayed, respiratory or cardiovascular deterioration. Most deep-learning studies on pneumothorax address classification or segmentation alone. This study proposes a holistic automatic radiological reporting system combining U-Net-based segmentation, Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2)-based boundary refinement, and a Vision-Language Model (VLM)-based reporting module for pneumothorax detection on computed tomography (CT) images. Methods: A MobileNetV2-encoder U-Net was trained on 224×224 CT patches from 171 patients (15,555 patches). A frozen, zero-shot SAM2 module, guided by a box prompt derived from the U-Net mask, was combined with U-Net via an Intersection over Union (IoU)-agreement rule. The refined mask and rule-based geometric features were passed to a frozen VLM (Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct) to generate structured reports with a combined confidence coefficient. Performance was evaluated with Accuracy, Dice, IoU, and Loss, over all patches and over pneumothorax-positive patches only. Results: U-Net achieved 93.09/92.09/99.71% (Dice/IoU/Accuracy) on validation and 93.68/92.79/99.79% on the test set; these largely reflect correct empty-mask prediction on negative patches. On positive patches only, Dice was 0.6295 (validation) and 0.6215 (test), with patch-level sensitivity of 82.2% (validation) and 79.9% (test) and specificity above 97%. SAM2 refinement achieved 92.44% Dice and 91.29% IoU on a random test subsample ( n ≈ 300), close to but not exceeding U-Net alone; an ablation analysis confirmed no consistent Dice/IoU or 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95) gain from SAM2. BLEU/ROUGE and Likert evaluation frameworks for the VLM reports were defined but not yet scored against reference reports. Conclusions: U-Net-based segmentation reliably identifies pneumothorax-containing patches with moderate boundary accuracy, while frozen SAM2 refinement adds limited value. The rule-based reporting layer is reproducible and shows triage-support potential, whereas the VLM free-text layer carries a documented hallucination risk and requires radiologist verification before clinical use.

title: Head-Mounted Augmented Reality in the Planning of Cerebral Cavernous Malformation Resections: Demonstrating Feasibility Through an Initial Case Series.
abstract: Objectives Lesion localization, associated vascular structures, and corticotomy selection pose key challenges when planning cerebral cavernous malformation (CCM) resections in eloquent areas. Head-mounted augmented reality (HMAR) may improve visualization without the gaze disruptions imposed by conventional neuronavigation. This study investigated the preoperative feasibility of HMAR in surgical plan modifications and educational value. Methods We performed a single-center retrospective review of all CCM patients with HMAR-assisted preoperative planning from 1 September, 2022, to 31 August, 2024. Three-dimensional reconstructions of patients' magnetic resonance imaging were viewed preoperatively using HMAR. Registration accuracy was confirmed against conventional neuronavigation. Surgical plan modifications entailed alterations of the operative goal, trajectory, or steps. Educational value of HMAR was appraised by trainees as "not helpful" when only confirming existing plans, "helpful" when facilitating a greater understanding of the lesion, and "very helpful" when spurring additional positioning or plan modifications. Results Of 19 patients with CCM resections, 14 patients with HMAR-assisted preoperative planning were included. The average age was 38.6 ± 14.5 years, with 6 males and 8 females. Three of 14 (21%) surgical approaches were modified following HMAR use: two to minimize cortical disruption and one to avoid injuring an associated developmental venous anomaly. Registration was accurate in all cases. Between registration and utilization, HMAR added an average of 2.7 ± 1.0 min in the operating room. The mean appraisal of the educational value of HMAR was "helpful." Conclusions Preoperative planning with HMAR prompted surgical plan modifications and often improved trainees' understanding without introducing significant workflow disruptions. Three-dimensional visualization offered dynamic spatial details beyond traditional two-dimensional multiplanar MRI.

title: Tractometric: A Diffusion Tractography Software Engine for Integration into a Neuronavigation System: Technical Development and Preliminary Clinical Feasibility.
abstract: Background Diffusion MRI tractography can support patient-specific neurosurgical planning, but implementation may be limited by workflow complexity, software requirements, and resource constraints. We describe Tractometric ® , a diffusion tractography software engine developed for integration with the Surgimetric ® neuronavigation planning environment. Methods Tractometric ® was developed through a multidisciplinary, iterative co-design process involving neurosurgeons and neuroimaging specialists. The software uses a modular Model-View-Controller architecture implemented in Python (version 3.11) and supports multiple diffusion reconstruction models, deterministic and probabilistic tracking, patient-specific and atlas-derived regions of interest (ROIs), visualization, and interoperable export. The present study was designed as a technical development and preliminary clinical feasibility report. Technical workflow characteristics were described retrospectively across 30 cases, while preliminary clinical feasibility was explored in 8 patients undergoing tractography-assisted surgical planning. Intraoperative direct cortical and subcortical electrical stimulation was used as a qualitative clinical reference rather than as a formal diagnostic-accuracy test. Results Tractometric ® implemented a complete workflow from diffusion data loading and preprocessing to tract reconstruction, filtering, visualization, and export to Surgimetric ® . The 30-case technical series illustrated variation in processing time and user interaction according to operator experience, reconstruction model, registration, ROI strategy, and manual cleaning. In 8 preliminary clinical cases, reconstructed motor and language pathways were qualitatively concordant with positive intraoperative stimulation findings. No formal sensitivity, specificity, spatial agreement, or test-retest reproducibility estimates were calculated. Conclusions Tractometric ® provides an integrated technical workflow for diffusion tractography and neuronavigation planning and was feasible to implement in a preliminary clinical series. The current data support technical feasibility and workflow integration, but do not establish anatomical accuracy, reproducibility, clinical efficacy, or cost-effectiveness. Independent, prospective validation using standardized acquisitions, predefined tractography parameters, quantitative spatial metrics, and systematic intraoperative mapping is warranted.

title: MedNeXt-Based Automated Tumor Segmentation and TMTV Prognostication in Hodgkin Lymphoma PET Images: A Retrospective Study.
abstract: Background/Objectives : To evaluate a deep learning-based method for automatic segmentation of Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) on PET images and to explore the prognostic value of total metabolic tumor volume (TMTV) derived from segmentation. Methods : PET datasets from two independent institutions were retrospectively collected and divided into training and validation cohorts. MedNeXt was trained for HL PET segmentation and benchmarked against five representative segmentation architectures under the same data split, preprocessing pipeline, and evaluation framework. Segmentation performance was assessed using the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), Jaccard index (JSC), 95th percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95), and average symmetric surface distance (ASSD). Bland-Altman and linear regression analyses evaluated agreement between ground-truth TMTV (gtTMTV) and predicted TMTV (pTMTV). Cox proportional hazards regression analysis was applied to assess the prognostic value of pTMTV. Results : In the validation cohort, the mean values (±standard deviation) of DSC, HD95, JSC, and ASSD were 0.702 ± 0.191, 67.998 ± 99.220, 0.561 ± 0.203, and 16.992 ± 31.659, respectively. Among the evaluated segmentation models, MedNeXt showed the best segmentation performance. Mean gtTMTV and pTMTV were 424.681 ± 498.811 cm 3 and 405.871 ± 466.984 cm 3 , showing good agreement. pTMTV was significantly associated with progression-free survival (PFS) ( p = 0.048), but not overall survival (OS) ( p = 0.163). Conclusions : MedNeXt achieved reliable HL segmentation, although tumor boundary delineation requires further improvement. The derived pTMTV may serve as a prognostic indicator for PFS but showed no significant association with OS. Further validation in larger cohorts is warranted.
