title: Comparative Evaluation of Feature Selection Algorithms for Predicting Radiation-Induced Complications in Head and Neck Cancer Using Multimodal CT and MRI Radiomics.
abstract: Head and neck cancer (HNC) presents a significant challenge due to its anatomic complexity and treatment-related complications such as sticky saliva and xerostomia, which critically impair patients' quality of life. Recent advancements in imaging technologies, using the concept of radiomics, offer promising approaches for predicting these complications and ultimately reducing their incidence. In this regard, robust feature selection is critical in radiomics-based predictive modeling due to the high dimensionality, redundancy, and instability of extracted imaging biomarkers. This study aims to evaluate nine distinct feature selection algorithms-Boruta, Kruskal, Recursive Maximum Relevance minimum redundancy (R-MRmr), Relief, Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE), Forward Selection (FS), Backward Elimination (BE), Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO), and Principal Component Analysis (PCA)-as a feature-transformation comparator for predicting sticky saliva and xerostomia in HNC patients using clinical, dosimetric, MRI and CT radiomics data. The study involved 250 HNC patients who underwent radiotherapy from three different institutions. From MRI and CT images, a total of 321 radiomic features (107 from each CT, T1, and T2-weighted MRI) along with 20 clinical and dosimetric features were extracted. The predictive robustness of feature selection methods was further evaluated across five machine-learning classifiers, including K-nearest neighbors (KNN), support vector machine (SVM), random forest (RF), logistic regression (LR), and eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), were initially benchmarked using a common feature selection procedure, after which SVM was selected as the reference classifier for systematic comparison of the feature-reduction approaches. Model performance was assessed using metrics objectives such as Area Under the Curve (AUC), accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity. Among the evaluated feature selection approaches, R-MRmr and Relief generally yielded better discrimination, although performance varied according to toxicity endpoint and imaging modality. The highest AUCs were 0.85 for early sticky saliva (R-MRmr, T1-weighted MRI), 0.96 for early xerostomia (R-MRmr, T1-weighted MRI), 0.65 for late sticky saliva (Relief, combined CT+T1+T2), and 0.88 for late xerostomia (Relief, T1-weighted MRI). T1-weighted MRI frequently provided better individual-modality performance, whereas combining all three imaging modalities did not consistently improve discrimination. These findings demonstrate that the choice of feature selection strategy and imaging modality can materially influence radiomics-based toxicity prediction.

title: GammaTile ® Brachytherapy as Spatially Fractionated Radiation Therapy for Postoperative Brain Cancer: A Paradigm for Precision Intracranial Radiotherapy.
abstract: Purpose: Tile-based radiation therapy (TBRT) delivers adjuvant radiation to brain tumor beds using evenly spaced cesium-131 (Cs-131) sources in collagen tiles. This study evaluated TBRT as spatially fractionated radiation therapy (SFRT) across tumor sizes and source counts. Methods and Materials: Dose distributions were generated from postoperative CT scans for 18 patients treated with TBRT, using 10-32 implanted Cs-131 sources per case (median, 20). The resection cavity (RC) was contoured on CT with registered postoperative T1-weighted MRI guidance. CTV_5mm was defined as the RC plus a 5 mm expansion excluding skull and surgical tract, and CTV_5mm_Eval as CTV_5mm minus the RC. Both volumes were analyzed using SFRT dose metrics from the Radiosurgery Society SFRT/Flash working group white paper, and planar high-dose core number density (HCND_A) was used to characterize TBRT spatial fractionation. Results : The mean dose indices of D5 (dose covering 5% of the target volume), D10, D50, D90, D95 and D100 were 175.8 ± 43.3, 148.8 ± 35.1, 86.7 ± 18.5, 56.1 ± 10.5, 50.2 ± 9.0 and 33.4 ± 7.2 Gy for the CTV_5mm_Eval, respectively. The heterogeneity indices, represented by the ratio of D5/D95 and D10/D90, were 3.5 ± 0.6 and 2.7 ± 0.4, respectively, which were in the range of the linac-based Lattice therapy. HCND_A was a constant, TBRT delivered one high dose core for every 1 cm 2 of tumor bed. All dose metrics in both the CTV_5mm and CTV_5mm_Eval were largely consistent across all plans. Conclusions : TBRT produced heterogeneous dose distributions comparable to conventional SFRT. A 60 Gy TBRT nominal prescription dose approximated the SFRT D90, or valley dose of the 5 mm expansion target volume, suggesting TBRT may provide an SFRT platform for tile-accessible cancers.

title: Cytoreductive Radical Prostatectomy in Oligometastatic Prostate Cancer and the Role of the Robotic Platform: A Narrative Review.
abstract: Background : Oligometastatic prostate cancer (OMPC) comprises biologically and clinically distinct states with a limited number of detectable metastases. Improved systemic therapy and prostate-specific membrane antigen positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PSMA PET/CT) have intensified interest in treating the primary tumor. Methods : In this narrative review we searched PubMed/MEDLINE from inception to 1 July 2026, reviewed current guidelines, and searched ClinicalTrials.gov, the ISRCTN registry and the EU Clinical Trials Register for ongoing surgical studies, prioritizing randomized trials, prospective studies, PSMA PET-staged cohorts, systematic reviews, guidelines, and studies of perioperative, functional and patient-reported outcomes. Results : Registry and institutional data generated the hypothesis that cytoreductive prostatectomy improves outcomes but are vulnerable to selection bias; prospective and PSMA PET-staged cohorts established feasibility. The phase II trial by Dai and colleagues supported radical treatment of the primary tumor but combined surgery and radiotherapy. RAMPP provided the first prostatectomy-specific randomized signal, with lower 5-year cancer-specific mortality after radical prostatectomy plus best systemic therapy than after systemic therapy alone (13% versus 23%; hazard ratio 0.39, 95% confidence interval 0.16-0.98), but accrual ended early, clinical progression was similar, overall survival was not significantly improved, systemic therapy predated contemporary intensification, and major surgery-related complications occurred in 14%. A randomized phase II trial with a predominantly surgical local-therapy arm found no progression-free or overall survival benefit, so randomized evidence is mixed. All randomized evidence concerns radical prostatectomy or local treatment irrespective of surgical approach; no trial has tested a robot-specific oncologic effect. Guidelines recommend prostate radiotherapy for selected low-volume de novo metastatic disease and restrict surgery to clinical trials. Conclusions : Cytoreductive prostatectomy, delivered mostly as robot-assisted radical prostatectomy (RARP), is feasible and may improve local control while providing complete pathology, but it remains investigational; the robotic approach is the surgical platform, not a modality with distinct oncologic efficacy. Appropriate use requires expert-center surgery, modern staging, guideline-concordant systemic therapy, multidisciplinary selection, transparent counseling and, preferably, trial participation. Future trials must establish whether prostatectomy adds meaningful benefit beyond modern systemic therapy, prostate radiotherapy and metastasis-directed treatment, while measuring morbidity, continence and quality of life.

title: Worsening of Oral Health Parameters After Head and Neck Radiotherapy-Findings from a Multidisciplinary Head and Neck Tumor Board: A Prospective Observational Study.
abstract: Objectives To evaluate (a) changes in caries experience, (b) changes in periodontal status, and (c) the need for dental extractions in a cohort of patients treated with radiotherapy (RT) and chemoradiotherapy (RTCT) for head and neck cancer (HNC). Methods This prospective cohort study was approved by the local Ethics Committee (Ref. 22858/18) and registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (ID: NCT04009161). The study population consisted of patients with HNC who, prior to RT, underwent a dental examination followed by the elimination of oral foci of infection and were then enrolled in a follow-up program. The primary outcome was oral health worsening, defined as the onset of severe periodontitis and/or a DMFt score ≥ 13. Oral cavity RT dose was obtained contouring the 'buccal mucosa' organ at risk (OAR). Results In total, 113 patients were included (median follow-up: 44.77 months). The sample mainly included oral, oropharyngeal, nasopharyngeal and laryngeal cancers (89/113, 78.8%). Salivary glands, hypopharynx and other sites accounted for a minority of the cases (24/113, 21.2%). Seventeen patients (34.7%) experienced worsening of oral health status over time, which was associated with smoking (OR = 4.7, 95% CI: 1.27-17.37; p = 0.02). The DMFt index increased (difference: 4.08; 95% CI: 1.60-6.56; p = 0.001), and this increase was associated with smoking (β = 2.05, 95% CI: 0.27-3.83; p = 0.02). Although worsening of periodontitis stage was not statistically significant ( p = 0.35), localized deterioration was observed, with an increase in sites with PPD ≥ 5 mm ( p = 0.02). Forty-nine patients (43.4%) experienced tooth loss. Mean tooth loss was 2.12 teeth per patient ( p = 0.05), primarily due to caries (48.5%) and periodontitis (48.1%). Independent risk factors for tooth loss were age ( p = 0.025) and an RT dose > 60 Gy to the 'buccal mucosa' OAR ( p = 0.023). Conclusions Patients treated with RT experienced significant deterioration in dental and periodontal health, and oral cavity dosimetric parameters might be associated with tooth loss, although this association requires confirmation in further studies.

title: PET Tumour Segmentation in Head and Neck Cancer: Reproducibility, Reader Dependence and Concordance with CT-Defined Tumour Volume in a 154-Patient Cohort.
abstract: Purpose: Volumetric PET biomarkers carry substantial prognostic value in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), yet their clinical implementation is hampered by segmentation heterogeneity. A fundamental and unresolved question is which segmentation method is most suitable for routine clinical use, both for a reader experienced in PET segmentation and for a reader without PET segmentation experience, such as an ENT surgeon or a radiation oncologist. This study addressed this question by assessing the intra- and interobserver reproducibility of four PET segmentation methods in MIM Maestro Software Version 7.4.2, identifying tumour-related determinants of variability, and examining concordance between PET-derived metabolic tumour volume (MTV) and CT-based gross tumour volume (GTV). Methods: Two readers with contrasting PET segmentation experience, a nuclear medicine physician experienced in PET segmentation (R1) and an ENT surgeon without prior PET segmentation training (R2), applied four methods to the primary tumours of 154 patients with HNSCC (oral cavity, oropharynx, hypopharynx or larynx) treated with definitive (chemo)radiotherapy between 2010 and 2021: fixed absolute thresholds at SUV 3.0 and 4.0, a relative threshold at 41% of the maximum standardised uptake value (SUVmax), and a gradient edge-detection algorithm (PET Edge+). R1 segmented twice with a washout of at least 4 weeks; R2 performed one session and delineated CT-GTV in the 85 patients whose PET/CT-derived CT served directly as the radiotherapy planning scan. The second session of R1 served as the reference for all interobserver and MTV-GTV analyses. Agreement was assessed by ICC (two-way mixed model), coefficient of variation, repeatability coefficient and Bland-Altman analysis; determinants of variability by a multivariable linear mixed-effects model with a random intercept per patient. Results: All four methods demonstrated excellent intraobserver (ICC 0.993 to >0.999) and interobserver (ICC 0.989-0.996) reproducibility. SUV3.0 generated significantly more relative error than SUV41% (β = +3.1%; 95% CI 0.89, 5.3). PET Edge+ was the only method for which a significant method × reader interaction was observed in this reader pair: the reader without PET segmentation experience generated more error than the reader experienced in PET segmentation (β = +7.1%; 95% CI 3.9, 10), an effect concentrated in smaller tumours (below approximately 15 mL); in the 85-patient GTV subset, where tumours were larger on average, the interobserver ICC for PET Edge+ was 0.997. GTV concordance was good for three of four methods (ICC 0.808-0.895); SUV41% showed only moderate concordance (ICC 0.572). Conclusions: All four methods provided excellent volumetric reproducibility within a single clinical software platform, but they differed in reader dependence and in agreement with CT-defined GTV. Rather than supporting a universal segmentation standard, these findings suggest that the method should be selected according to its intended application, pending multicentre confirmation.

title: Interpretable CT-Based Radiomics for Prediction of High-Affinity Neoantigens Associated Immunogenic States in Advanced Hepatocellular Carcinoma Treated with TACE Plus Targeted Therapy and Immunotherapy.
abstract: Objectives: To develop and validate a CT radiomics-based machine learning model for the noninvasive prediction of HANS status in advanced HCC and to investigate the prognostic and genomic characteristics associated with HANS status. Materials and Methods: This retrospective study included patients with advanced HCC treated with TACE-based triplet therapy. Patients were followed until death or last follow-up. Tumor tissue underwent whole-exome sequencing for HANS calculation, and arterial-phase CT images were used for radiomic feature extraction. A radiomics model (HANS-Rad), a clinical model (HANS-Clin), and a combined model (HANS-RC) were developed using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression. Model performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic curve analysis. Calibration and decision curve analyses were performed to assess model reliability and clinical utility. Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) were used for model interpretation. Genomic analyses were conducted to explore differences between predicted HANS subgroups. Results: A total of 129 patients were included (median age, 54 years; IQR, 44-62 years; 90% men). The HANS-High group demonstrated longer overall survival compared with the HANS-Low group (median, 23.0 vs. 10.0 months; hazard ratio, 0.60; p = 0.026). The combined HANS-RC model achieved the best performance, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.964 in the training set and 0.869 (95% CI, 0.716-1.000) in the test set, outperforming the radiomics-only and clinical models. The model also showed favorable calibration and net benefit. Genomic analyses revealed that HANS-High tumors exhibited higher tumor mutational burden and enrichment of immune-related and oncogenic pathways, whereas HANS-Low tumors were associated with distinct mutational patterns and pathway alterations. Conclusions: A radiomics-based machine learning model using CT images enables the noninvasive prediction of HANS status in advanced HCC, with strong prognostic relevance and biologic interpretability supported by genomic analyses.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Pancreatic Cancer: From Predictive Performance to Clinical Translation.
abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is now applied across the pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) pathway, yet the literature has grown faster than the evidence needed to act on it. The question is not whether an algorithm can predict an endpoint, but whether it yields information reliable, generalizable, and actionable enough to change a clinically meaningful decision. Methods In this narrative, in a non-systematic review of PDAC-specific literature, we grade applications on an author-defined evidence-readiness framework (development, internal, external, prospective validation, clinical impact, and implementation) and on four dimensions-validation, comparator, actionability, and impact. Findings Contemporary meta-analyses show high pooled accuracy for AI-based early detection and for distinguishing PDAC from mass-forming pancreatitis (sensitivity ~0.88-0.92, specificity ~0.90-0.93), but with extreme heterogeneity, low radiomics quality, scarce external validation, and-for electronic health-record risk models-positive predictive values often below 1% at population prevalence. Computed tomography (CT)-based detection and risk enrichment are among the more mature applications identified, yet none has been shown to improve stage distribution, resection rate, or survival. Treatment prediction is held to a strict standard, distinguishing prognostic association from a validated treatment-by-biomarker interaction. Conclusions The rate-limiting steps are no longer algorithmic but translational-external and prospective validation, calibration, appropriate comparators, and workflow integration.

title: Vitreoretinal Lymphoma: From Pathobiology to Integrated Diagnosis.
abstract: Vitreoretinal lymphoma (VRL) is a rare, high-grade intraocular malignancy able to mimic intermediate and/or posterior uveitis. Diagnosis is difficult because lymphomatous cells in ocular samples are scarce, fragile and rapidly degraded, particularly after corticosteroid exposure. This review examines how current knowledge of VRL pathobiology is reflected in its clinical, imaging and laboratory features and how these can inform diagnosis. Cytology remains the confirmatory test, while multimodal imaging helps localise vitreous, intraretinal and sub retinal pigmented epithelium (RPE) involvement and guides ocular sampling. Diagnostic yield depends on appropriate sample collection, handling and timely processing. Cytokine and molecular testing, including interleukin-10 (IL-10)/interleukin-6 (IL-6) assessment and detection of recurrent lymphoma-associated alterations such as MYD88 and CD79B, can provide diagnostic support when morphology is inconclusive. We also examine newer approaches designed to increase the information obtained from small-volume ocular samples through quantitative imaging and high-dimensional molecular profiling. The diagnostic value of each test depends on the anatomical distribution of disease and the characteristics of the specimen and is greatest when complementary findings are interpreted together.

title: MRI-Based Prediction of Immunotherapy Response in Breast Cancer: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Background: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have been shown to improve long term outcomes and pathological complete response (pCR) rates in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). However, treatment response remains heterogeneous. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has emerged as a promising noninvasive biomarker for predicting response to immunotherapy-containing treatment regimens. Purpose: To systematically review studies evaluating MRI biomarkers for predicting response to immunotherapy-containing treatment regimens in breast cancer. Methods: A PRISMA-guided systematic review of PubMed was performed for studies published between June 2019 and June 2026 evaluating MRI-based prediction of pCR or immunotherapy response in breast cancer. Data regarding study design, MRI techniques, predictive performance, and study characteristics were extracted and qualitatively synthesized. Results: Across the ten included studies, conventional MRI generally demonstrated moderate predictive performance (AUC 0.65-0.75), whereas multiparametric radiomics models achieved the highest predictive performance (AUC up to 0.88). Several consistent themes emerged. Studies evaluating neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy (NACI) reported increased MRI-pathology discordance and reduced reliability of enhancement-based assessment alone, suggesting that conventional MRI response assessment may require refinement in this treatment setting. Functional MRI biomarkers, including diffusion-weighted imaging and dynamic enhancement metrics, identified treatment response earlier than baseline morphologic imaging, while radiomics models integrating MRI with clinical or molecular biomarkers consistently demonstrated the strongest predictive performance. However, evidence remained limited by heterogeneous imaging protocols, small study populations, and limited external validation. Conclusions: MRI, particularly multiparametric and radiomics-enhanced approaches, is evolving beyond conventional morphologic assessment to provide complementary information regarding tumor biology and treatment response in patients undergoing NACI. However, standardized imaging protocols and prospective multicenter validation are needed before MRI-derived biomarkers can be incorporated into routine clinical decision-making.

title: Precision Cardio-Oncology: A Multimodal Approach to Cancer Therapy-Related Cardiovascular Toxicity Prediction and Assessment.
abstract: Cancer therapy-related cardiovascular toxicity (CTR-CVT) is associated with morbidity, mortality, and interruptions to cancer treatment. Current cardio-oncology clinical assessment tools generally rely on a limited range of clinical data; however, in the era of precision medicine, it may be possible to leverage multimodal data, including imaging and multi-omic inputs, to personalise CTR-CVT prediction and assessment. In this review, we examine the genotypic and phenotypic predictors of CTR-CVT and the evidence supporting their incorporation into multimodal risk models. Most research focuses on cancer therapy-related cardiac dysfunction (CTRCD). We identify a strong evidence base for multimodal imaging-guided prediction, particularly cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) and transthoracic echocardiography (TTE)-derived global longitudinal strain measurements. Emerging evidence also supports the potential value of novel imaging parameters, including computed tomography (CT) and TTE-derived radiomic features. From the genomic and proteomic perspective, truncating titin variants and microRNA-126 may be informative predictors of cancer therapy-related cardiac dysfunction (CTRCD). At the same time, the literature also highlights potential epigenomic markers of CTR-CVT. Finally, we consider how these diverse data can be integrated into multimodal risk models and how digital innovation and advanced machine learning methods may further improve model predictive performance. However, a large implementation gap remains, with challenges such as data privacy and a lack of external validation studies preventing routine clinical implementation.

title: Microcystic Adnexal Carcinoma of the Head and Neck: Diagnostic Work-Up and Contemporary Treatment Strategies-A Narrative Review.
abstract: Background: Microcystic adnexal carcinoma (MAC) is a rare cutaneous adnexal malignancy characterized by slow clinical growth but pronounced local aggressiveness, extensive subclinical infiltration, and a propensity for perineural invasion. Owing to its rarity and often inconspicuous clinical presentation, diagnosis and treatment remain challenging, particularly in the anatomically complex head and neck region. Methods: A narrative review of the literature was performed using PubMed/MEDLINE and Embase, covering publications available up to August 2026. Relevant studies addressing the clinical presentation, diagnostic work-up, histopathology, imaging, surgical and non-surgical treatment, recurrence, and follow-up of MAC were reviewed, with particular emphasis on MAC arising in the head and neck region. Results: Adequate deep biopsy extending into the subcutaneous tissue is essential for reliable diagnosis, as superficial sampling may result in misdiagnosis. Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging may be considered when deep infiltration or clinically significant perineural spread is suspected, although MAC-specific imaging evidence is limited. Complete surgical excision with comprehensive microscopic margin assessment represents the cornerstone of treatment. Mohs micrographic surgery or staged excision with comprehensive peripheral and deep margin assessment may be favored when technically feasible; comparative evidence is retrospective and does not establish a survival advantage. More extensive oncological resection may be required for tumors involving deep structures or major nerves. Elective treatment of the clinically negative neck is generally not indicated because regional metastases are uncommon. Radiotherapy has a selective role in patients with high-risk features, unresectable disease, or inadequate surgical margins, but supporting evidence remains predominantly retrospective. Conclusions: Management of head and neck MAC should focus on accurate diagnosis and durable local and perineural disease control. Available evidence and expert guidance favor margin-controlled surgery, with radiotherapy considered selectively; the optimal treatment and surveillance strategies have not been prospectively established. Given the potential for late recurrence, prolonged clinical surveillance is warranted.

title: Is PET/CT Useful in Detecting Pneumocystis jirovecii Colonization in Patients with Primary Lung Cancer?
abstract: Background/Objectives: Pneumocystis jirovecii colonization induces persistent low-grade pulmonary inflammation, which may alter fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) uptake in positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT). We aimed to evaluate whether asymptomatic infection influences the maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax) or clinicopathological parameters of primary lung cancer. Methods: In this prospective single-center observational study, 107 consecutive patients undergoing surgical resection for primary lung cancer were enrolled. Preoperative FDG PET/CT scans were obtained within four weeks prior to surgery. Intraoperative respiratory secretions and lung tissue samples were analyzed for P. jirovecii , using nested polymerase chain reaction (nested-PCR) targeting the mitochondrial large subunit rRNA gene. Propensity score matching (PSM) adjusting for age, sex, and body mass index was performed across 1:1, 1:2, and 1:3 matching models. Results: Pneumocystis jirovecii colonization was confirmed in 12 of 107 patients (11.21%). In the unadjusted cohort, no significant differences in primary lesion SUVmax were identified between positive and negative patients (10.38 ± 6.50 vs. 8.86 ± 6.58, p = 0.411), nor across matched models (1:1: p = 0.555; 1:2: p = 0.951; 1:3: p = 0.926). Following PSM, patients without colonization exhibited significantly larger maximum tumor diameters in both 1:2 (30.71 ± 19.23 vs. 18.25 ± 6.63 mm, p = 0.035) and 1:3 matching models (29.08 ± 17.47 vs. 18.25 ± 6.63 mm, p = 0.035). Conclusions: We did not find any association between P. jirovecii colonization and preoperative metabolic tumor staging on FDG PET/CT. However, asymptomatic carriage was associated with smaller primary tumor dimensions following propensity adjustment in 1:2 and 1:3 matching models, warranting further exploration of host-fungal interactions within the pulmonary tumor microenvironment.

title: Transformer-Convolution Pyramid Network for Multi-Class Kidney, Tumor, and Cyst Segmentation.
abstract: Background/Objectives : Chronic kidney diseases are fatal disorders, and early treatment is crucial for reducing mortality. Segmenting kidneys, tumors, and cysts from computed tomography scans has a significant role in assessing these diseases' progression, determining their severity, and planning surgeries. However, accurate segmentation is challenging for many reasons. The objective of this study is to develop a hybrid network that can overcome these challenges. Methods : The proposed network was designed using (i) a patch-joining and swin transformer block to capture global features efficiently, (ii) a Dynamic Channel Attention block to emphasize significant feature locations with the help of channel-wise attention, (iii) a block to perform complementary fusion of features coming from different layers, (iv) an edge-detection block to improve the performance by paying extra attention to edge features, and (v) an efficient activation function to overcome dying neuron and bias-shifting problems caused by the commonly used rectified linear unit. Extensive experiments were conducted using images from KiTS-2023 and Kaggle databases. Also, state-of-the-art techniques were applied to identical datasets and evaluated using identical metrics for fair comparisons. In addition to the commonly used Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC), the Normalized Surface Distance (NSD) was used for evaluation. Results : The proposed method yields DSC/NSD scores of 98.35 ± 0.65%/97.62 ± 0.55%, 94.88 ± 0.57%/93.84 ± 0.50%, and 81.99 ± 0.45%/80.93 ± 0.40% for kidneys, tumors, and cysts, respectively. Conclusions : The results indicate the superiority of the proposed approach in segmenting kidneys, tumors, and cysts. The proposed method has the potential to support medical experts by providing quantitative and objective segmentation results.

Methods: The proposed network was designed using (i) a patch-joining and swin transformer block to capture global features efficiently, (ii) a Dynamic Channel Attention block to emphasize significant feature locations with the help of channel-wise attention, (iii) a block to perform complementary fusion of features coming from different layers, (iv) an edge-detection block to improve the performance by paying extra attention to edge features, and (v) an efficient activation function to overcome dying neuron and bias-shifting problems caused by the commonly used rectified linear unit. Extensive experiments were conducted using images from KiTS-2023 and Kaggle databases. Also, state-of-the-art techniques were applied to identical datasets and evaluated using identical metrics for fair comparisons. In addition to the commonly used Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC), the Normalized Surface Distance (NSD) was used for evaluation. Results: The proposed method yields DSC/NSD scores of 98.35 ± 0.65%/97.62 ± 0.55%, 94.88 ± 0.57%/93.84 ± 0.50%, and 81.99 ± 0.45%/80.93 ± 0.40% for kidneys, tumors, and cysts, respectively. Conclusions: The results indicate the superiority of the proposed approach in segmenting kidneys, tumors, and cysts. The proposed method has the potential to support medical experts by providing quantitative and objective segmentation results.

title: Prognostic Value of Baseline High-Uptake PSMA Tumor Volume Fraction in Metastatic Castration-Resistant Prostate Cancer Patients Treated with [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA Radioligand Therapy.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Lutetium-177 prostate-specific membrane antigen radioligand therapy ([ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA-RLT) is an effective treatment for patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC), but no validated PSMA-PET/CT-based biomarker currently identifies patients at risk of early treatment failure. The aim of this study was to assess whether semi-quantitative PSMA-PET/CT parameters, in particular the fraction of PSMA-positive tumor volume with high uptake, are associated with early biochemical progression (EBP) and PSA50 response and secondarily with PSA-PFS and OS. Methods: Semiquantitative PSMA-PET parameters comprised reference lesion SUVmax (RL-SUVmax), SUVmean, total PSMA tumor volume (tPSMA-TV), tPSMA-TV above a fixed SUV threshold of 20 (tPSMA-TV20), the percentage of tPSMA-TV20 within tPSMA-TV (tPSMA-TV%), total lesion quotient (TLQ), TLQ20, and rTLQ%. The co-primary endpoints were EBP, defined as PSA progression according to the PCWG3 criteria within 4 months of the start of treatment, and PSA50 response, defined as a reduction in PSA of at least 50% compared with baseline. PSA-PFS (PCWG3-defined PSA progression or death from any cause) and OS were secondary endpoints. Results: 63 patients were retrospectively included (median follow-up, 20.9 months). In univariable analyses, higher baseline tPSMA-TV% was significantly associated with lower odds of EBP (OR per 10% increase, 0.71; 95% CI, 0.57-0.87; p = 0.001) and higher odds of PSA50 response (OR, 1.31; 95% CI, 1.07-1.61; p = 0.009). It was associated with longer PSA-PFS (HR, 0.75; 95% CI, 0.67-0.84; p < 0.001) and longer OS (HR, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.72-0.91; p < 0.001). Exploratory ROC analysis identified a tPSMA-TV% cut-off of 47.54% for EBP (AUC, 0.73 [95% CI, 0.57-0.86]; sensitivity, 0.61; specificity, 0.93), although this threshold requires external validation. In exploratory models including tPSMA-TV and SUVmean, tPSMA-TV% remained associated with PSA-PFS and OS but not with EBP or PSA50 response. Conclusions: Baseline tPSMA-TV% was associated with EBP, PSA50 response, PSA-PFS and OS in mCRPC patients undergoing [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA-RLT, and these associations remained after adjustment for baseline PSA and metastatic presentation. tPSMA-TV% is a candidate prognostic imaging biomarker that requires external validation.

title: Is the MRI Phenotype Associated with Survival in Patients with Different Breast Cancer Subtypes?
abstract: Background Breast cancer exhibits marked molecular and phenotypic heterogeneity, with important implications for prognosis and therapeutic response. Although magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is widely used for detection and staging, its potential role as a prognostic biomarker across molecular subtypes remains incompletely understood. This study aimed to evaluate the association between MRI-defined tumor imaging phenotypes and disease-free survival (DFS) among different breast cancer molecular subtypes. Methods This retrospective single-center study included 407 patients with invasive breast carcinoma of no special type who underwent pre-treatment breast MRI between October 2015 and May 2021. Tumors were classified into molecular subtypes and three MRI phenotypes based on lesion morphology and distribution. Associations between imaging phenotype, molecular subtype, and DFS were assessed using Kaplan-Meier analysis and Cox proportional hazards models. Results Type 3 was the most prevalent imaging phenotype overall (60%), followed by Type 2 (21.9%) and Type 1 (18.2%). Imaging phenotype distribution differed significantly among molecular subtypes. Over a median follow-up of 57 months, imaging phenotype was not associated with DFS in Luminal A, Luminal B, or HER2-overexpressed tumors. However, in the triple-negative/ER-low subgroup, imaging phenotype demonstrated an independent association with DFS. In multivariable analysis, patients with the Type 1 phenotype had an 8.16-fold higher risk of recurrence compared with those with the Type 2 phenotype (95% CI: 1.49-44.60; p = 0.015). Type 2 lesions showed the most favorable survival outcomes. Conclusions In this exploratory analysis, MRI phenotype was associated with disease-free survival in triple-negative and ER-low breast cancers. Circumscribed, unifocal tumors are associated with improved survival, whereas spiculated or multifocal patterns are associated with worse outcomes. However, given the small number of events in this subgroup, these exploratory findings need to be confirmed in larger studies before MRI morphology can be considered a prognostic imaging biomarker in aggressive breast cancer subtypes.

title: BCIW-Net: Boundary-Conditioned Adaptive CT Windowing for Hepatocellular Carcinoma Segmentation.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the most common primary liver malignancy, and accurate tumour segmentation in contrast-enhanced computed tomography is essential for treatment planning, assessment of ablation margins, and post-treatment evaluation. Existing deep learning methods typically use fixed-intensity CT preprocessing, overlooking the adaptive windowing employed by radiologists to enhance tumour visibility. To address this limitation, we propose BCIW-Net, a boundary-conditioned intensity-windowed network that integrates spatially adaptive and differentiable intensity windowing into the segmentation process as a clinically motivated inductive bias. Methods: The proposed framework first generates complementary soft-tissue and tumour-enhancing intensity representations using differentiable sigmoid-based transformations. A primary encoder-decoder module predicts tumour guidance, boundary probabilities, and pixel-wise error proxy maps, which collectively guide the dynamic estimation of spatially varying window centre and width parameters. The resulting adaptively windowed features are selectively blended with fixed-intensity representations through an error-gated mechanism before final refinement in a secondary encoder-decoder network. A multi-task objective jointly optimises tumour segmentation, boundary prediction, error-proxy estimation, and adaptive window regularisation in an end-to-end manner. Results: Experiments on the primary liver cancer (PLC)-CECT dataset demonstrate that BCIW-Net achieved a mean Dice similarity coefficient of 78.68% and an intersection over union (IoU) of 64.85% across five-fold patient-level cross-validation, outperforming the seven evaluated CNN-, Transformer-, and state-space baselines. Evaluation on LiTS2017 without dataset-specific fine-tuning yielded a tumour Dice score of 89.84%, providing preliminary evidence of cross-dataset generalisation. Conclusions: Qualitative feature visualisations show that adaptive windowing enhances tumour representation and boundary delineation, demonstrating the effectiveness and interpretability of BCIW-Net for HCC segmentation.

title: Advances in Interventional Oncology for Hepatocellular Carcinoma.
abstract: Locoregional therapies are used across the hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) treatment spectrum, including for curative treatment of small tumors, as bridging or downstaging therapy before liver transplant, for treatment of intermediate-stage disease, and as part of combination treatment with systemic therapy in selected patients. This narrative review summarizes recent developments in transarterial radioembolization (TARE), transarterial chemoembolization (TACE), and percutaneous ablation techniques and separates established clinical advances from early investigational work. The strongest evidence supports personalized TARE dosimetry and radiation segmentectomy, selective TACE with reassessment before repeat treatment, and image-guided thermal ablation with objective margin assessment. Phase 3 trials of TACE combined with antiangiogenic and immune checkpoint therapy demonstrated improved progression-free survival in selected patients with unresectable, nonmetastatic HCC, although the survival benefit of these combinations so far extends only to progression-free survival, and the best treatment sequence remains to be defined. Histotripsy, pulsed electric-field ablation, electrochemotherapy, cryoablation, high-intensity focused ultrasound, imageable or alternative radioembolic microspheres, new embolic agents, robotics, and artificial intelligence remain at different stages of clinical development. Most supporting data are derived from single-arm studies, retrospective cohort studies, trials in mixed liver-tumor populations, or studies in preclinical models. Treatment selection should account for tumor burden and location, liver function, portal hypertension, vascular invasion, transplant candidacy, available alternatives, local expertise, and patient preferences. Future studies should focus on durable local control, preservation of liver function, quality of life, transplant eligibility, overall survival, and cost.

title: Paired [ 18 F]FDOPA and [ 18 F]FDG PET Shows Complementary Prognostic Associations at Recurrence in IDH-Wildtype Glioblastoma.
abstract: Background/objectives Prognostic PET biomarkers in glioblastoma remain mostly as a single tracer and poorly characterized at recurrence. We investigated whether paired [ 18 F]FDOPA/[ 18 F]FDG PET captures complementary metabolic information associated with survival in IDH-wildtype glioblastoma. Methods Sixty-five consecutive patients underwent paired [ 18 F]FDOPA/[ 18 F]FDG PET/MR at baseline and/or recurrence. Survival was analyzed from baseline PET/MR (OS1, n = 36) and recurrence PET/MR (OS2, n = 55); longitudinal analyses used the paired subgroup ( n = 26). FDOPA and FDG tumor masks were independently segmented within a FLAIR-derived tumor box, and metrics were extracted from tracer-specific masks, their intersection, and their union. Metrics significant in Kaplan-Meier or univariable Cox analyses were tested in adjusted Cox models. Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction was used as a sensitivity analysis for the continuous Cox screening tests. Results In exploratory screening, prognostic associations were sparse at baseline and more prominent at recurrence. At OS2, three metrics remained independently associated with survival after adjustment: the FDOPA/FDG union-domain SUV mean union ratio (HR, 1.50; p = 0.0168), MTV inter (HR, 1.63; p = 0.0154), and MTV DOPA (HR, 1.58; p = 0.0191). The SUV mean union ratio and MTV DOPA showed limited correlation, suggesting complementary information. Their integration into IR-MTV DOPA , defined as FDOPA/FDG SUV mean union ratio × log(MTV DOPA ), showed higher apparent OS2 discrimination (HR, 1.73; log-rank p = 0.0001; C-index, 0.730; bootstrap .632-corrected C-index, 0.684; 12-month AUC, 0.863). Conclusions In this exploratory single-center cohort, paired [ 18 F]FDOPA/[ 18 F]FDG PET showed prognostic associations at recurrence. Inter-tracer intensity balance and metabolic tumor burden provided partially complementary survival information, and their exploratory integration showed higher apparent discrimination. External validation is required before clinical implementation.

title: Qualitative Dynamic Contrast-Enhanced MRI Time-Intensity Curve Analysis for Differentiating Non-Progressive Treatment-Related Changes from Tumor Progression After Stereotactic Radiotherapy for Brain Metastases.
abstract: Background : This exploratory study assessed whether qualitative dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI (DCE-MRI) time-intensity curves (TICs) differentiate non-progressive treatment-related changes (NPTRC) from tumor progression after stereotactic radiotherapy for brain metastases. Methods : Thirty-two patients with 51 treated lesions underwent DCE-MRI. Five neuroradiologists independently delineated a volume of interest and classified the resulting TIC as Type A-D. Longitudinal clinical and MRI follow-up provided the reference outcome, which was recorded before the TIC framework was finalized. An A/B versus C/D grouping was evaluated as a secondary exploratory analysis. Results : Thirty-five lesions were classified as NPTRC and 16 as tumor progression. All 17 Type A lesions were NPTRC, whereas all 13 Type C/D lesions showed progression. Type B was observed in 21 of 51 lesions (41.2%), including 18 NPTRC and 3 progressive lesions, representing a substantial indeterminate subgroup. The exploratory A/B versus C/D grouping yielded 81.3% sensitivity and 100% specificity. The ordinal TIC analysis yielded an AUC of 0.952. Interobserver agreement was high within the present reader group (Fleiss' κ = 0.889). Conclusions : Type A was associated with NPTRC, Types C/D were associated with progression, and Type B represented an indeterminate pattern. These descriptive findings require independent validation before clinical use.

title: Peritumoral Radiomic Deviation on DCE-MRI Exceeds the Bilateral Normal-Appearing Parenchymal Distance in Breast Cancer: A Within-Patient Multi-Metric Study.
abstract: Background The imaging-defined peritumoral region may contain quantitative imaging information beyond that captured by the tumor core, but its radiomic deviation from normal-appearing breast parenchyma remains insufficiently characterized. This retrospective single-center study investigated whether peritumoral-to-normal radiomic distances exceed the within-patient bilateral normal-appearing parenchymal reference distance. Fifty-six patients with histopathologically confirmed breast cancer and preoperative bilateral dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI were included. Methods Single-slice radiomic analysis was performed for four predefined regions: tumor core (T), peritumoral microenvironment (M), remote ipsilateral normal-appearing parenchyma (I), and contralateral normal-appearing parenchyma (C). After quality control, 101 radiomic features were standardized and analyzed using standardized Euclidean, Manhattan, cosine, and Ledoit-Wolf Mahalanobis distances. Peritumoral-to-ipsilateral (dMI) and peritumoral-to-contralateral (dMC) distances were compared with the within-patient bilateral normal-appearing parenchymal distance (dIC). Results Across all four metrics, both dMI and dMC exceeded dIC, and all eight primary paired Wilcoxon comparisons remained significant after Benjamini-Hochberg correction (q≤1.07×10-6), with matched-pairs rank-biserial correlations ranging from 0.749 to 0.989. The principal pattern was broadly preserved across alternative Mahalanobis covariance formulations, reduced-dimensional PCA analyses, particularly when three or four principal components were retained, exclusion of all 13 retained shape features, separate radiomic feature-family analyses, and replacement of selected non-normalized non-uniformity features with normalized counterparts. Conclusions These findings show that, in the present cohort, peritumoral-to-normal radiomic distances exceeded the within-patient bilateral normal-appearing parenchymal reference distance. Because the four analyzed regions differed in size, shape, and sampling geometry, the reported distances should be interpreted as region-level radiomic differences under the present ROI definitions rather than as geometry-independent tissue properties. Larger multi-institutional studies using full-volume three-dimensional radiomics and standardized imaging and preprocessing strategies are needed to assess reproducibility, clarify the biological correlates of this radiomic pattern, and evaluate its potential clinical relevance.

title: Prediction Models for Pathological Response to Neoadjuvant Chemoradiotherapy in Locally Advanced Rectal Cancer: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: Background : Accurate pretreatment prediction of pCR is critical for stratifying patients with LARC and selecting candidates for organ-preserving approaches. However, pCR is a postoperative pathological endpoint, whereas watch-and-wait strategies are based on cCR. Despite a rapidly expanding literature encompassing gene expression signatures, MRI radiomics, deep learning, and multi-modal fusion models, no prior systematic review has comprehensively evaluated predictive performance across all modalities using contemporary meta-analytic techniques for diagnostic test accuracy. Methods : Systematic review and random- effects meta-analysis of studies developing or validating predictive models for pCR in LARC treated with neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (nCRT) were conducted. Summary AUC was estimated using logit-transformed random-effects models. Heterogeneity was quantified by I 2 and τ 2 . Subgroup analyses were performed according to model modality and validation strategy. Publication bias was assessed with Egger's linear regression test. Sensitivity analyses were performed using leave-one-out cross-validation. Results : Forty-three studies with 67,302 patients were included. The pooled AUC across all models was 0.874 (95% CI: 0.855-0.892), with substantial heterogeneity (I 2 = 94.3%, τ 2 = 0.247). Deep learning models showed the highest pooled AUC (0.919, 95% CI: 0.877-0.948), with MRI radiomics (0.885, 95% CI: 0.852-0.911), multi-modal (0.875, 95% CI: 0.813-0.919), gene expression (0.855, 95% CI: 0.797-0.898), and clinical factors (0.820, 95% CI: 0.788-0.849) showing progressively lower pooled estimates. External validation cohorts had a lower pooled AUC (0.864) than internal validation (0.884). Significant publication bias was detected (Egger's test p < 0.001). Leave-one-out sensitivity analysis confirmed robustness of the overall estimate. Conclusions : Deep learning and MRI radiomics models demonstrate promising diagnostic accuracy for predicting pCR after nCRT in LARC. However, the predominance of retrospective, single-center designs with limited external validation represents a critical translational gap, and the lack of studies in the total neoadjuvant therapy era limits generalizability. Prospective, multicenter validation studies incorporating standardized endpoints and class imbalance-appropriate metrics are urgently needed.

title: Convolutional, State-Space and Transformer Liver-Tumor Segmentation Models Trained on Hepatocellular Carcinoma Fail on the Same External Cases: Lesion Size Outweighs Architecture in Cross-Dataset Generalization.
abstract: Background/objectives Architectural innovation is widely assumed to improve the cross-institutional generalization of tumor segmentation models, yet this is rarely tested. We compared three architectural families under an identical, leak-safe protocol in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) segmentation. Methods Convolutional (nnU-Net ResEnc-M), state-space (U-Mamba Bot) and transformer (SwinUNETR) models were trained on HCC-TACE-Seg ( n = 103) with identical patient-disjoint five-fold splits, then applied without adaptation to 3D-IRCADb ( n = 15) and LiTS ( n = 118). We assessed discrimination, case-level failure concordance, lesion-volume dependence, calibration and selective prediction. Results Internal performance differed (Dice 0.685, 0.662, 0.479; Friedman p = 0.022) but external performance was low and largely convergent: the convolutional and state-space models were formally equivalent on both external cohorts (pre-specified margin ±0.05 Dice), whereas the transformer was inferior on LiTS (0.222; p < 0.0001) and inconclusive on 3D-IRCADb. Case-level Dice was highly concordant across all pairings (Spearman ρ = 0.84-0.96; 0.67-0.81 on LiTS after adjustment for lesion volume), the same cases failing across architectures. Lesion volume predicted performance in all six architecture × cohort combinations; lesions < 5 mL failed completely in 61-76% of cases and formed 1.9% of the development cohort against 31.4% of LiTS. Neither liver-mask constraint nor ensembling recovered performance. Deferring the 30% least-confident LiTS cases raised Dice to 0.516 (0.450 when only empty predictions were removed). Conclusions Under a single-source, TACE-treated HCC training regime, cross-dataset failure of liver-tumor segmentation was governed primarily by lesion size rather than by architectural family; confidence-based selective prediction offers a deployable mitigation.

title: Active Surveillance in Low- and Intermediate-Risk Prostate Cancer: Comparative Oncologic Safety, Patient Selection, and Predictors of Treatment Conversion in the Era of Multiparametric MRI: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: Background/objectives Active surveillance (AS) is the preferred management strategy for localized low-risk prostate cancer. However, clinical debate persists regarding long-term oncologic safety beyond 10 years, the diagnostic reliability and false-negative risk of serial multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) for biopsy deferral, and the prognostic magnitude of adverse pathological patterns such as invasive cribriform morphology. This study aimed to provide a comprehensive meta-analytic synthesis of long-term oncologic survival, dynamic imaging performance, multivariable progression predictors, and longitudinal patient-reported functional outcomes. Methods Registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261479059) and conducted per PRISMA 2020 and GRADE guidelines, electronic searches were performed across PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus, and Cochrane CENTRAL through January 2026. Twenty-nine prospective cohorts, randomized trials, and diagnostic imaging studies comprising 46,318 patients were included. Time-to-event survival outcomes were synthesized using Generalized Linear Mixed Models (GLMMs) and random-effects inverse-variance models (REML). Diagnostic accuracy of serial mpMRI was modeled via bivariate random-effects meta-analysis (Reitsma approach). Multivariable-adjusted hazard ratios (aHRs) and longitudinal EPIC-26 domain scores were quantitatively pooled. Results Across 10 cohorts reporting long-term outcomes ( N = 24,987), pooled 10-year prostate cancer-specific survival (PCSS) was 98.9% (95% CI: 98.4-99.4%), demonstrating comparable oncologic efficacy to radical therapy. Pooled 10-year metastasis-free survival (MFS) was 96.2% (95% CI: 94.7-97.4%), and 10-year treatment-free survival (TFS) was 54.2% (95% CI: 48.1-60.3%; 95% prediction interval: 31.4-75.8%; I 2 = 88.1%). Serial mpMRI demonstrated a pooled sensitivity of 85.6% (95% CI: 74.2-92.6%) and a negative predictive value of 93.4% (95% CI: 89.1-96.3%) for PRECISE 1-3, supporting selective biopsy deferral while recognizing a 6.6% residual risk of missed occult high-grade disease. Invasive cribriform morphology in Grade Group 2 was the strongest independent multivariable predictor of progression (aHR: 12.67, 95% CI: 4.77-33.64; two studies, 1420 patients, 184 progression events). AS preserved baseline urinary continence (+3.0 points at 12 months) and sexual function (-2.0 points at 12 months) compared to profound declines observed after radical prostatectomy (-17.0 and -35.0 points, respectively). Conclusions Active surveillance provides comparable 10-year oncologic safety to immediate radical therapy while robustly preserving quality of life. Sequential mpMRI facilitates selective biopsy deferral, though invasive cribriform histology and visible target lesions indicate aggressive disease phenotypes that require proactive definitive intervention.

title: Automated RANO 2.0-Aligned Response Assessment for Glioblastoma Clinical Trials: External Evaluation Against Expert Annotations.
abstract: Background/objectives Reliable and reproducible imaging-response assessment is essential for endpoint evaluation in glioblastoma clinical trials. The Response Assessment in Neuro-Oncology (RANO) criteria provide a rule-based framework for standardisation, but their implementation can still yield variable outputs between readers and across timepoints and trial sites. This partly reflects differences in lesion definition, measurement geometry, longitudinal tracking, and new-lesion adjudication. We externally evaluated an automated pipeline for auditable, RANO 2.0-aligned imaging-only response assessment using pre-existing segmentation masks. Methods This retrospective feasibility and pilot evaluation used longitudinal glioblastoma magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) studies from the public single-centre LUMIERE dataset. Dataset-provided tumour segmentation masks were retained unchanged. An expert neuroradiologist visually reviewed the masks against the corresponding MRI images, and timepoints with segmentations clearly non-representative of tumour tissue were excluded. Deterministic rule-based processing performed lesion definition, admissibility-filtered measurement extraction, longitudinal tracking, new-lesion detection, and provisional response classification. Expert RANO imaging annotations and bidimensional measurements served as comparators rather than complete clinical RANO 2.0 adjudications. Analyses assessed agreement in the sum of products of diameters (SPD), longitudinal burden change, response classification, progression timing, new-lesion agreement, and failure modes, with patient-level clustered bootstrap resampling. Results Visual segmentation quality control excluded 57 timepoints across 42 patients, leaving 542 evaluable timepoints, including 506 matched to expert annotations. Across 84 expert-measured timepoints from 47 patients, the constrained maximum product of perpendicular diameters (Max-PPD-c) correlated with expert SPD (Pearson r = 0.753; Spearman ρ = 0.861), although the concordance correlation coefficient (CCC) was 0.680 and the median absolute percentage difference was 36.8%. Overall, 73.8% of measurements were within ±50% of expert SPD. Across 31 consecutive pairs from 17 patients, correlations for longitudinal percentage change were r = 0.715 and ρ = 0.874. Per-timepoint four-class response agreement was 48.1% (κ = 0.173), whereas final-timepoint binary progressive disease (PD) agreement was 76.0%. Among patients with PD by both methods, the pipeline assigned PD earlier more often than later, although the median timing difference was 0.0 weeks and the paired comparison was not statistically significant ( p = 0.068). New-lesion detection had a positive predictive value (PPV) of 22.3% and negative predictive value (NPV) of 89.0%. Conservative patient-level later-positivity estimates were 10.8% within 12 weeks and 27.0% within 24 weeks, without same-lesion verification. Conclusions This study supports the value of a deterministic pipeline for standardising imaging-derived response outputs in glioblastoma clinical trials. Future work will focus on prospective multi-institutional validation incorporating clinical variables, non-enhancing disease assessment, and adjudicated outcomes.

title: Optic Nerve Sheath Meningiomas: A Narrative Review of Clinical Features, Imaging Advances, and Current Management.
abstract: Optic nerve sheath meningioma (ONSM) is a rare orbital tumor that can pose a significant threat to visual function due to its close relationship with the optic nerve and surrounding vascular structures. Early and accurate diagnosis is essential to preserve vision and guide individualized management. The objective of this narrative review is to provide a comprehensive overview of the current evidence on the clinical presentation, diagnostic evaluation, imaging characteristics, and management of ONSM, with a particular focus on recent advances in imaging techniques and their implications for clinical decision-making. This review synthesizes current knowledge on clinical presentation, diagnostic workup, and evolving treatment strategies for ONSM, with particular emphasis on advanced imaging modalities. Magnetic resonance imaging remains the cornerstone of diagnosis, yet functional imaging, especially somatostatin receptor--based techniques such as 68GaDOTATATE PET/CT have shown potential as a useful adjunct in the diagnostic evaluation of ONSM, especially for assessing tumor characteristics, extent, and treatment planning in selected cases. We discuss the emerging role of DOTATATE imaging in differentiating ONSM from other optic nerve and orbital pathologies, as well as its potential application in monitoring therapeutic response. We also highlight contemporary management approaches, including fractionated radiotherapy and the selective role of surgical intervention, underscoring the importance of multidisciplinary decision-making in optimizing visual outcomes. Emerging molecular insights from meningioma research may inform future therapeutic strategies for ONSM; however, clinical evidence specific to ONSM remains limited.

title: Lymphatic Microvascular Density, Lymphatic Invasion and Endothelial Cell Proliferation as Prognostic Biomarkers in Cutaneous Melanoma: A Systematic Review and Evidence Map.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Cutaneous melanoma spreads preferentially through the lymphatic system, and sentinel lymph node status is among the strongest prognostic factors. Whether tumour angiogenesis and lymphangiogenesis add prognostic information beyond conventional histopathology has been examined in many immunohistochemical studies, with heterogeneous results. We conducted a systematic review, reported according to PRISMA 2020 and not registered, of blood microvascular density (MVD), lymphatic vessel density (LVD) in the intratumoral and peritumoral compartments, proliferating (Ki-67-positive) lymphatic vessels and lymphatic invasion (LI) as prognostic markers in primary cutaneous melanoma. Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE was searched to 10 September 2026, supplemented by a Web of Science export and by citation tracking of the reference meta-analysis by Pastushenko et al. (2014). Twenty-one cutaneous study units (25 reports) and four ocular studies providing indirect evidence were included, and risk of bias was rated with the QUIPS tool. Results: In the reference meta-analysis, peritumoral LVD and LI, but not MVD or intratumoral LVD, were associated with metastasis. The newer cohorts confirmed this pattern and provided adjusted effect sizes: peritumoral LVD predicted disease-free (HR 2.14) and melanoma-specific survival (HR of 2.74; 95% CI 1.31 to 5.73), immunohistochemically detected LI predicted sentinel node metastasis (33% vs. 11% positive nodes) and overall survival, and a Ki-67-positive lymphatic endothelium predicted melanoma-specific mortality (adjusted HR of 2.03; 95% CI 1.33 to 3.10) in 264 patients. Blood MVD and blood endothelial proliferation were not prognostic. Heterogeneity of markers, counting methods and effect measures precluded re-pooling. Conclusions: Peritumoral LVD, LI and proliferating lymphatics are promising adjunct biomarkers for selecting patients for sentinel node biopsy, adjuvant therapy and closer follow-up, pending standardised, digital-pathology-based quantification.

title: Clinical Utility of 18F-FDG PET/CT for Staging and Restaging of Pediatric Malignant Melanoma: A Single-Center Retrospective Study.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Malignant melanoma is a rare entity in the pediatric population, accounting for approximately 1-3% of all childhood malignancies. Despite its rarity, it is the most common skin cancer in children. Accurate staging and monitoring are essential for treatment planning and prognosis. This study aimed to evaluate the clinical value of 18F-FDG PET/CT in staging and restaging of pediatric malignant melanoma. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed pediatric patients aged 18 years or younger who underwent 18F-FDG PET/CT imaging between 2010 and 2025 with histopathologically confirmed malignant melanoma. Demographic data, primary lesion localization, PET/CT findings, pathology reports, and clinical outcomes were recorded. Lesions were categorized as positive and negative in the final analysis. Diagnostic performance parameters (with 95% confidence intervals (CIs)) were calculated using histopathological confirmation or clinical follow-up as the reference standard, and categorical associations were assessed using Fisher's exact test. Results: A total of 20 patients (12 females, 8 males; mean age: 11 years, range: 4-18) and 31 PET/CT examinations were included, with a mean follow-up duration of approximately 98 months. PET/CT was performed for initial staging in 17 examinations and for restaging in 14. On an examination-based analysis, PET/CT findings were negative in 22/31 (71.0%) and positive in 9/31 (29.0%) examinations. On a patient-based analysis, 12/20 (60%) patients had all examinations classified as true negative and remained disease-free throughout follow-up. 18F-FDG PET/CT demonstrated a sensitivity of 80.0% (95% CI: 49.0-94.3%), specificity of 95.2% (95% CI: 77.3-99.2%), positive predictive value of 88.9% (95% CI: 56.5-98.0%), negative predictive value of 90.9% (95% CI: 72.2-97.5%), and overall accuracy of 90.3% (95% CI: 75.1-96.7%) for the detection of clinically active disease. Agreement between PET/CT findings and clinical outcomes was substantial (Cohen's κ = 0.77). Among the nine PET-negative restaging examinations, one was subsequently confirmed as false-negative; the remaining eight showed no evidence of active disease during the available follow-up period. Conclusions: In this exploratory retrospective study, 18F-FDG PET/CT demonstrated promising diagnostic performance for staging and restaging of pediatric malignant melanoma, with high specificity and negative predictive value. These findings should be interpreted with caution given the small sample size and retrospective design but suggest a potentially meaningful role for 18F-FDG PET/CT in the multidisciplinary management of this rare pediatric malignancy.

title: Gut Failure During Pediatric Critical Illness: Toward a Phenotype-Driven Framework for Early Recognition, Prognostication, and Prevention.
abstract: Gastrointestinal dysfunction is common during critical illness, yet gut failure remains poorly defined, inconsistently diagnosed, and incompletely integrated into organ dysfunction frameworks. Current clinical approaches often recognize gut failure only after overt manifestations such as feeding intolerance, ileus, abdominal distension, gastrointestinal bleeding, or radiographic bowel injury have developed. However, these signs may represent late manifestations of distinct and potentially evolving pathophysiologic pathways. In this narrative review, we propose a phenotype-driven framework for gut failure during critical illness, with emphasis on pediatric critical care. We conceptualize gut failure as a dynamic syndrome comprising overlapping phenotypes: motility-dominant dysfunction, perfusion-ischemic injury, epithelial barrier failure, dysbiosis, absorptive-nutritional failure, treatment-modified dysfunction, and mixed evolving states. Linking these phenotypes to clinical presentation, prognosis, and management may improve early diagnosis and allow clinicians to anticipate progression before irreversible injury occurs. Pediatric patients represent a particularly vulnerable population because gut failure may affect not only short-term outcomes such as infection, mechanical ventilation, and mortality, but also nutrition delivery, growth, microbiome development, and recovery. A phenotype-based approach may shift gut failure from a late symptom-based diagnosis toward an earlier, mechanism-informed, and potentially preventable process.

title: MRI-Based Radiomics Model for Pretreatment Prediction of Pathological Lymph Node Metastasis in Neuroendocrine Carcinoma of the Cervix: Dual-Center Development and External Validation.
abstract: Objectives: To develop and externally validate MRI-based radiomics and clinicoradiomics models for predicting pathological lymph node metastasis (LNM) in neuroendocrine carcinoma of the cervix (NECC). Methods: This retrospective two-center study included 133 patients who underwent pretreatment pelvic MRI and pathological nodal assessment: 93 for development and 40 for external validation. Intratumoral and peritumoral features were extracted from T2-weighted, diffusion-weighted, and contrast-enhanced T1-weighted images. Stratified nested fivefold cross-validation evaluated the complete revised selection process. Locked models were assessed for discrimination, calibration, and exploratory net benefit, with conventional MRI nodal assessment as a comparator. Results: Pathological LNM was present in 54/133 patients (40.6%). The selected radiomics-only k-nearest neighbors (KNN) model had an external AUC of 0.783 (95% CI, 0.630 to 0.935), accuracy of 0.800, sensitivity of 0.813, and specificity of 0.792. The complete selection procedure yielded an out-of-fold AUC of 0.731. External AUCs were 0.727 for the clinical/MRI model and 0.767 for the clinicoradiomics model; neither fusion model differed significantly from the clinical/MRI comparator. Conventional MRI sensitivity was 0.563, with no significant paired difference from the selected model ( p = 0.125). External calibration was imperfect (Brier score, 0.186; slope, 0.672). Conclusions: MRI radiomics showed moderate external discrimination of pathological LNM in NECC. Adding clinical variables did not demonstrate further benefit. Multicenter validation, recalibration, and clinical-impact assessment are needed before clinical application.

title: CSFINet-Based Multimodal MRI Image Segmentation and Survival Prediction.
abstract: Background : Brain tumors are highly lethal malignant neoplasms, for which accurate tumor segmentation and survival-day prediction are critical to treatment planning and prognostic assessment. This study establishes an exploratory two-stage analytical framework spanning multimodal MRI tumor segmentation and survival-day prediction. Methods : The study is based on the BraTS 2020 multimodal MRI dataset, employing four imaging modalities-T1, T1ce, T2, and FLAIR-with patient age and extent-of-resection status as candidate clinical features. The 235 cases with survival labels were split at the patient level (188 training, 47 test; single 80:20 split). In the first stage, CSFINet is used for brain tumor segmentation; in the second stage, the resulting binary whole-tumor mask, age, and resection status serve as inputs for survival-day prediction. The survival models are trained on the ground-truth whole-tumor masks but evaluated on the masks predicted by CSFINet, and the survival training runs were not seeded. Four models-image-only, image with age, image with resection status, and image with both-are constructed for ablation experiments, and Gradient SHAP is introduced for interpretability analysis. Results : CSFINet achieves a Mean Dice, Mean Precision, and Mean Recall of 0.7849±0.1937, 0.8739±0.1978, and 0.7480±0.1936, compared with 0.5084, 0.8676, and 0.3822 for a U-Net baseline trained in this study under an identical configuration. The gains are in Dice and recall; the precision difference (+0.0063, 95% CI -0.0601 to 0.1086) is not distinguishable from zero. This comparison is internal to the present study; published BraTS 2020 results were obtained under different evaluation protocols and are not directly comparable. The model combining imaging features with age yields the lowest error, achieving a mean absolute error of 251.69 days (95% CI [186.56, 336.79])-lower than the 279.41 days obtained by the image-only model-whereas incorporating resection status does not lead to further improvement. Conclusions : CSFINet improves whole-tumor segmentation relative to this identically configured U-Net baseline-not relative to the published state of the art-and the inclusion of age was associated with a lower survival-day prediction error in this study. The survival findings are exploratory and cohort-specific: an MAE of 252 days is roughly 57% of the reported median survival of glioblastoma and is not clinically actionable, and the web interface is a research prototype. This study establishes an integrated analytical pipeline spanning tumor segmentation, survival-day prediction, and result visualization, serving as a preliminary reference for brain tumor image analysis and prognostic assessment. These are exploratory, single-cohort associations obtained from BraTS 2020; they do not establish a causal relationship between the clinical variables and survival, and they have not been externally validated.

title: Preoperative White Matter Disease Severity Predicts Intraoperative Cerebral Desaturation During Carotid Endarterectomy.
abstract: Objective : Carotid endarterectomy carries the risk of cerebral ischemia during carotid clamping. Traditional risk stratification relies on anatomic factors such as contralateral stenosis, yet these predictors demonstrate limited sensitivity for intraoperative hypoperfusion. White matter hyperintensities (WMH), quantified by the Fazekas scale, reflect chronic cerebral small vessel disease and impaired cerebrovascular reactivity. Whether baseline WMH burden predicts intraoperative cerebral oxygen desaturation during carotid clamping remains unknown. Methods : This prospective, single-center cohort study enrolled patients undergoing carotid endarterectomy with continuous bilateral near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) monitoring. The primary outcome was the maximum contralateral regional cerebral oxygen saturation (rSO 2 ) decrease within 2 min after carotid clamp placement compared with the pre-clamp baseline. The primary predictor was the contralateral hemisphere Fazekas score assessed on preoperative brain MRI. Multivariable linear regression adjusted for age, contralateral carotid stenosis, clamping time, and shunt use. Results : Of 173 patients screened, 58 with complete data were included in the final analysis. Th average age was 69. 2 ± 7 years, 37.9% were female, significant contralateral stenosis was present in four cases, and the average exclusion time was 30.1 ± 9.7 min. In multivariable regression, a higher contralateral Fazekas score was independently associated with greater contralateral rSO 2 desaturation during carotid clamping (unstandardized β = 0.008, standardized β = 0.287, p = 0.035). The association remained statistically significant after adjustment for all covariates. The overall model explained 8.8% of variance in contralateral desaturation (R 2 = 0.088). Conclusions : Contralateral white matter disease severity, quantified by Fazekas score, was independently associated with greater contralateral cerebral oxygen desaturation during carotid clamping. This finding supports the concept that baseline microvascular disease modifies acute ischemic tolerance independent of large-vessel anatomy. Preoperative Fazekas scoring may enhance risk stratification and inform individualized neuromonitoring strategies during carotid endarterectomy.

title: Skene's Gland Malignancy from Imaging Diagnosis to Management: A Narrative Review.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Skene's gland malignancies are extremely rare tumors of the female paraurethral region, known almost exclusively from case reports and small case series. Their diagnosis is often delayed because symptoms are nonspecific and may mimic benign periurethral disorders, urethral diverticula, primary urethral carcinoma or anterior vaginal wall tumors. This narrative review focuses on the role of imaging, particularly pelvic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), in the diagnosis, differential diagnosis, staging and treatment planning of Skene's gland malignancies, distinguishing evidence from confirmed Skene's gland cases from evidence extrapolated from female urethral carcinoma. Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus and Web of Science were searched on 27 September 2026 (publication years 2015-2026) and supplemented by reference-list screening; an explicit case definition was applied. Results: Of 191 records (93 after de-duplication), 17 reports of Skene's gland malignancy were included (15 case reports or series and 2 systematic reviews); fewer than thirty cases have been published overall. Patients were mostly postmenopausal (median age about 70 years, range 45-91), presenting with an asymptomatic periurethral nodule, hematuria or vaginal bleeding, or lower urinary tract symptoms; no uniform staging system has been applied. Most tumors were prostatic-type adenocarcinomas treated by local excision alone; radiotherapy, chemotherapy or androgen deprivation were used mainly for nodal, metastatic or recurrent disease. After examination, ultrasonography can detect and characterize a paraurethral mass, whereas MRI best defines tumor epicenter, urethral, periurethral and anterior vaginal wall involvement and regional spread, and should precede cystourethroscopy and biopsy; CT and PET/CT are complementary for systemic staging. No single immunohistochemical marker establishes Skene's gland origin. Conclusions: MRI is central to localizing and staging suspected Skene's gland malignancy and thus to guiding biopsy and the choice between local excision and radical surgery, but most imaging recommendations are extrapolated from female urethral carcinoma and require validation in pooled multicenter data.

title: Development and Patient-Level Internal Validation of an MRI-Based Radiomics Machine Learning Model for Preoperative Prediction of Cervical Lymph Node Metastasis in Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma: A Pilot Study.
abstract: Background / Objectives : Cervical lymph node metastasis (LNM) is the main prognostic factor in oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) and guides the extent of neck treatment. This retrospective pilot study aimed to develop MRI-based radiomics machine learning models for the preoperative prediction of LNM in OSCC and to validate them internally at the patient level. Methods : Preoperative MRI of 74 patients (32 LNM-positive, 42 LNM-negative on histopathology) was analysed. In each patient the largest morphologically suspicious cervical lymph node was segmented volumetrically on axial contrast-enhanced T1-weighted images, and 1409 IBSI-compliant radiomic features were extracted. Performance was estimated by 10 repeats of 5-fold nested cross-validation with the patient as the unit of partitioning; standardisation, correlation pruning, LASSO selection, hyperparameter tuning and threshold choice were confined to the training folds. Six classifiers were compared. Results : LASSO retained a median of nine features (range 6-13). SVM performed best, with an AUC of 0.781 (95% CI 0.667-0.884), a sensitivity of 0.72, a specificity of 0.76 and a balanced accuracy of 0.74; XGBoost (AUC 0.774) and logistic regression (AUC 0.769) performed comparably. A slice-level analysis of the same data, in which slices from the same patient could fall into both training and test sets, gave an apparent AUC of 0.878 but a specificity of only 0.33. Conclusions : MRI radiomic features of cervical lymph nodes carry moderate patient-level information on LNM in OSCC, and slice-level designs can substantially misrepresent performance. External validation in larger multicentre cohorts is required before clinical use.
