title: Understanding Venous Remodeling After Minimally Invasive and Noninvasive Treatments for Varicose Veins: A Mechanistic Narrative Review.
abstract: The absence of detectable flow on duplex ultrasound after venous ablation may correspond to different tissue states. This mechanistic narrative review examines histopathological and immunohistochemical responses after thermal, chemical, mechanochemical, adhesive, and focused ultrasound treatments. The PubMed search, conducted on 6 September 2026 for publications available through 31 August 2026, resulted in the inclusion of 45 tissue-based publications; six additional references provided clinical context. Study selection and data extraction were performed by a single author. Human and experimental data were organized by wall compartment, treatment modality, and time point. Depending on the technique, the initial signatures comprised thermal injury, endothelial detergent toxicity, mechanical abrasion, adhesive polymerization, or cavitation. Luminal organization, fibrosis, and recanalization followed heterogeneous trajectories. Cyanoacrylate was distinguished by a biomaterial response with variable persistence. Early occlusion does not demonstrate mature fibrous obliteration. The depth-continuity-topography framework is a working hypothesis without validated predictive value. Combining longitudinal duplex ultrasound follow-up with end-point histological analysis of the same segment, including morphometry, immunohistochemistry, and matrix assessment, could better relate tissue status to clinical outcome.

title: The Glial Coupling in the Developing Brain: Astrocytes, Oligodendrocytes and Myelin Formation.
abstract: Astrocytes and oligodendrocytes contribute to the metabolic, homeostatic and structural organization of the developing brain, yet their interactions evolve across development and remain incompletely characterized during the earliest stages of life. This narrative review examines astrocyte-oligodendrocyte coupling in relation to myelin development and addresses the question of which cellular and metabolic mechanisms support oligodendrocyte maturation and white-matter metabolism before mature astrocytic functions are fully established. Evidence from preterm and ill term neonates is considered together with experimental and adult or elderly studies used exclusively for secondary mechanistic comparison. Astrocytes and oligodendrocytes participate in interconnected metabolic, developmental and homeostatic processes, while perinatal white-matter injury may combine reactive astrogliosis, pre-oligodendrocyte injury and maturation arrest. Neuroimaging, including quantitative susceptibility mapping, synthetic MRI, cranial ultrasound and molecular or myelin-sensitive imaging, provides complementary but indirect information on the structural and maturational consequences of these processes, whereas omics approaches may characterize their molecular environment. Radiomics similarly provides indirect tissue-level biomarkers rather than cell-specific measures of glial biology. Dysglycaemia further illustrates the dependence of developing white matter on coordinated cellular energy handling and the potential relevance of immature astrocyte-oligodendrocyte interactions during metabolic instability. Evidence from very early development suggests that oligodendrocyte maturation occurs within a changing cellular environment in which astroglial maturation, neuronal and vascular processes, and immune and metabolic mechanisms coexist. The Crossword and Foil Effects are proposed as hypothesis-generating frameworks to organize these intersecting developmental, metabolic, cellular, imaging and molecular dimensions rather than as experimentally validated causal models. Overall, no single cellular substitute for mature astrocytic functions is identified; instead, oligodendrocyte maturation appears to emerge within a developmentally changing division of metabolic, homeostatic and signaling labour across astroglial, neuronal, vascular and immune compartments.

title: The Preterm Brain Is Also What It Eats: A Systematic Review of Nutrition and Neuroimaging Outcomes in Preterm Infants.
abstract: Background : Nutrition is one of the most modifiable determinants of brain development in preterm infants. Although increasing evidence supports associations between early nutritional exposures and neurodevelopment, studies remain heterogeneous regarding nutritional interventions, imaging biomarkers, and long-term outcomes. This systematic review aimed to summarize contemporary evidence on the relationship between nutrition and brain development in preterm infants using neuroimaging as the primary assessment tool while proposing an integrated translational framework to guide future research. Methods : Following a PECO framework, a systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and CINAHL: population, infants born before 37 completed weeks of gestation; exposure, any enteral or parenteral nutritional exposure, supplementation strategy, fortification approach, or individualized nutritional intervention; comparator, an alternative nutritional strategy, lower or absent exposure, standard care or, when relevant, a term-born reference group; outcomes, MRI- or CUS-based measures of brain growth, maturation, connectivity, or injury. Studies reporting volumetric, morphometric, diffusion, connectivity, spectroscopy, or quantitative ultrasound outcomes were eligible. The methodology was adapted from the PROSPERO-registered review by Ottolini et al. Original studies published between 2020 and 2026 (1 January 2020-4 September 2026) evaluating nutritional exposures or interventions in preterm infants with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and/or cranial ultrasound (CUS) outcomes were included. Risk of bias was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS), ROBINS-I and RoB 2 according to study design. Quantitative imaging studies were screened for eligibility for ATLAS assessment. Given the substantial heterogeneity in nutritional exposures, imaging protocols, timing of assessments, and neurodevelopmental outcomes, meta-analysis was not performed. Certainty of evidence was assessed at the level of each causal question and neuroimaging outcome domain using the GRADE framework. Randomized intervention evidence and observational exposure evidence were evaluated according to the design and target contrast contributing to each body of evidence. Judgments considered risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, publication bias, and, where applicable, factors that could increase certainty. Statistical significance was not used to determine certainty, and studies arising from shared or partially overlapping parent populations were not counted as independent replication. Results : We found 33 reports that met the inclusion criteria: 4 evaluated randomized treatment contrasts, 5 non-randomized intervention comparisons, and 24 observational nutritional exposure analyses. Greater exposure to human milk and selected strategies involving early protein and lipid provision, docosahexaenoic acid, omega-3 fatty acids, and individualized nutritional support were associated in several studies with favorable MRI measurements, including larger total or regional brain volumes, more advanced white-matter maturation, and differences in structural or functional connectivity. Some studies also reported associations with later neurodevelopment. However, findings were not uniform, and GRADE certainty across outcome-specific nutrition-neuroimaging questions ranged from very low to low, principally because of risk of bias, imprecision, heterogeneous exposure and imaging definitions, and limited independent replication. Although causal inference cannot be directly drawn, neuroimaging may provide quantitative measures of brain development that can be investigated alongside long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes. We propose the Roadmap for Imaging-Guided Enhancement of Neurodevelopment (RIGEL), an integrative research framework combining imaging, molecular biomarkers, standardized neurodevelopmental assessment, and epidemiological evidence across developmental stages. RIGEL should be regarded as a hypothesis-generating research framework that requires prospective validation before any clinical implementation.

title: Gut Microbiome in Sporadic Cerebral Small Vessel Disease: MRI-Defined Phenotypes, Mechanistic Evidence, and Nutritional Implications for Brain Aging.
abstract: Background/objectives Cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD) is a major vascular component of brain aging, yet potentially modifiable systemic contributors remain incompletely understood. Growing evidence links the gut microbiome to magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-defined CSVD, but interpretation is complicated by heterogeneity in microbiome profiling, clinical populations, analytical methods, and neuroimaging phenotypes. This review critically integrates the available human evidence with complementary multi-omics, ex vivo, and experimental findings. Methods PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched through 4 August 2026; 12 eligible reports representing eight cohort families were included and evaluated using a structured study-level methodological appraisal. Results Across the available literature, ecological and host-related biological processes show greater qualitative convergence than individual taxa, although this pattern has not been formally quantified across independent cohorts. Among reported alpha diversity measures, Chao/Chao1 showed the same numerical disease-versus-control direction across four cohort families, with statistical significance in two, suggesting a recurrent but still preliminary richness-related signal; Shannon and Simpson indices were less consistent. No single genus or species has been consistently replicated across the available, largely cross-sectional cohorts. Complementary studies implicate intestinal barrier, immune-metabolic, neurovascular, and perivascular clearance pathways but do not establish a unified causal pathway in human sporadic CSVD. Conclusions These observations support a hypothesis-generating ecosystem-level framework. Because diet is an important modifiable determinant of the gut microbial ecosystem, these findings may have relevance for nutrition-based strategies targeting vascular brain aging. However, no CSVD-specific dietary or microbiome-directed intervention has yet been shown to modify disease progression or related MRI outcomes.

title: Diagnostic Methods for Muscle Wasting in COPD: Strengths, Limitations and the Role of Nutritional Assessment.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Skeletal muscle wasting is a frequent and clinically consequential comorbidity in COPD, affecting 15-50% of patients and predicting reduced exercise tolerance, impaired quality of life, hospitalization, and mortality. However, no consensus exists on the optimal diagnostic approach, and the role of nutritional assessment remains underemphasized despite its contribution to muscle depletion. Methods: This narrative review synthesizes evidence from original research, systematic reviews, and consensus statements on diagnostic methods for evaluating muscle mass, strength, physical performance, and nutritional status in COPD. Results: Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging offer accurate assessment of muscle mass but are limited by cost and accessibility. Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry provides a low-radiation alternative but cannot assess muscle quality. Bioelectrical impedance analysis and ultrasound are portable and inexpensive, yet lack standardized COPD-specific cut-offs. Functional tests provide clinically meaningful performance data but do not directly measure muscle mass. In parallel, nutritional screening tools and dietary assessment can identify modifiable risk factors and are associated with sarcopenia prevalence and prognosis in COPD. The choice of diagnostic approach significantly influences prevalence estimates. Conclusions: Optimal assessment of muscle wasting in COPD requires a multimodal approach combining muscle mass quantification, strength measurement, physical performance evaluation, and nutritional assessment. Standardized COPD-specific diagnostic criteria are needed. A practical algorithm integrating simple screening tools with targeted confirmatory assessments, including nutritional evaluation, may help guide clinical practice.

title: Diagnosis of Extrapulmonary Tuberculosis at the Interface of Pathogen Detection and Host Response: Molecular, Microbiological, and Histopathological Advances.
abstract: Extrapulmonary tuberculosis (EPTB) accounts for approximately 16% of notified tuberculosis (TB) cases worldwide and disproportionately affects children and immunocompromised populations. Paucibacillary disease, anatomically diverse sites, and nonspecific presentations make EPTB one of the most persistent diagnostic challenges in TB control. This review integrates microbiological, molecular, sequencing-based, and histopathological approaches to EPTB diagnosis within the context of site-specific immunopathology, including granuloma biology and the microenvironment of caseous necrosis. Comparative evidence is synthesized across osteoarticular, lymph node, pleural, central nervous system, and disseminated EPTB, focusing on Xpert MTB/RIF and Ultra, targeted and metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS), and emerging host-response biomarkers and AI-assisted histopathology. Pragmatic, tiered diagnostic algorithms are proposed for resource-limited settings, where most EPTB occurs, and unresolved gaps in current international guidance are identified. Aligning diagnostic modality choice with anatomical site, specimen quality, pathological subtype, and laboratory capacity can shorten the time to EPTB diagnosis and inform host-directed diagnostic strategies.

title: From Fiber Architecture to Digital Twins: Characterization, Orientation Modeling, and Artificial Intelligence in Short Fiber-Reinforced Polymer Composites.
abstract: Short fiber-reinforced polymer composites (SFRPCs) are widely used in lightweight components because they combine low density, good mechanical performance, and high-volume processability. Their local properties, however, are governed by a fiber architecture-fiber length, orientation, dispersion, and defects-that is created during processing and varies within each molded part. This review examines how this architecture can be measured, predicted, and carried into digital representations of the manufacturing process. It covers the mechanisms that form the orientation state during injection molding; two- and three-dimensional characterization, with emphasis on X-ray micro-computed tomography; orientation models from the Jeffery and Folgar-Tucker equations to anisotropic rotary diffusion and slow-kinetics formulations; and multiscale homogenization. Applications of artificial intelligence are then assessed for image segmentation, orientation prediction, micromechanical surrogates, and physics-informed learning. Finally, published Digital Twin implementations for composite and polymer manufacturing are classified by their level of data integration, and a layered architecture for SFRPCs is proposed. Most existing systems are digital models or digital shadows rather than bidirectionally coupled twins. The main obstacles are the scarcity of paired process-microstructure-property datasets, the lack of uncertainty propagation across scales, and the limited transferability of data-driven models.

title: Intravenous Leiomyomatosis-A Single Centre Experience and Literature Review.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Intravenous leiomyomatosis (IVL) is a rare, histologically benign proliferation of uterine smooth-muscle cells that extend intravascularly. The clinical significance of IVL lies in the potential for mechanical obstruction of the major veins and heart, as well as possible thromboembolic complications. Methods: A retrospective case series included four patients with confirmed IVL, treated at the Clinic for Gynaecology and Obstetrics "Narodni front" between 1 January 2020 and 31 December 2025. The following were recorded: medical history, imaging diagnostics (ultrasound, MRI), operative findings, histopathology, and follow-up data. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee, and written informed consent for participation in the study was obtained from all the patients. Results: The series included four patients aged 40 to 73 with histologically confirmed IVL who were treated surgically. In one patient, an intraoperative complication occurred in the form of sigmoid colon lesion and consequential resection, requiring surgical reconstruction, while the remaining procedures were completed without major complications. Histopathological findings in all cases indicated benign smooth-muscle differentiation with the presence of intravascular nodules of smooth-muscle cells (IVL). Residual disease and recurrence were documented in one patient. Conclusions: Our cases reflect a diverse spectrum of clinical presentations of IVL indicating the heterogeneity of the disease and the importance of a multimodal, multidisciplinary approach to the optimal management of this rare entity. The absence of further disease progression in our patients following bilateral oophorectomy, i.e., iatrogenic menopause, suggests the possible hormonal dependence of IVL.

title: Preliminary Clinical Case Series for Evaluation of a Novel Bi-Dimensional Archwire During Miniscrew-Supported En-Masse Retraction of the Maxillary Anterior Teeth.
abstract: Background/objectives Efficient en-masse retraction of the maxillary anterior teeth requires adequate anchorage control while maintaining acceptable incisor torque. This prospective clinical case series aimed to provide an initial clinical evaluation of a novel laser-welded bi-dimensional archwire designed for miniscrew-supported en-masse retraction in adult patients with Class II Division 1 malocclusion. Methods Six patients requiring extraction of the maxillary first premolars were treated using a custom-made stainless-steel archwire consisting of a 0.019 × 0.025-inch anterior segment and 0.016 × 0.022-inch posterior segments. Retraction was performed using nickel-titanium closed-coil springs delivering approximately 250 g of force per side. The primary outcome was the monthly rate of maxillary anterior retraction measured on three-dimensional digital models. The secondary outcome was the change in maxillary incisor torque assessed on lateral cephalometric radiographs using the bracket-archwire angle. Results Repeated measurements showed no statistically significant systematic error, with method errors ranging from 0.14 to 0.31 mm for linear variables and from 0.72° to 1.08° for angular variables; intraclass correlation coefficients ranged from 0.91 to 0.97. The overall mean retraction rate was 0.97 ± 0.05 mm/month, and the mean retraction duration was 5.78 ± 0.79 months. The mean change in maxillary incisor torque was 7.08 ± 1.29°. Conclusions Within the limitations of this six-participant clinical case series, the novel bi-dimensional archwire was associated with a relatively stable observed rate of anterior retraction, although a measurable change in the bracket-archwire angular relationship remained. These descriptive findings should be regarded as preliminary and hypothesis-generating and require confirmation in adequately powered controlled studies. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT07664215; retrospectively registered on 24 June 2026.

title: Idiopathic Segmental Megacolon-Intestinal Neuronal Dysplasia Type B, Cajal Cells Abnormality, or Still "Idiopathic" Disease?-Case Report and Literature Review.
abstract: Background and Clinical Significance: Idiopathic megacolon (IM) in adults is a rare disease with an unknown aetiology. The condition remains poorly understood, with ongoing debate over the specificity of its histopathology. Case Presentation: Case 1: A 40-year-old man was admitted due to moderate lower abdominal pain and a distended, asymmetric abdomen. X-ray demonstrated the sigmoid colon with a diameter of 13 cm. Colonoscopy found a significantly enlarged and elongated sigmoid colon, which precluded the examination of the entire colon due to the insufficient length of the colonoscope. All blood assays were within the normal range. Intraoperatively, there was a significantly dilated sigmoid colon measuring 20 cm in width with a length of 60 cm. A sigmoid resection with mechanical T-T anastomosis between the descending colon and proximal rectum circular stapler was performed. The patient had an uneventful recovery. Seven years after the operation, he is symptom-free. The histopathological examination revealed a slight oedema of the lamina propria, submucosal fibrosis, hyperplastic submucosal ganglia and nerve fibres, hypertrophy of the muscle layers and hyperplastic myenteric nerve plexuses and ganglion cells. Case 2: A 28-year-old otherwise healthy man was admitted due to intermittent diffuse abdominal pain that manifested suddenly during a military mission. There was no remarkable medical history. The abdominal contrast CT revealed a segmental sigmoid megacolon with a diameter of 10 cm without any other noteworthy pathology. All organic causes for megacolon were excluded. No conservative treatment was applied. The intraoperative finding was a dilated sigmoid measuring 15 cm in diameter. A sigmoid resection was performed, followed by T-T anastomosis between the descending colon and proximal rectum. During the postoperative course, there was significant anastomotic bleeding, which was managed successfully by blood transfusion and haemostatic clips. The patient was discharged on the 8th postoperative day. Eighteen months after the operation, he is symptom-free. The histopathological examination was performed using Formalin-Fixed Paraffin-Embedded (FFPE) tissue, cut at 3 µm. Immunohistochemistry was performed on an autostainer Leica Bond with ready-to-use reagents-CD117 clone EP10 and S100 clone EP32. The dilated part revealed a fibrotic submucosa with hyperplastic vessels and nonspecific inflammatory changes, hypertrophy of the muscle layers, and hyperplastic submucosal and myenteric ganglia and plexuses, but did not fulfil the criteria for IND. The same picture was observed in both the distal narrowed part and the resection lines. There was no obvious abnormality of the Cajal cells in both parts of the specimen. Conclusions: We were unable to identify a specific cause of IM in the presented cases. The histopathological findings were not compatible with IND, Hirschsprung disease, or other neuromuscular pathology. The critical analysis of the literature does not support IND as a possible cause of IM. Due to the heterogeneity of colonic motility disorders and the lack of a consistent histological pattern in IM, we hypothesise that it has a multifactorial aetiology.

title: Double Iatrogenic Ethmoid-Orbito-Frontal Mucocele: The Role of Neuronavigation System in Revision of Endoscopic Sinus Surgery-A Case Report.
abstract: Background and Clinical Significance: Frontal sinus disease remains one of the most challenging conditions in rhinology due to its complex and variable anatomy and high tendency toward postoperative stenosis. Paranasal sinus mucoceles are uncommon, delayed complications following functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS), most often involving the frontal or anterior ethmoidal sinuses. They may arise from obstruction or scarring of natural drainage pathways, producing recurrent sinusitis or headache; Case Presentation: A 21-year-old male presented with persistent left-sided frontal headache and nasal obstruction after two previous FESS procedures. Radiologically, CT and MRI demonstrated chronic left-sided sinonasal inflammatory disease and two frontal-ethmoidal mucoceles. Revision endoscopic sinus surgery was performed with an image-guided (neuronavigation-assisted) technique, including Draf IIb frontal sinusotomy, mucocele marsupialization, and corrective septoplasty. The postoperative course was uneventful with rapid clinical improvement; Conclusions: Double postoperative mucoceles following ESS are rare. Neuronavigation-assisted revision surgery can be used for effective management in scarred, anatomically distorted sinus regions. However, this single case cannot establish superiority over conventional endoscopic guidance or demonstrate an effect on safety, efficacy, or recurrence.

title: An Artificial Intelligence Framework for Detection of Leukemia with Comparison Between Segmented and Non-Segmented Images.
abstract: Background Accurate classification of Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) subtypes from peripheral blood smear (PBS) images using deep learning may support automated image-based analysis of this blood malignancy. Methods We developed a custom lightweight Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to classify white blood cells into four subtypes: Benign, Early Pre-B ALL, Pre-B ALL, and Pro-B ALL. We assessed performance using accuracy, ROC curves, and explainability techniques, including upsampled feature map activations, occlusion sensitivity, and SHAP-style explanation overlays, comparing original (Non-segmented) and HSV-Segmented images. To mitigate patient-level data leakage without explicit patient identifiers, we further used unsupervised K-means clustering of HSV color histograms to group 3256 images into 89 "proxy-patient" clusters. Consequently, we implemented rigorous subject-level grouped 5-fold cross-validation and Hold-Out protocols alongside standard image-level evaluations. Results Under standard image-level evaluation, the model achieved 98.8% accuracy on non-segmented images and 91.3% on segmented images. Crucially, this performance advantage was maintained under strict subject-level cross-validation (97.9% vs. 89.7%), confirming the robustness of the findings against data leakage. Explainability visualizations demonstrated that HSV segmentation discarded vital contextual morphological cues, increasing confusion between closely related subtypes. Conclusions A lightweight CNN can accurately classify ALL subtypes directly from raw PBS images. The evaluated HSV segmentation degraded performance by removing contextual information. This study underscores the necessity of subject-level evaluation in medical imaging and indicates that mandatory preprocessing should be empirically justified rather than assumed beneficial.

title: A Dual-Modal Hybrid Marker for Automatic Registration and Coordinate Hand-Over in C-Arm CT-Guided Spinal Navigation.
abstract: An asymmetric hybrid registration frame (RF) integrates radiopaque and optical markers to automate computed tomography (CT) registration and coordinate hand-over to a dynamic reference frame (DRF). We compared automatic and manual fiducial selection using three fixed CT datasets of a rigid sawbone phantom. Ten operators performed five manual registrations per CT, alongside one automatic benchmark per CT. Both methods used the same five registration fiducials, rigid registration procedure, and three evaluation centers excluded from transform estimation. Target registration error (TRE) was the root mean square distance between transformed design centers and CT-detected centers, without probe contact. Across equally weighted CT datasets, mean TRE was 0.538 mm for automatic and 1.565 mm for manual registration. The manual-minus-automatic difference was 1.027 mm (95% operator-bootstrap confidence interval, 0.951-1.148 mm). Mean registration processing times were 2.817 and 22.589 s, respectively. Under these common evaluation conditions, automatic fiducial detection reduced on-frame center discrepancy and registration time. These findings support the integrated registration and handover workflow as a basis for further validation at independent anatomical targets.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Cardiac Ischemia Detection: A Review of Biosensor, Biomarker, and Imaging Applications.
abstract: Ischemic heart disease is the leading cause of global mortality, yet accurate and timely detection remains constrained by incomplete signal capture, noise, operator dependence, and imperfect reference standards. Artificial intelligence (AI) may enhance cardiovascular sensing by extracting latent diagnostic information from routinely acquired signals. This narrative review examines AI-enabled approaches to ischemia detection across three sensing modalities: the electrocardiogram as a bioelectric sensor, cardiac troponin as a biochemical marker, and cardiac imaging technologies (echocardiography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance, and nuclear imaging) as structural and functional sensors. For each modality, we evaluate the sensing pipeline, the reference standards, the endpoint actually measured (from acute coronary occlusion to functional ischemia), and reported performance metrics, separating diagnostic accuracy from effects on clinical workflow, patient outcomes, and cost. We also discuss emerging directions, including foundation models and multimodal fusion, together with translational challenges such as limited prospective validation, regulatory hurdles, and uncertain cost-effectiveness. Most evidence comes from retrospective, frequently single-center studies of diagnostic performance; few studies have measured effects on workflow, and fewer still on patient outcomes or cost. Routine clinical adoption will require prospective multicenter trials, standardized performance benchmarks, and evidence of clinical and economic benefit.

title: Representation Alignment with Hybrid Perturbation for Semi-Supervised Medical Image Segmentation.
abstract: Given the scarcity of labeled data and the high cost of annotation in medical imaging, semi-supervised learning (SSL) has become a promising approach for semantic segmentation tasks. In this paper, we propose RAHP, a representation stabilization framework for semi-supervised medical image segmentation, which addresses perturbation-induced representation inconsistency by integrating hybrid perturbation learning with explicit intermediate representation alignment. Our method adopts a cross-teaching architecture in which two sub-networks guide each other through pseudo-labeling to ensure stable training. To improve consistency across diverse perturbed views, we employ a hybrid perturbation strategy to generate complementary training views. Rather than relying only on prediction-level consistency between these perturbed views, we further introduce a Region-aware Patch Alignment Loss (RPAL) to explicitly align spatially corresponding decoder representations at the patch level. By combining prediction-level supervision with region-aware representation alignment, RAHP constrains not only the output predictions but also the intermediate semantic representations induced by heterogeneous perturbations. Experiments on three public datasets, including ACDC, Synapse, and MMWHS, show that RAHP achieves favorable mean performance compared with the evaluated semi-supervised methods under the reported limited-label settings.

title: CT-Referenced Diagnostic Performance and Complementary Error Patterns of Artificial Intelligence Versus a Single Emergency Physician in Chest Radiograph Interpretation: A Retrospective Paired Diagnostic Accuracy Study.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to support chest radiograph interpretation, but its clinical value depends not only on stand-alone accuracy but also on whether its errors differ from those of clinicians. We evaluated CT-referenced, target-specific diagnostic performance and complementary error patterns of a commercial chest radiograph AI system and a single emergency physician. Methods: In this retrospective, single-center, paired diagnostic accuracy study, 920 consecutive adults who underwent posteroanterior chest radiography and thoracic computed tomography (CT) within 4 h during the same emergency department encounter were included. A commercial AI system (hChestXR version 1) and a single blinded emergency physician independently assessed eight prespecified thoracic findings using CT as the reference standard. Paired differences were estimated with 10,000 patient-level bootstrap resamples and tested with exact McNemar tests with Holm adjustment. Exact-target complementarity and simulated same-target OR/AND rules were secondary exploratory analyses. Results: Across 7360 patient-target assessments, including 1232 CT-positive findings, AI had significantly greater Holm-adjusted sensitivity for pneumothorax (90.8% vs. 50.8%), nodule/mass (63.3% vs. 32.7%), and rib fracture (77.2% vs. 46.5%). AI-only detections were most frequent for pneumothorax (47.7%), nodule/mass (44.9%), and rib fracture (43.6%), whereas physician-only detections were most frequent for atelectasis (24.8%), pulmonary edema (21.0%), and lung opacity (19.7%). In exploratory pooled analyses, sensitivity was 73.0% for AI and 62.0% for the physician. Exploratory simulated same-target OR/AND analyses demonstrated a sensitivity-specificity trade-off across pooled patient-target assessments but did not represent observed AI-assisted clinical performance. Conclusions: The AI system and the single emergency-physician reader in the study showed target-dependent, partly non-overlapping error patterns in this CT-selected emergency cohort. The findings support prospective multireader evaluation of AI as a second-reader tool but do not establish benefit from real-time AI-assisted interpretation.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted ACR TI-RADS Assessment of Thyroid Nodules: Potential for Reducing Unnecessary Biopsies in a Prospective Single-Center Study.
abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI)-based ultrasound risk stratification has emerged as a promising tool for improving the evaluation of thyroid nodules. However, prospective evidence regarding its performance in routine clinical practice and its potential impact on biopsy recommendations remains limited. Methods In this prospective single-center observational study, 1009 thyroid nodules undergoing ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration between May 2025 and May 2026 were independently evaluated using ChatGPT Plus as an investigational AI-assisted decision-support tool. Representative ultrasound images, including dimensional and Doppler images, were submitted to the AI without disclosure of the radiologist-assigned TI-RADS category or subsequent cytological or histopathological findings. AI-assisted and radiologist-assigned TI-RADS classifications were compared with Bethesda cytology, while postoperative histopathology served as the reference standard in the surgically treated subgroup. Diagnostic performance and discordance in risk classification between AI and routine radiologist assessment were evaluated. Results The study included 1009 thyroid nodules from patients with a mean age of 51.5 ± 13.4 years, of whom 80.7% were female. Bethesda II was the most frequent cytological category (93.6%). AI classified 227 nodules (22.5%) as high risk (TR4-TR5), compared with 761 nodules (75.5%) by routine radiologist assessment ( p < 0.001). Among Bethesda II nodules, AI assigned 172 (18.2%) to TR4-TR5 compared with 701 (74.2%) by radiologists. When ACR TI-RADS category-specific size thresholds were applied, FNA would have been recommended for 469 nodules (46.5%) according to AI-assisted classification and 993 nodules (98.4%) according to radiologist-assigned classification ( p < 0.001), corresponding to 524 fewer modeled FNA recommendations with AI-assisted assessment. Histopathological evaluation was available for 73 surgically treated nodules, including 48 malignant and 25 benign lesions. Within this surgically verified subgroup, both AI-assisted and radiologist-assigned TI-RADS achieved a sensitivity of 100.0%, while specificity was 72.0% for AI-assisted assessment and 60.0% for radiologist assessment. Because histopathological verification was available only for surgically treated nodules, these diagnostic performance estimates apply specifically to the surgically verified subgroup and cannot exclude false-negative disease among nonoperated nodules. Conclusions AI-assisted ACR TI-RADS assessment produced substantially fewer high-risk assignments than routine radiologist assessment, with the greatest divergence observed among cytologically benign nodules. These findings suggest a potential role for AI as a second-reader decision-support tool for refining thyroid nodule risk stratification and biopsy selection. However, because all nodules had already undergone FNA and histopathological verification was limited to surgically treated cases, the present study cannot establish the safety of AI-guided biopsy de-escalation or exclude false-negative disease among nonoperated nodules. Prospective management studies with longitudinal outcome verification are required to determine whether AI-assisted assessment can safely reduce unnecessary FNA.

title: Cytologically Suggested Vulvar Involvement in a Dog with Multicentric Lymphoma After a Nodal Response to CHOP-Based Chemotherapy, with Discordant Clonality Results: A Case Report.
abstract: Involvement of the female reproductive tract is rare in canine lymphoma. A 9-year-old spayed female Maltese dog was presented with generalized lymphadenopathy. Cytology of a mandibular lymph node aspirate indicated large cell lymphoma, whereas PCR for antigen receptor rearrangement (PARR) of the same sample was polyclonal. Splenectomy confirmed splenic large cell lymphoma, classified as World Health Organization clinical stage IVa. After 12 cycles of a CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisolone)-based protocol, restaging computed tomography showed a marked reduction in all measurable lymph nodes, whereas gastric and subcutaneous nodules persisted. On Day 181 (168 days after the start of chemotherapy), vulvar swelling was noticed and progressed despite antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory treatment, together with inguinal lymphadenopathy. Disease progression was diagnosed by inguinal lymph node cytology, and rescue chemotherapy was started; however, the dog developed acute dyspnea and died two days later. Results reported after death showed a mixed monoclonal and polyclonal immunoglobulin heavy chain (IgH) pattern in the inguinal lymph node and a clonal IgH rearrangement in the vulvar aspirate, which was cytologically consistent with lymphoma. In dogs treated for lymphoma, vulvar swelling may reflect neoplastic infiltration, and PARR results may differ between samples obtained at different sites and time points.

title: Diagnostic accuracy of computed tomography in patients with non-specific symptoms of cancer referred directly from general practice: a retrospective follow-up study.
abstract: Background The urgent-referral Cancer Patient Pathway for Non-Specific Symptoms and Signs of Cancer (NSSC-CPP) was introduced in Denmark in 2012 to reduce delays in cancer diagnoses. In Region Zealand, it includes direct referral from GPs to contrast-enhanced computed tomography of thorax, abdomen, and pelvis (ceCT-TAP). In 2013, the NSSC-CPP cancer prevalence was 20%, but easy access to computed tomography (CT) may change referral patterns. Aim To examine cancer prevalence, diagnostic accuracy of ceCT-TAP, and changes in NSSC-CPP referral patterns. Design and setting Retrospective cohort study conducted in Region Zealand, Denmark. Method We included patients with non-specific symptoms or signs of cancer who were referred by GPs between 1 July and 31 December 2019. Primary endpoints were cancer prevalence and diagnostic accuracy of ceCT-TAP. Secondary endpoints were cancer types, referral trends between 2012 and 2019, and prevalence of GP-reported symptoms and clinical findings. Patients were followed up until cancer diagnosis or up to 12 months after ceCT-TAP, whichever came first. Results In total, 729 referrals were recorded, a five-fold increase compared with 140 referrals in the same period of 2013. Malignancy was diagnosed in 95 (13%) patients. Twelve patients had a false-negative ceCT-TAP result, yielding a negative likelihood ratio (LR) for malignancy of 0.15. Conclusion Despite a five-fold increase in GP referrals for ceCT-TAP since 2012, it remains an important diagnostic tool, identifying malignancy in one in seven patients. However, as the LR- was >0.10, a normal ceCT-TAP does not convincingly rule out cancer and should not stand alone as the only decision-support tool.

title: APOL1 Risk Genotypes and Sickle Cell Trait are Associated with Kidney Disease Progression in an Afro-Brazilian Population.
abstract: Background Apolipoprotein L1 (APOL1) risk alleles and sickle cell trait (HbAS) are established risk factors for CKD, but their distribution and clinical impact in admixed populations remain incompletely defined. We conducted a Brazilian population-based study integrating APOL1 genotypes, sickle cell trait, kidney histopathology, and longitudinal clinical outcomes. Methods We studied 889 newborns from a population-based survey and 424 patients with biopsy-proven kidney disease. APOL1 genotypes and hemoglobin variants were determined by PCR-based sequencing and high-performance liquid chromatography, and their associations with histopathologic chronicity markers and clinical outcomes were evaluated. Results The prevalence of the APOL1 high-risk genotype was higher among patients than among the general population (4.7% vs. 1.2%; P < 0.001), whereas HbAS frequency was similar in both groups (4.7%). Among patients, the APOL1 high-risk genotype was associated with greater histopathologic chronicity, including increased tubular atrophy and interstitial fibrosis. A progressive increase in the frequency of progression to ESKD was observed in accordance with the number of APOL1 risk alleles (10%, 14%, and 56% for individuals carrying 0, 1, and 2 risk alleles, respectively; p < 0.001). Progression to ESKD was more frequent among individuals with sickle cell trait than among those with HbAA (39% vs. 13%; p = 0.01). Under univariate analysis, carrying two APOL1 alleles (RR = 4.8; 95% CI: 2.8, 8.4; p < 0.001) or possessing the sickle cell trait (RR = 2.7; 95% CI: 1.4, 5.1; p = 0.03) were significantly associated with the composite outcome of ESKD or death. Conclusions In this Afro-Brazilian population, APOL1 high-risk genotypes were enriched among individuals with kidney disease, whereas sickle cell trait prevalence resembled that of the general population. Both APOL1 risk alleles and sickle cell trait were associated with adverse kidney outcomes, highlighting their clinical relevance in admixed populations.

The prevalence of the APOL1 high-risk genotype was higher among patients than among the general population (4.7% vs. 1.2%; P < 0.001), whereas HbAS frequency was similar in both groups (4.7%). Among patients, the APOL1 high-risk genotype was associated with greater histopathologic chronicity, including increased tubular atrophy and interstitial fibrosis. A progressive increase in the frequency of progression to ESKD was observed in accordance with the number of APOL1 risk alleles (10%, 14%, and 56% for individuals carrying 0, 1, and 2 risk alleles, respectively; p < 0.001). Progression to ESKD was more frequent among individuals with sickle cell trait than among those with HbAA (39% vs. 13%; p = 0.01). Under univariate analysis, carrying two APOL1 alleles (RR = 4.8; 95% CI: 2.8, 8.4; p < 0.001) or possessing the sickle cell trait (RR = 2.7; 95% CI: 1.4, 5.1; p = 0.03) were significantly associated with the composite outcome of ESKD or death.

Conclusions

In this Afro-Brazilian population, APOL1 high-risk genotypes were enriched among individuals with kidney disease, whereas sickle cell trait prevalence resembled that of the general population. Both APOL1 risk alleles and sickle cell trait were associated with adverse kidney outcomes, highlighting their clinical relevance in admixed populations.

title: The Current Status and Evaluation of Artificial Intelligence in Bladder Cancer: Clinical Applications and Research.
abstract: Bladder cancer ranks as the 10th most common malignancy worldwide. Advances in technology are continuously reshaping its diagnosis, treatment selection, and prognosis assessment. In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has demonstrated marked potential in transforming bladder cancer care. By integrating and analyzing multi-source data, AI enhances the precision and efficiency of disease management. This review comprehensively examines the current applications of AI across various domains, including radiographic imaging analysis, pathological diagnosis, cystoscopic image processing, molecular subtyping, drug development, organoid research, prognostic modeling, and medical device innovation. It highlights the advantages of AI over conventional methods, outlines model development strategies, and summarizes commonly employed algorithms. Furthermore, we discuss the key challenges in translating AI tools into real-world clinical practice. This narrative review aims to inform the future development of AI-driven digital health systems, ultimately contributing to the realization of precision medicine and personalized management for bladder cancer patients.

title: Intraoperative Trajectory Realignment Algorithm for Minimizing Screw Misplacement in Cervical Spinal Fusion.
abstract: Spinal fusion is a surgical procedure designed to stabilize the spine by connecting vertebrae with screws and rods, where placement accuracy is critical, as even small deviations can cause severe neurovascular complications. The accuracy of traditional preoperative image-based navigation is limited by intraoperative alignment shifts, particularly in the highly mobile cervical spine. This study presents an intraoperative trajectory realignment algorithm that reconciles preoperative computed tomography data with simulated and phantom-derived intraoperative 2-dimensional (2D) projections by integrating forward kinematics, digitally reconstructed radiographs, and optimization-based search strategies. The algorithm was evaluated through computational simulations and physical experiments using a modular 3D-printed cervical spine phantom, with accuracy evaluated through clinical grading and assessment metrics, including entry/end point displacement, angular deviation, and minimum inter-trajectory distance. Results demonstrated high accuracy, with all screws graded as perfectly placed and deviations consistently below clinically relevant thresholds. While these findings confirm the feasibility of this approach under controlled experimental conditions, future validation using cadaveric models and real intraoperative fluoroscopic imaging remains necessary prior to clinical integration.

title: QuRad: Radiomics Feature Extraction for QuPath.
abstract: Radiomic features provide a quantitative description of tissue organization in histopathology images. QuPath, a widely used open-source platform for whole-slide image analysis, offers morphology, intensity, and Haralick texture measurements but no standardized radiomic feature set such as that of PyRadiomics. Researchers must therefore export data to external Python pipelines, interrupting their QuPath workflow. QuRad extracts radiomic features from cell detections and annotation regions directly inside QuPath. The extension and equivalent Groovy script implement 119 features: 103 two-dimensional features enabled by default and 16 optional legacy shape descriptors. We compared QuRad 0.4 with PyRadiomics 3.0.1 on identical grayscale images and pixel masks. All 103 default features met a 10 -9 absolute-or-relative agreement tolerance on a breast-cancer benchmark tile (410 cells). On 20 melanoma tiles (8,644 nuclei), 97 of 103 features met this tolerance and 6 polygon-derived shape features differed from PyRadiomics' raster-derived mesh (minimum concordance correlation coefficient 0.942). The 22 synthetic regions accepted by PyRadiomics reproduced the expected intensity and texture values. A single-threaded server benchmark reached about 1,900 nuclei per second, and processing the 184,242 cells of a whole-slide image took 2.7 min on a laptop. A random forest distinguished tumor cells from lymphocytes in melanoma (pooled macro-F1 0.853) and classified 197 tissue regions of 6 breast-cancer slides into 3 compartments (0.696). QuRad exports the features with object coordinates and extraction settings for use in QuPath or downstream analyses.

title: Integrated CT Foundation Model and Radiomic Features Define Clinically and Biologically Distinct Colorectal Cancer Subtypes.
abstract: Colorectal cancer is clinically heterogeneous, and current risk stratification does not fully capture differences in recurrence, survival, or treatment response. Molecular subtyping has improved biological classification, but sequencing-based workflows are not always available before treatment or at the population scale. We developed a survival-informed computed tomography (CT) phenotyping framework that combines CT foundation-model representations with PyRadiomics descriptors of tumor shape, intensity, and texture. Across 4 nonoverlapping cohorts, including SYSU6H cohort 1 ( N = 902), SYSU6H cohort 2 ( N = 3,267), external Ningbo cohort 1 ( N = 509), and SYSU6HNAT neoadjuvant-treatment cohort ( N = 709), fused CT features were selected and integrated to derive survival-informed CT imaging phenotypes, followed by evaluation of survival, adjusted prognostic associations, molecular correlates, phenotype assignment, and treatment response. The fused representation identified 2 survival-informed imaging phenotypes with marked survival differences. Compared with CT-S1, CT-S2 was associated with worse disease-free survival and overall survival (disease-free survival hazard ratio = 11.16, 95% confidence interval 9.19 to 13.55; overall survival hazard ratio = 14.29, 95% confidence interval 10.83 to 18.85; both P < 0.0001) and remained associated with outcomes after adjustment for clinicopathologic variables and measured tumor size. CT-S2 was enriched for consensus molecular subtype 4-like composition and stromal/extracellular matrix programs, suggesting transcriptomic and microenvironment-associated correlates linked to the adverse imaging phenotype. A flexible phenotype-assignment model reproduced prognostic separation in internal and external cohorts, and assigned phenotypes were associated with survival and pathological response in SYSU6HNAT. These findings suggest that integrated CT phenotyping may provide a noninvasive approach for identifying survival-informed colorectal cancer imaging phenotypes with exploratory molecular correlates, supporting further independent validation.

title: First clinical implementation of histotripsy for liver tumors in Japan.
abstract: Histotripsy is a nonthermal therapy that mechanically disrupts and liquefies tumor tissue by generating focused microbubbles using extracorporeal ultrasound. Following U.S. Food and Drug Administration approval for the treatment of liver tumors in 2023, its clinical use has rapidly expanded. Here, we report the first clinical implementation of histotripsy in Japan, focusing on its safety and feasibility. The first treatment was performed for a 1.8-cm postoperative recurrent hepatocellular carcinoma in segment 8, followed by a second treatment for a 2.5- cm recurrent colorectal liver metastasis in segment 2 after multiple resections of intra- and extra-hepatic metastases. Histotripsy treatment times were 22 and 40 min, respectively. Target tumor coverage was confirmed by intraoperative ultrasonography, and reduced tumor enhancement was confirmed by contrast-enhanced computed tomography performed the day after treatment. The patients were discharged on postoperative days 1 and 2, respectively. No major complications occurred during follow-up to postoperative days 14 and 19, respectively, although both patients experienced mild treatment-related pain and one developed fever. These initial experiences suggest feasibility of implementing histotripsy for liver tumors in Japan.

title: Redefining axillary management by selecting patients for omission of sentinel lymph node surgery in early breast cancer.
abstract: Axillary staging has traditionally been performed routinely in early breast cancer to provide prognostic information and guide adjuvant therapy. In the era of targeted anti-tumor therapy and biology-driven treatment selection, however, the therapeutic relevance of nodal status has diminished in selected patients with clinically node-negative disease. Recent randomized trials, including Sentinel node vs. Observation after axillary UltraSouND (SOUND), INtergroup SEntinel MAmma trial (INSEMA), and Dutch Breast Cancer Research Group (BOrstkanker Onderzoek Groep; BOOG) 2013-08, have demonstrated that omission of sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) in carefully selected patients undergoing breast-conserving surgery with planned whole-breast radiotherapy (WBRT) does not compromise local or distant disease control and rarely alters adjuvant systemic or radiotherapy management. The most robust evidence applies to postmenopausal women aged ≥ 50 years with ductal tumors ≤ 2 cm, grade 1-2, hormone receptor (HR)-positive, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-negative and clinically node-negative disease. In this biologically favorable population, the therapeutic impact of nodal findings is limited as systemic therapy and radiotherapy decisions are predominantly driven by tumor subtype and genomic risk stratification rather than minimal nodal involvement. Based on evidence from recent randomized trials and current guidelines, this position paper proposes a practical four-step framework for decision-making regarding omission of SLNB. Redefining the axilla in this context represents a precision-oncology approach to surgical de-escalation, aligning local treatment intensity with biological risk while preserving oncologic safety.

title: [Clinical and genetic characteristics of 6 children with acrodysostosis].
abstract: Objective: To analyze the clinical, radiographic, and genetic characteristics of children with acrodysostosis (ACRDYS). Methods: This case series study enrolled 6 children with ACRDYS from Capital Center for Children's Hospital of Capital Institute of Pediatrics, Beijing Children's Hospital Affiliated of Capital Medical University, and the Second Affiliated Hospital of Guangxi Medical University. Diagnosis was confirmed by whole-exome sequencing between July 2023 and April 2026. Clinical data, laboratory findings, radiographic features, treatment details, and genetic test results were reviewed. Results: Among the 6 ACRDYS children, 5 had PRKAR1A gene variation (ACRDYS1) and 1 had PDE4D gene variation (ACRDYS2). There were 3 boys and 3 girls. The age at diagnosis was 6.3 (5.3,9.1) years. Four children presented with short stature and 2 with short hands and feet. One child was born preterm, 1 was small for gestational age, and 1 had a positive family history. All 6 children had brachydactyly and characteristic facial features, including depressed nasal bridge, upturned nasal tip, long philtrum, and micrognathia. Two children were obese. The 4 children with ACRDYS1 had parathyroid hormone resistance and 3 had thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) resistance (1 child was not tested for TSH). The child with ACRDYS2 had mild intellectual developmental delay and no hormone resistance. Hand radiographs showed shortened metacarpals and phalanges with cone-shaped epiphyses in all patients. Bone age was advanced in 3 children and delayed in 1. Genetic testing showed PRKAR1A variants in 5 children and a PDE4D variant in 1 child. The PRKAR1A nonsense variant p.Arg368* was the most common, detected in 3 of the 5 children. One PDE4D variant was previously unreported. Conclusions: Children with ACRDYS typically present with brachydactyly or brachytelephalangy, midfacial hypoplasia, and hand radiographic abnormalities. ACRDYS1 is often accompanied by mild hormone resistance, while ACRDYS2 features neurodevelopmental delay without obvious endocrine abnormalities.

title: [Clinical analysis of infectious endocarditis in children with concomitant septic pulmonary embolism].
abstract: Objective: To analyze the clinical characteristics, diagnosis, and treatment of infectious endocarditis (IE) with septic pulmonary embolism (SPE) in children. Methods: A case series study was conducted. Clinical data of 10 children with IE complicated by SPE admitted to the Department of Cardiovascular Medicine, Shanghai Children's Medical Center, Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine from January 2023 to September 2025 were analyzed. The detection rates of three pathogen detection methods, including blood culture, metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS), and vegetation culture, were compared. The clinical diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up outcomes were summarized. Results: Among the 10 children, there were 3 males and 7 females, with an age at presentation of 8.5 (6.6, 11.0) years. Congenital heart disease was present in 9 cases, and intracardiac implants were present in 4 cases. The main clinical manifestations included fever in 10 cases, cough in 4 cases, dyspnea in 4 cases, and chest pain in 3 cases. Six cases had dental caries. A total of 10 pathogens were detected in 9 children, including 2 fungi, 7 bacteria, and 1 Coxiella burnetii . Blood culture was positive in 7 cases, mNGS was positive in 8 cases, and vegetation culture was positive in 4 cases. Echocardiography revealed right-sided vegetations in all cases, and cardiac CT angiography showed multiple pulmonary lesions, including pulmonary artery filling defects, patchy opacities, and streaky shadows. Nine children underwent surgical treatment, and the duration of antimicrobial therapy was 3.0 (2.5, 8.0) months in 10 children. Under multidisciplinary management, 4 cases were cured, 5 cases improved, and 1 case was under control at discharge. After 6 months of follow-up, pulmonary lesions resolved in 9 cases, and valvular regurgitation improved in 8 cases. Conclusions: Embolization of right-sided IE vegetations is an important cause of SPE in children. Adjunctive mNGS testing, when required, contributes to a higher pathogen detection yield in patients with IE.For right-sided IE, early surgical intervention is often required in addition to antimicrobial therapy.

title: [Clinical and radiological analysis of 55 children of basal ganglia germ cell tumors presenting as predominant atrophy].
abstract: Objective: To analyze the clinical, laboratory, and radiological characteristics of intracranial germ cell tumors (iGCT) patients with the basal ganglia atrophy as the predominant imaging manifestation. Methods: In this case series study, clinical data of 55 children diagnosed with iGCT and predominant basal ganglia atrophy (without cystic change or mass effect) admitted to the Department of Pediatrics, Beijing Tiantan Hospital, Capital Medical University, from January 2018 to December 2025 were analyzed retrospectively. Descriptive analysis was conducted on demographic, clinical, radiological and laboratory data. Chi-square test was applied to compare β-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-HCG) positive rates in serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Results: All 55 children were male, including 50 (91%) germinomas and 5 (9%) non-germinomatous germ cell tumors (NGGCT). The age at diagnosis was 11 (8, 12) years, with a disease duration of 7 (3, 10) months. Forty-nine children (89%) presented with progressive limb weakness or motor deficit. The β-HCG from serum was increased in 27 children (49%), meanwhile β-HCG from CSF was elevated in 43 children (78%); β-HCG positive rate from CSF was higher than that of β-HCG from serum ( χ ²=10.06, P =0.002). Only 2 children were tested elevated AFP from serum. All 55 children were tested normal AFP from CSF. The markers of β-HCG and AFP from serum and CSF were both negative in 12 children (22%). Among them, 7 children were confirmed as germinoma by biopsy and 5 children were clinically diagnosed based on comprehensive evaluation. Among the 43 children (78%) with CSF β-HCG positive, 8 germinoma children were confirmed by stereotactic brain biopsy. Despite pathological confirmation of germinoma, 4 of the 8 children were found to meet the diagnostic standard of NGGCT, based on tumor marker levels. Those children were ultimately clinically diagnosed as NGGCT. Left-sided lesions were observed in 35 children (64%), right-sided in 15 children (27%), and bilateral in 5 children (9%). The whole 55 children manifested atrophy of the basal ganglia, T2-weighted and fluid attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensity, and ipsilateral cerebral peduncle atrophy, without definite mass or cystic components from MRI. title: [Clinical characteristics of intracranial suppurative infections caused by Streptococcus intermedius in 4 children].
abstract: Objective: To investigate the clinical features, therapeutic strategies, and outcomes of intracranial suppurative infections caused by Streptococcus intermedius ( S. intermedius ) in children. Methods: A case series study was conducted involving 4 children diagnosed with central nervous system (CNS) infections attributed to S. intermedius at the Capital Center for Children's Health, Capital Medical University from January 2020 to January 2026. Their demographics, clinical presentations, laboratory findings, neuroimaging features, microbiological results, treatment regimens, and prognoses were reviewed. Results: Among 4 children 3 were male and 1 was female, aged 10-15 years. All 4 children presented acutely with fever and headache as the initial symptoms; 3 children presented with vomiting, 2 children with drowsiness and seizures. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed elevated white blood cell counts in all 4 children, elevated protein levels in 3 children. Brain MRI revealed sinusitis in all 4 children, with predominant right-sided involvement. All intracranial suppurative lesions were adjacent to the right-sided sinus inflammatory foci, including multiple brain abscesses in 1 child, subdural empyema in 2 children, and concurrent brain abscess with subdural empyema in 1 child. S. intermedius was confirmed in all 4 children via various microbiological methods: metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) of subdural pus in 1 child, targeted NGS (tNGS) of CSF in 1 child, culture of deep sinus pus obtained intraoperatively in 1 child, and both culture and tNGS of brain abscess pus in the remaining child. All 4 children received comprehensive treatment, including targeted antimicrobial therapy, anticonvulsant therapy, intracranial pressure reduction management, and multidisciplinary surgical interventions including craniotomy with abscess excision, burr-hole drainage of subdural empyema, and endoscopic sinus surgery. One child developed secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis during the disease course. After a follow-up period of 1.5-5.5 years, all 4 children achieved clinical recovery, resumed normal academic and daily activities, and exhibited no significant neurological sequelae. Conclusions: Pediatric intracranial infections caused by Streptococcus intermedius primarily affecting older children and adolescents. These infections are highly associated with adjacent infectious foci, particularly sinusitis, and exhibiting a propensity for localized abscesses or empyema formation. Timely and targeted antibiotic therapy coupled with surgical intervention is associated with favorable prognosis in this population.

title: [Autoantibody positivity with bilateral pulmonary ground-glass opacities and consolidations].
abstract: A 52-year-old male patient presented with a 6-month history of cough and exertional dyspnea that had worsened over 2 days. Six months earlier, he had developed exertional dyspnea accompanied by a paroxysmal dry cough. At another hospital, anti-RNP/Sm and anti-Jo-1 antibodies were weakly positive, anti-Ku antibodies were positive, and the rheumatoid factor level was elevated. High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of the chest demonstrated pulmonary emphysema, honeycomb pattern in the lower lobes, scattered patchy ground-glass opacities and consolidations, as well as traction bronchiectasis. Bronchoalveolar lavage culture, tuberculosis-related investigations, and liquid-based cytology were all negative for pathogens and malignant cells. He was treated first with glucocorticoids and subsequently with glucocorticoids plus mycophenolate mofetil; however, follow-up chest CT revealed that the pulmonary lesions had increased in extent and density. Upon admission, physical examination revealed crackles bilaterally. Repeat autoantibody testing remained positive. Following multidisciplinary discussion, repeat bronchoscopy was performed, and a transbronchial lung biopsy established the diagnosis of pulmonary adenocarcinoma involving both lungs.

title: [Chinese expert consensus on the clinical application of lung biopsy in interstitial lung disease].
abstract: Interstitial lung disease (ILD) comprises a highly heterogeneous group of pulmonary disorders, whose diagnosis often requires the integration of clinical, radiologic, and pathologic evidence. Lung biopsy is a key method for obtaining a histopathologic diagnosis, but unified standards are lacking for determining indications, selecting biopsy techniques, managing patients perioperatively, and integrating pathologic and clinical information. To address these gaps, the Respiratory Physicians Branch of the Chinese Medical Doctor Association and the ILD Group of the Chinese Thoracic Society spearheaded this initiative, collaborating with national experts in respiratory medicine, radiology, pathology, thoracic surgery, and rheumatology to formulate this consensus. Developed in strict adherence to evidence-based medicine principles, this consensus is founded on systematic literature reviews and evidence grading, utilizing the Delphi method for anonymous voting. It culminates in 15 recommendations, each explicitly annotated with the level of evidence and strength of recommendation. This consensus systematically delineates the multidisciplinary discussion (MDD)-centered full-process management of lung biopsy. The main contents encompass: assessment of the necessity and feasibility of lung biopsy; indication stratification strategies based on HRCT patterns; applicability scenarios and selection pathways for the four major lung biopsy techniques; shared decision-making; perioperative comprehensive management; management strategies for acute exacerbation of ILD (AE-ILD); standardization of tissue processing and pathological reporting; the post-biopsy MDD process for integrated diagnosis; and biopsy decision-making in special clinical contexts, such as ILD complicated by lung cancer or connective tissue disease-associated ILD (CTD-ILD). This consensus aims to provide clinicians with clear, safe, and practical guidance on lung biopsy, promote standardized and precise decision-making, and improve patient outcomes. Summary of Recommendations Recommendation 1: For patients with suspected ILD, a comprehensive multidisciplinary discussion (MDD) is mandatory prior to lung biopsy. This evaluation should establish the diagnostic certainty of the preliminary clinical assessment, evaluate the clinical utility of the biopsy, and facilitate shared decision-making (SDM) that incorporates patient preferences (Level of evidence: 3, Recommendation: strong). Recommendation 2: For ILD patients in whom the diagnosis remains uncertain following a comprehensive non-invasive evaluation, or when precise histopathologic subtyping is required, a lung biopsy is recommended to establish a definitive diagnosis and guide the therapeutic management (Level of evidence: 4, Recommendation: strong). Recommendation 3: For patients with an interstitial pattern, a lung biopsy is strongly discouraged if HRCT demonstrates a definite UIP pattern and secondary etiologies have been excluded. A conditional recommendation for a lung biopsy applies to patients with a probable UIP patterns in whom NSIP or fibrotic HP cannot be ruled out. A lung biopsy is strongly recommended to achieve a definitive diagnosis in patients with an indeterminate or non-UIP patterns and insufficient clinical evidence (Level of evidence: 4, Recommendation: conditional). Recommendation 4: For patients with an alveolar filling pattern, a lung biopsy is recommended to clarify the etiology once infection, alveolar hemorrhage, and pulmonary edema have been systematically excluded, and there is either a lack of response to empirical therapy or a clinical necessity to differentiate the lesion from malignancy (Level of evidence: 2, Recommendation: strong). Recommendation 5: For suspected rare ILDs, including PAP, iEP, LAM, and LIP, non-invasive or minimally invasive diagnostic modalities should be prioritized; a lung biopsy is conditionally recommended if these approaches are non-diagnositic. Conversely, a lung biopsy is strongly recommended for patients with clinically suspected AFOP or PLCH (Level of evidence: 2, Recommendation: conditional). Recommendation 6: Lung biopsy is not recommended for patients with acute respiratory failure, severe pulmonary functional impairment, recent cardiovascular events, hemodynamic instability, significant pulmonary hypertension, severe coagulopathy, or end-stage systemic debilitation (Level of evidence: 1, Recommendation: strong). Recommendation 7: Site selection for lung biopsy should target active lesions identified on HRCT (e.g., ground-glass opacities or fine reticulation). Specimens must include the interface between diseased and normal parenchyma to facilitate pattern assessment. High-risk areas, such as major vessels and severe bullae, must be strictly avoided. Multi-lobar sampling from at least two sites of varying severity is recommended to adequately capture disease heterogeneity (Level of evidence: 4, Recommendation: strong). Recommendation 8: A TBLB is recommended as the first-line diagnostic approach for suspected granulomatous diseases (e.g., sarcoidosis) and specific alveolar filling patterns. If a TBLB is non-diagnostic, escalation to TBLC or SLB is advised. A TBLB is not recommended for the evaluation of predominantly fibrotic ILDs (e.g., UIP or NSIP) (Level of evidence: 4, Recommendation: strong). Recommendation 9: TBLC is recommended as the preferred modality in expert centers, particularly for patients who are poor candidates for or are averse to SLB. The procedure should be standardized under general anesthesia with prophylactic balloon placement for hemorrhage control and integrated with imaging or navigational guidance to optimize diagnostic yield while minimizing procedural complications (Level of evidence: 2, Recommendation: strong). Recommendation 10: SLB is recommended for patients in whom TBLC yields a non-diagnostic result, provided their cardiopulmonary physiological reserve permits surgical intervention. Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) is the preferred approach, requiring sampling from at least two distinct lobes. Biopsies should prioritize the dependent segments of the upper lobes or the superior segments of the lower lobes; sampling from the lingula or the right middle lobe should only be considered if these sites harbor the most representative lesions and no superior alternatives exist (Level of evidence: 2, Recommendation: strong). Recommendation 11: PTNB is recommended for the diagnosis and differential diagnosis in ILD patients presenting with solitary nodules, masses, or focal consolidations, particularly to rule out malignancy. However, it is not recommended for the histopathological evaluation of diffuse fibrosing ILDs (Level of evidence: 2, Recommendation: strong). Recommendation 12: A shared decision-making model is recommended throughout the biopsy selection process. Clinicians should thoroughly counsel patients regarding the benefits, risks, and alternatives of the procedure, ultimately formulating a clinical plan that aligns medical evidence with patient values (Level of evidence: 4, Recommendation: strong). Recommendation 13: Histological or imaging patterns of usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP), active disease phase, and reduced diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO) are the main risk factors for acute exacerbation of interstitial lung disease (AE-ILD). Routine prophylactic use of glucocorticoids or antifibrotic therapy is not recommended for all patients; instead, meticulous perioperative management is recommended to prevent acute exacerbations. Once AE occurs, the underlying cause should be promptly investigated, and high-dose glucocorticoids along with supportive therapy may be considered (Level of evidence: 2, Recommendation: strong). Recommendation 14: Histopathological reports must adhere to current international standardized nomenclature, prioritizing the description of the predominant histological patterns and their salient features, while specifically noting any findings indicative of a specific etiology. Diagnostic limitations secondary to suboptimal specimen quality must be explicitly stated. Pathologists are required to provide a systematic and standardized microscopic description of the tissue pathology, formulate a histopathological classification, and offer etiological insights whenever feasible (Level of evidence: 4, Recommendation: strong). Recommendation 15: Post-biopsy MDD is central to formulating an integrated diagnosis and should be conducted by the same cohort of clinicians, radiologists, and pathologists involved in the initial evaluation. A systematic correlation between the histopathology and the clinical andradiologic data is required; any discordances must be thoroughly analyzed to achieve a consensus integrated diagnosis and guide therapeutic planning. If an integrated diagnosis cannot be established, a subsequent MDD or referral to an expert center for a repeat biopsy is warranted (Level of evidence: 2, Recommendation: strong).

title: [ Mycobacterium persicum pulmonary disease misdiagnosed as tuberculosis: a case report].
abstract: Mycobacterium persicum ( M. persicum ) is a nontuberculous mycobacterium that predominantly affects the lungs, causing pulmonary lesions, and is readily misdiagnosed as tuberculosis. Here we report a 48-year-old man with AIDS and M. persicum pulmonary disease who was initially misdiagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis and received standard anti-TB therapy, yet showed no radiological or clinical improvement. Sputum specimens were subsequently subjected to targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS), which identified M . persicum and established the definitive diagnosis. After switching to an anti- M . persicum regimen, the pulmonary lesions gradually resolved, and the patient was cured. This case highlights that in immunocompromised individuals, M . persicum pulmonary disease closely mimics tuberculosis in both imaging and clinical presentation, and reliance solely on CT and sputum acid-fast staining readily leads to misdiagnosis. Molecular diagnostics are central to precise diagnosis and treatment, and this case offers a valuable clinical reference.

title: [Acute respiratory distress syndrome secondary to severe pneumonia: how to perform precise and individualized assessment].
abstract: Severe pneumonia is the most common cause of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), and precise and individualized assessment is a prerequisite for improving therapeutic outcomes. Of all bedside assessment tools, respiratory physiological indicators are the most readily available and widely adopted, covering key metrics including gas exchange, respiratory mechanics, respiratory drive, and inspiratory effort. Recent prospective cohort investigations have validated that physiological metrics, including driving pressure, mechanical power, respiratory drive, and inspiratory effort, correlate strongly with mortality among patients with ARDS. Furthermore, thoracic imaging technologies (such as chest CT, ultrasound, and electrical impedance tomography) can accurately evaluate morphological alterations in ARDS lung tissue and dynamically visualize regional lung ventilation function. These tools have demonstrated considerable clinical utility for facilitating precise diagnosis, tailoring individualized ventilation settings, and assessing weaning readiness. Additionally, evaluating inflammatory immune status and biological subphenotypes not only helps elucidate the core pathophysiological mechanisms underlying ARDS secondary to severe pneumonia, but also provides a rationale for precision therapies using medications such as glucocorticoids. Bedside assessment indicators are growing in variety and availability. Artificial intelligence can efficiently integrate and analyze these large-scale multimodal datasets to construct predictive models. These models can track disease progression trajectories, optimize ARDS management, and advance the translation of Clinical Decision Support Systems into clinical practice. This approach represents a vital direction for future research.
